<SYSTEM>This is the full developer documentation for Nearhost</SYSTEM>

# Introduction

> What Nearhost does, who it is for, and how to get a remote project open in your browser.

Nearhost opens your dev servers at trusted `https://name.test` addresses, whether they run on this machine or on another one you reach over SSH. For a remote server it uses the SSH access you already have and installs nothing there.

## Who it is for

You run dev servers on your laptop, or somewhere else: a desktop under the desk, a home server, a VPS. Over there the app listens on `localhost`, and your browser is over here.

Without Nearhost that means an `ssh -L` flag per port, a certificate warning, and hot reload that fails to connect. With it, each project has a name, a certificate your browser trusts, and forwards that reconnect on their own.

## What you get

* **One address per project.** `https://myapp.test` today, tomorrow and after a reboot.
* **Real HTTPS.** Secure cookies, OAuth callbacks and service workers behave as they do in production.
* **Hot reload and WebSockets.** They travel through the same SSH connection.
* **Nothing installed on the server.** No daemon, no open ports, and nothing written to your project unless you run `nearhost export`. Nearhost only keeps a socket in `~/.nearhost` there, so a coding agent on the server can reach it. If `ssh <host>` works without a prompt, Nearhost works.
* **Any stack.** Nearhost routes ports. It finds them in `.env`, and [presets](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/) teach it Compose files, Vite and Laravel Sail. You can set routes by hand for anything else.

## Quick start

Install the binary:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://nearhost.dev/install.sh | sh
```

Start it. The first time, it offers to trust its local certificate authority so your browser accepts its certificates:

```sh
nearhost
```

Then press `s` to add a server, `n` to add a project on it or on this machine, and `o` to open it. Nearhost starts each project as soon as it is added, and every enabled project each time it opens. `q` quits. If this window started Nearhost, it asks whether to stop it or leave it running in the background. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/#quitting).

The same steps from the command line, which offers to add `mini` when it is not a server yet:

```sh
nearhost add --server mini ~/code/myapp
nearhost up myapp
```

`nearhost doctor` checks your setup at any time.

## Where to go next

* [Install](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) covers the installers, Homebrew, npm, and Linux and Windows setup.
* [Add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) and [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-project/) walk through each screen.
* [Presets and registries](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/) explains how Nearhost learns a framework’s ports.
* [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/) explains how assets and live reload reach your browser.
* [SSO callback fails on a remote dev server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/sso-callback-on-a-remote-dev-server/) fixes sign-in that breaks on a remote dev server. [HTTPS on a local dev domain](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/https-on-a-local-dev-domain/) and [ngrok loads the page, but assets point at localhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/ngrok-assets-on-localhost/) cover the HTTPS name and the asset URLs.

## When to use something else

Nearhost serves your own browser on your own machine. To show a page to a client or a teammate, use a public tunnel service. To reach a database or another non-HTTP port, a plain `ssh -L` forward is still the right tool.

# Install

> Install the Nearhost binary on macOS, Linux or Windows, including the extra steps Linux and Windows need.

Nearhost is one static binary for macOS, Linux and Windows 11, built for amd64 and arm64. Pick whichever of these fits how you install tools.

## Shell installer

On macOS and Linux:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://nearhost.dev/install.sh | sh
```

The script detects your OS and CPU, downloads the matching release from GitHub, verifies its checksum and installs to `/usr/local/bin` when that is writable, otherwise to `~/.local/bin`. It tells you when that folder is not on your `PATH`.

Three environment variables change what it does:

| Variable               | Effect                                                   |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NEARHOST_VERSION`     | Install this release instead of the latest, as `v0.8.0`. |
| `NEARHOST_INSTALL_DIR` | Install into this folder.                                |
| `NEARHOST_SKIP_SETCAP` | Set to `1` to skip the Linux port step below.            |

Check the install with:

```sh
nearhost --version
```

`nearhost --version` needs Nearhost 0.8.0 or later. `nearhost version` prints the same, and works on releases before 0.8.0 too.

## PowerShell installer

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://nearhost.dev/install.ps1 | iex
```

The script detects your CPU, downloads the matching release from GitHub, verifies its checksum and installs `nearhost.exe` to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\nearhost`. It adds that folder to your user `PATH`, so open a new terminal before you run `nearhost`: a terminal that is already open keeps its old `PATH`. It runs in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7, and if anything fails it stops with the reason and leaves an existing install as it was.

These environment variables change what it does. Set them before the command; a variable stays set for the rest of that PowerShell window:

```powershell
$env:NEARHOST_VERSION='v<version>'; irm https://nearhost.dev/install.ps1 | iex
```

| Variable               | Effect                                                       |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `NEARHOST_VERSION`     | Install this release instead of the latest, as `v<version>`. |
| `NEARHOST_INSTALL_DIR` | Install into this folder.                                    |
| `NEARHOST_NO_PATH`     | Set to `1` to leave your `PATH` alone.                       |

## Windows zip

Each release on [GitHub](https://github.com/nearhost/nearhost/releases) has a zip for each Windows build, `nearhost_<version>_windows_amd64.zip` and `nearhost_<version>_windows_arm64.zip`. Each holds `nearhost.exe`, `LICENSE` and `README.md`. Extract `nearhost.exe` to a folder on your `PATH`, or add its folder to your `PATH` in Settings, then open a new terminal.

To check the zip against the release’s `checksums.txt`, print its SHA-256 hash and compare it with the zip’s line there. PowerShell prints it in capitals and the file in lower case, which is the same hash:

```powershell
Get-FileHash nearhost_<version>_windows_amd64.zip
```

## Homebrew

On macOS and Linux:

```sh
brew install nearhost/tap/nearhost
```

## From source

With Go:

```sh
go install github.com/nearhost/nearhost/cmd/nearhost@latest
```

Nearhost needs Go 1.27.4 or later, the version the release binaries are built with. Go 1.21 to 1.27.3 downloads it first, unless `GOTOOLCHAIN` forbids it (some distributions’ Go packages set it to `local`). Then install Go 1.27.4 or later yourself.

A copy built this way reports its release version, rather than `dev`, so `nearhost update` can tell whether it updated.

## npm

```sh
npx @nearhost/cli
```

or `npm install -g @nearhost/cli` to keep the `nearhost` command. This works the same in PowerShell on Windows. npm installs the binary for your machine as a platform package, such as `@nearhost/cli-linux-x64` or `@nearhost/cli-win32-x64`, with no install script, so pnpm, bun and `--ignore-scripts` work too.

To try the next release before it ships, install a beta with `npm install -g @nearhost/cli@next`, or run `nearhost update --next` on a copy installed with npm, pnpm, bun, `go install` or an installer. Homebrew has no betas. A new beta is published each time a change lands for the next release. Right after a release, `next` points at that release until the next beta. On a beta, `nearhost update` moves to newer betas and then to the release, and stays on releases from there.

## Verifying a download

The shell and PowerShell installers check the archive against the release’s `checksums.txt`. They do not check the attestation. Releases also carry build provenance attestations, and you can check any file you downloaded with the GitHub CLI:

```sh
gh attestation verify <file> --repo nearhost/nearhost
```

Each archive comes with a software bill of materials, `<archive>.sbom.json`, listing the modules it was built from. The attestation covers the archives, their SBOMs and `checksums.txt`. From Nearhost 0.8.0.

The macOS binaries are signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarised by Apple, so Gatekeeper runs them however you download them. A copy downloaded in a browser may need an internet connection the first time it runs, while macOS checks the notarisation with Apple. From Nearhost 0.9.0.

The Windows binaries are code signed, with ECS Software Consulting Ltd. as the publisher, so Smart App Control runs them. From Nearhost 0.16.0. See [Code signing](#code-signing) below.

## Updating

```sh
nearhost update
```

updates Nearhost the way you installed it, after asking. Afterwards it checks the version of the copy your next command runs. If that copy is unchanged, it fails with `Error: The update ran, but <path> is still <old>.` and exits 1. On Windows, for a copy from the PowerShell installer or a zip, `nearhost update` downloads the release’s zip itself, checks it against the release’s `checksums.txt` and only then replaces `nearhost.exe` where it is, so a failed or cancelled download leaves your copy as it was. See [`nearhost update`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

If Nearhost is running in the background, `nearhost update` restarts it on the new version, and asks first when that would close open passthroughs or forwards. See [Updating](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/#updating).

`nearhost update --check` only reports, for scripts: it exits 0 when Nearhost is up to date, 1 when a newer release is out, and 2 when it could not check.

## Linux setup

Linux needs three things that macOS handles with a single prompt. `nearhost doctor` checks all of them.

### Allow binding ports 80 and 443

Nearhost serves HTTPS on 443 and redirects 80. A normal user cannot bind those ports, so grant the binary that one capability:

```sh
sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep "$(command -v nearhost)"
```

Run it again after each upgrade, because replacing the binary clears the capability. After any update, `nearhost update` prints the command, naming the real binary file, even for Homebrew, npm, pnpm and bun installs. It prints nothing when the binary still has the capability, or when the system lets any user bind port 80. The shell installer prints it as it installs, also when `nearhost update` runs it. Run from a downloaded copy at a terminal, rather than through `curl | sh`, the installer asks whether to run it, and only uses `sudo` if you say yes.

`nearhost up` stops with the same command when it cannot bind port 80 or 443 for want of the capability, and says `Do not run nearhost with sudo.` So does `nearhost service install`, which refuses a copy without the capability. See [nearhost up](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-up). Running Nearhost with `sudo` leaves files owned by root in your config and data folders.

Installed from npm, `command -v nearhost` finds the Node launcher rather than the binary, so run the command `nearhost doctor` prints instead: it names the binary itself.

### Trust the certificate authority

```sh
nearhost trust
```

This adds the Nearhost Local CA to the system trust store and asks for your password through `sudo`, which must be in `/usr/bin`, `/bin`, `/usr/local/bin` or `/run/wrappers/bin` and owned by root, from Nearhost 0.8.0. It uses your distribution’s own tool:

| Distribution   | Command it runs           |
| -------------- | ------------------------- |
| Debian, Ubuntu | `update-ca-certificates`  |
| Fedora, RHEL   | `update-ca-trust extract` |
| openSUSE       | `update-ca-certificates`  |
| Arch           | `trust extract-compat`    |

### Trust it in your browser

Firefox and Chromium-based browsers on Linux keep their own certificate databases and ignore the system store. Nearhost fills them in when `certutil` is installed:

```sh
sudo apt install libnss3-tools   # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install nss-tools       # Fedora, RHEL
```

Then run `nearhost trust` again. It prints whether the browser stores were updated. Restart the browser afterwards.

The CA’s key is not in your config folder. See [The local CA](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/#the-local-ca) for where it is and how to look after it.

## macOS and Firefox

`nearhost trust` adds the CA to the System keychain, which Safari and Chrome use. Firefox keeps its own store. To cover it, install `certutil` and run trust again:

```sh
brew install nss
nearhost trust
```

## Windows setup

Nearhost needs Windows 11, and Windows Terminal is the terminal it supports. `nearhost doctor` checks the parts below that it can.

### Code signing

From Nearhost 0.16.0, `nearhost.exe` is code signed through Microsoft’s Artifact Signing, with ECS Software Consulting Ltd. as the publisher. That holds however you install it: the PowerShell installer, the zip or npm. Smart App Control runs it. If you downloaded the zip in a browser, SmartScreen may still ask you to confirm the first run while the certificate builds a reputation. It names the publisher when it does: choose More info, check the publisher, then Run anyway. The PowerShell installer and npm don’t trigger it.

To check a copy, run this in PowerShell, with the path to your `nearhost.exe`:

```powershell
Get-AuthenticodeSignature "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\nearhost\nearhost.exe"
```

`Status` should be `Valid`, and the signer certificate’s subject should name ECS Software Consulting Ltd. Installed from npm, the binary is in the `@nearhost/cli-win32-x64` or `@nearhost/cli-win32-arm64` package under your global `node_modules`.

Earlier releases are not signed. Where Smart App Control is on, Windows blocks them outright, with no Run anyway, so install 0.16.0 or later.

### OpenSSH

Nearhost uses the OpenSSH client that ships with Windows 11, `ssh.exe`, and your `~/.ssh/config`, as on macOS and Linux. If `ssh` is missing, add OpenSSH Client in Settings > System > Optional features. `nearhost doctor` reports the version, and warns about one older than the 9.5 that Windows 11 ships.

Nearhost runs the first `ssh` on your `PATH`. Git for Windows puts its own ssh there, which reads another config and agent, so forwards can fail in ways that are hard to follow. `nearhost doctor` warns, under `ssh vendor`, when the `ssh` it finds is not in `%SystemRoot%\System32\OpenSSH` or `%ProgramFiles%\OpenSSH`, and gives its path. Put `%SystemRoot%\System32\OpenSSH` first on your `PATH`.

Windows’ `ssh.exe` cannot share one connection, so Nearhost logs in once for the server, once for each forward and once for each file it reads over SFTP. A key that needs a touch or an approval at each login asks once for each forward, and again for each forward every time the server reconnects. See [SSH transport](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/ssh-transport/#on-windows).

A key with a passphrase needs the ssh-agent service, which Windows installs disabled. In PowerShell run as administrator, start it and have it start with Windows:

```powershell
Get-Service ssh-agent | Set-Service -StartupType Automatic; Start-Service ssh-agent
```

Then add your key, in an ordinary terminal:

```powershell
ssh-add
```

A key without a passphrase needs no agent. `nearhost doctor` shows whether the service is running.

The OpenSSH in Windows 11, version 9.5, does not resolve a `ProxyJump` host given as an alias from your `~/.ssh/config`. If a server is reached through a jump host, give `ProxyJump` the jump host’s address, or use a `ProxyCommand`. `nearhost doctor` says so when this is why a server fails.

### Trust and the hosts file

`nearhost trust` adds the CA to your user’s certificate store, and Windows asks you to confirm it in a dialog of its own. It needs no administrator rights. Edge and Chrome use that store, and so does Firefox 120 and later, so no browser needs anything more. If Firefox has been set not to read Windows’ trusted roots, `nearhost doctor` warns and says which setting to change.

Each change to the hosts file, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`, needs administrator rights, so Windows shows a User Account Control prompt for it. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/#on-windows).

### Ports 80 and 443

Windows lets Nearhost bind ports 80 and 443 with no extra step. The proxy listens on loopback addresses only, so Windows Firewall does not ask about it. If port 80 is held by HTTP.sys, often for IIS, `nearhost doctor` names it and says how to find and stop the service that holds it.

### Projects in WSL

Nearhost runs on Windows itself, not inside WSL. To serve a project inside a WSL2 distribution, run sshd in the distribution and [add it as a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/), as you would any machine you reach over SSH. Nearhost installed inside WSL is the Linux build, and the Linux setup above applies to it.

## Next

Run `nearhost`. The first time, it offers to trust the certificate authority for you. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/).

# First run

> What Nearhost shows the first time you start it, and when it asks for your password or, on Windows, your approval.

Start the interface with:

```sh
nearhost
```

It shows Nearhost, which serves your projects. With none running, it starts one in the background first, so the proxy and every enabled project run whether or not this window stays open. It creates the local certificate authority, “Nearhost Local CA”, if it does not exist yet. Its key is kept in Nearhost’s data folder, not in `~/.config`. See [The local CA](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/#the-local-ca).

## Nothing to serve yet

With no projects, the screen shows the Nearhost mark and “Nothing to serve yet.”, with the two ways in:

```text
n  add a project on this machine or a server
s  add a server you reach over SSH
```

From Nearhost 0.12.0, once you have added a server, a third line appears:

```text
c  connect a server, so its agents reach Nearhost
```

Press `c` to connect the server without adding a project first, so a coding agent working there can ask Nearhost to add one. With several servers, Nearhost asks which. See [Coding agents](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/).

Below them are the folder you started in, whether the certificate authority is trusted, the proxy’s ports, and, from Nearhost 0.8.0, a link to Nearhost’s page at `https://nearhost.localhost:6327`, or on the port `--web-port` gives, unless that port was taken or `--web-port 0` turned it off. See [TLS and the proxy](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/). Press `n` to serve a project from this machine, or from a server you have added. Press `s` first if the project is on a machine you reach over SSH. See [Add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) and [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-project/).

## Welcome to Nearhost

While your system does not trust the certificate authority, a box titled “Welcome to Nearhost” opens over the screen. It says what will ask for your password:

* now: trusting the local certificate authority, so browsers accept HTTPS from Nearhost’s web server
* later: adding names to `/etc/hosts`

On Windows it says both ask for your approval, and names the hosts file as `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`.

Press `enter` to trust it now, or `s` to skip. Skipping lasts until you next start Nearhost, and the box comes back while the authority is still untrusted. Once it is trusted you see “The local CA is now trusted.” and the box does not appear again.

Trusting installs the authority’s root certificate into your system trust store: the System keychain on macOS, your distribution’s certificate store on Linux, your user’s certificate store on Windows. It is what lets your browser open `https://<alias>` without a warning.

Firefox, and Chromium-based browsers on Linux, keep their own stores. Nearhost updates those too when `certutil` is installed. See [Install](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) for the one-line setup. On Windows, every browser uses the Windows store, Firefox from version 120, so there is usually nothing more to set up. Firefox can be set not to read it, and `nearhost doctor` warns when it is.

If you skip, the proxy still runs and Home shows `local CA ● not trusted. Run nearhost trust`. You can trust it from a terminal at any time, and `nearhost untrust` reverses it:

```sh
nearhost trust
```

## The password box

On macOS and Linux, two things need root: trusting the certificate authority, and adding your projects’ names to `/etc/hosts`. For both, Nearhost asks in a box titled “Password needed”, which says why:

```text
Nearhost needs your password to add myapp.test to /etc/hosts.
```

Type your password and press `enter`, or `esc` to cancel. The password goes straight to `sudo` and nowhere else: it is not shown, logged or saved.

* **A wrong password** shows “Sorry, try again.” After three, the step stops and nothing is changed.
* **Cancelling** leaves things as they were. The certificate authority stays untrusted, or the project stays stopped until you start it again.
* **sudo remembers it** for a few minutes, as it does in a terminal, so a second step soon after does not ask again.
* **If sudo asks every time**, because it is set up not to remember, Nearhost hands over to the terminal for the password, then comes back.

`/etc/hosts` is only changed when a project starts and its names are missing, so most starts ask for nothing. See [The hosts file](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/).

## On Windows

On Windows, Nearhost shows no password box. Windows asks in its own dialogs instead:

* **Trusting the certificate authority** opens a Windows security warning that asks whether to install the certificate. Choose Yes. It needs no administrator rights.
* **Each change to the hosts file** opens a User Account Control prompt, because the file needs administrator rights. Windows does not remember the approval, so each change asks again, including one a coding agent asks for. If you choose No, the hosts file stays as it was and the project stays stopped.

As on macOS and Linux, the hosts file is only changed when a project starts and its names are missing, so most starts ask for nothing.

## Touch ID on a Mac

macOS can let `sudo` take your fingerprint instead of your password, but it is off until you turn it on. Copy the template that macOS ships:

```sh
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/sudo_local.template /etc/pam.d/sudo_local
```

Then edit `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local` as root and remove the `#` from this line:

```text
auth       sufficient     pam_tid.so
```

Check it in an ordinary terminal. This should show the Touch ID dialog:

```sh
sudo -k; sudo -v
```

With it on, Nearhost may still ask for your password the first time, then use Touch ID when it next needs root. Typing the password always works. Touch ID only works at the Mac itself, not over SSH. Inside tmux or another terminal multiplexer it may also need [pam_reattach](https://github.com/fabianishere/pam_reattach).

## Home

Once a project exists, the screen has a sidebar on the left, with Home at the top and each server’s projects below, and the selected row’s details on the right. Home shows:

* `proxy`: whether it is serving, and on which ports
* `page`: a link to Nearhost’s page at `https://nearhost.localhost:6327`, or the port `--web-port` gives, once the proxy is serving. It is left out when that port was taken, or when `--web-port 0` turned the page off. Needs Nearhost 0.8.0 or later.
* `local CA`: whether it is trusted, and when it expires
* `hosts`: whether the hosts file has every project’s name
* `config`: the path of the config file
* `running`: how many projects are running, on how many servers

Two rows stay at the bottom of the sidebar, `passthroughs` and `documents`, which show what coding agents have opened, and `none` when nothing is. See [Browser previews](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/browser-previews/#see-what-is-open).

When something needs you, a problems section lists it, with why it happened and how to fix it. When something you do fails, such as a save or a start, an alert box opens over the screen with the same: `enter` or `esc` closes it, and `c` copies its command. Below that is the recent log. Press `l` for the full-screen log, `/` to filter the sidebar by name, and `h` to come back to Home. `?` lists every key. See [Keyboard shortcuts](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/keyboard-shortcuts/).

## Quitting

Press `q` to quit. What happens to the Nearhost behind the interface depends on who started it:

* **The interface started it,** because none was running, and no other interface follows it. Nearhost asks `Stop Nearhost, or leave it running in the background?` Choose `Stop` to stop it, as quitting always did, or `Leave running` to keep your projects served with no terminal open. Tick `Don't ask again` to save the choice as [`keep_running`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/) in the config.
* **Anything else started it:** `nearhost -d`, a service, or another interface that is still open. Quitting leaves it running, and prints `Nearhost is still running in the background. Stop it with nearhost stop.`

`ctrl+c` never asks: where `q` would ask, it stops Nearhost. To stop one that runs in the background, from any terminal, run `nearhost stop`. `nearhost status` shows what it serves. See [Run Nearhost in the background](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/).

Next: [Add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) or, for a project on this machine, [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-project/).

# Add a server

> Register a remote machine that Nearhost reaches through your existing SSH setup.

A server is a remote machine you can reach with OpenSSH. Nearhost runs your own `ssh`, so your `ssh_config` applies, including `Include`, `Match`, `ProxyJump` and `IdentityAgent`.

The `local` server is this machine. It always exists, needs no configuration, and cannot be removed or renamed.

## Before you start

`ssh <host>` must work without prompting for anything, and the server must allow SFTP, which most do. Nearhost reads project files over SFTP. Check the first part with:

```sh
ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 <host> true
```

If it exits 0, Nearhost can connect. If it asks about a host key or a passphrase, answer it in a normal `ssh <host>` session first.

## From the interface

Press `s`. A box titled “Add server” opens over the screen, in three steps.

1. **Host.** The hosts in `~/.ssh/config` that you have not added yet are listed under the field, and typing filters them. Choose one with `↑` and `↓`, or type a host such as `dev@build.lan`. Wildcard hosts are not listed, and neither are hosts in files that `~/.ssh/config` includes, so type those.
2. **Name.** The name shown in the sidebar. It starts as the host without the user, and you can change it. `local` is taken.
3. **Check.** Nearhost connects with your SSH setup and opens SFTP. When that works, the server is saved and selected.

`esc` goes back a step, and from the first step closes the box. Nothing is saved until the check passes.

Adding a project can add a server on the way: choose **New server…** on its first step.

## What Nearhost stores

Only the name and the host, in `~/.config/nearhost/config.yaml`, or `%APPDATA%\nearhost\config.yaml` on Windows. No keys, passwords or sockets are stored.

```yaml
servers:
  - name: mini
    ssh_host: mini
```

For a port other than 22, give the host an entry in `~/.ssh/config` with a `Port` line and use its alias.

## If the check fails

The box shows OpenSSH’s error, followed by what to do: run `ssh <host>` once in a terminal to fix access. That is where OpenSSH handles unknown host keys, `ssh-add` and similar. Fix it there, then press `r` to check again.

## Afterwards

Select the server in the sidebar to see its host, its projects and its log.

| Key | Action                                                           |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `r` | Reconnect.                                                       |
| `c` | Drop the connection, or connect it again.                        |
| `e` | Edit the host and name. A new name carries over to its projects. |
| `d` | Remove the server and its projects, after you confirm.           |
| `n` | Add a project on this server.                                    |

From the command line, `nearhost add --server <name>` run at a terminal offers to add a server it does not know yet.

Nothing is installed on the remote machine. Nearhost makes a private `~/.nearhost` folder there and keeps a socket in it, so a coding agent on the server can reach Nearhost. See [How agents reach Nearhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/). The only file it ever writes to a project is a `.nearhostrc`, and only when you run [`nearhost export`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-export).

# Add a project

> Register a directory on this machine or a server and serve it at an alias.

A project is a directory, on this machine or on a server, that runs an HTTP service. Nearhost reads the project’s files to work out its ports, then serves it at an alias, `<name>.test` unless you choose another. The service can be anything that listens on a port.

## From the interface

Press `n`. A box titled “Add project” opens over the screen. Its steps are counted at the top, and steps that have nothing to ask are skipped. `esc` goes back a step.

1. **Server.** Pick `local` for this machine, or a server you have added. The selected server, or the selected project’s, is chosen already. **New server…** adds one on the way. See [Add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/).
2. **Path.** The project’s directory. On `local` it starts as the folder you ran `nearhost` in, and on a server as `~/`. See [Typing a path](#typing-a-path).
3. **Presets.** Nearhost reads ports from `.env` by itself. While no preset registry is trusted, it asks once whether to trust the official presets, which add Compose files, Vite and Laravel Sail. Choose Yes, No, or Don’t ask again. With a registry trusted, it lists the presets that suit this project, ticked. `space` unticks one, and `enter` enables the rest. See [Presets and registries](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/).
4. **Routes.** The ports found, with a role, what each opens on this machine and a label. Ticked ports are served. The project’s web port opens `https://<alias>`, and any other `web` port opens the names it is given. A `loopback` port opens `localhost:<port>`, and an `ignore` port opens nothing. See [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/) for what each does. The line under the table says what the selected port’s role does. `space` ticks or unticks a port, and `←` or `→` changes its role. Changing one port’s role leaves the others as they are. At least one port must be `web`, and only one `web` port can go without names of its own; `enter` says so if two do. One port is the project’s web port. To serve another port as well, make it `web` and give it names of its own with `h`. If no ports were found, give the web port yourself. The opens column and the line under the table need Nearhost 0.8.0 or later.
5. **Name.** The project’s name and its alias. The name is what Nearhost calls the project: in the sidebar, the log and `nearhost up <name>`. The alias is the address your browser opens, shown after `https://`. It follows the name until you change it, unless it comes from the project’s `.nearhostrc`. `tab` moves between them. Names and aliases must be unique. The alias is the project’s [main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name) and can be any lowercase domain name, such as `local.myapp.com`, but not a wildcard, `localhost` or an IP address. A real domain asks for approval, which typing it here gives. One that comes from the project’s [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/) is asked about on the last step. The hints under the name and alias need Nearhost 0.8.0 or later.
6. **Confirm.** The server, path, address and routes, with any advice. It also lists anything that needs approval, such as a host or option from the project’s `.nearhostrc`, and `enter` approves it as it adds the project.

The project is selected and starts at once. If its alias is not in `/etc/hosts` yet, Nearhost asks for your password to add it. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/#the-password-box).

## Typing a path

Nearhost suggests directories as you type, on this machine and on servers alike. It reads each folder in the background, so typing never waits.

```text
path      ~/code/bl▏og/
          blog  blob
```

The rest of the suggested name appears faint after the cursor. When several directories match, they are listed under the field.

| Key        | Action                                                  |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tab`, `→` | Accept the suggestion.                                  |
| `↑`, `↓`   | Choose between the matches.                             |
| `enter`    | Use the path exactly as typed, without the suggestion.  |
| `ctrl+r`   | Reconnect to the server, if the connection has dropped. |

`tab` with nothing suggested lists the folder again, which picks up a directory made since. Hidden directories are suggested once you type the `.`.

## From the command line

`nearhost add` takes a path and discovers its routes the same way. Run without a terminal, as in a script, it prints:

```text
$ nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp' --web 8080
No preset registries are trusted. To use the official presets: nearhost preset registry add nearhost/presets


Routes found for myapp (mini:/home/dev/code/myapp):
  PORT  ROLE    LABEL
  3307  ignore  forward-db (FORWARD_DB_PORT)
  5174  ignore  vite (VITE_PORT)
  8080  web     app (APP_PORT)


Added myapp on mini at https://myapp.test
Start it with `nearhost up`.
```

With no registry trusted, only the `.env` port variables are found, and every port but the web one is `ignore`. Here the Vite port should reach the browser as `localhost:5174`, so change it to `loopback` afterwards: select the project, press `tab`, choose the route and press `space`. The [Vite and Sail presets](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/) do that for you.

If Nearhost is already running, the last line says so instead: `The running Nearhost picks it up in a moment.` Before that, `nearhost add` brings the hosts file up to date, as `nearhost hosts update` does, since the background Nearhost never asks for your password. If it cannot, it tells you to run `nearhost hosts update` in a terminal. A `nearhost up` started with project names does not reload: stop it and start it again.

At a terminal it asks what the interface asks: whether to trust the official presets, which suggested presets to enable, and which port is the web app when that is not clear. It also offers to add a server it does not know, and asks you to approve, one at a time, any real domain, wildcard, `localhost` or Docker access that the project’s `.nearhostrc` or presets ask for, and any loopback port its `.nearhostrc` adds. Without a terminal it takes the defaults, and stops if it cannot tell which port is web or if something needs approval. See [Approval](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#approval).

| Flag              | Effect                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--server <name>` | The server the path is on. The default is `local`.                                                                                                                           |
| `--name <name>`   | The project name. The default is the directory’s name.                                                                                                                       |
| `--alias <alias>` | The main name. The default is `<name>.test`. Any lowercase domain name works, but not a wildcard, `localhost`, `nearhost.localhost` or an IP address. Typing it approves it. |
| `--web <port>`    | The port to serve at the alias.                                                                                                                                              |
| `--host <host>`   | Add this host to the primary web route. Repeat for more. Typing it approves it.                                                                                              |
| `--preset <name>` | Enable this preset without asking. Repeat for more.                                                                                                                          |
| `--no-presets`    | Use no presets and suggest none.                                                                                                                                             |
| `--disabled`      | Add it disabled: `nearhost up` starts it only when named.                                                                                                                    |

A directory whose name has letters or digits outside ASCII, such as `café`, needs `--name` with only a-z, 0-9 and `-`, or `--alias`, or an `alias` in its `.nearhostrc`. From Nearhost 0.8.0, `nearhost add` stops and says so.

A `~` in the path means the server’s home directory, even when your shell has already turned it into this machine’s.

## Route roles

| Role       | What happens                                                                                             |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `web`      | Served through the proxy. The first is served at `https://<alias>`, and each later one at its own hosts. |
| `loopback` | Raw forward to the same port on your laptop’s `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`. Skipped for local projects.       |
| `ignore`   | Listed, not forwarded.                                                                                   |

Discovery proposes the roles, and you can change them at any time. See [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/).

A project can have several web routes, each served at hosts of its own. In the form, choose a web route on the routes step and press `h` to type its hosts. On the command line, `--host` adds a host to the primary web route. See [Multi-host projects](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/multi-host-projects/).

Advisories are shown, never applied. See [Advisories](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/advisories/). Nothing on the remote machine is edited.

## What gets written

Every project lives in `~/.config/nearhost/config.yaml`, or `%APPDATA%\nearhost\config.yaml` on Windows. You can edit it by hand too.

```yaml
projects:
  - name: myapp
    server: mini
    path: /home/dev/code/myapp
    alias: myapp.test
    enabled: true
    routes:
      - { port: 3307, role: ignore, label: 'forward-db (FORWARD_DB_PORT)' }
      - { port: 5174, role: loopback, label: 'vite (VITE_PORT)' }
      - { port: 8080, role: web, label: 'app (APP_PORT)' }
```

See [config.yaml](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/) for every key.

# Coding agents

> Let Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent add projects, open browser previews and show documents through Nearhost, on this machine or on a server, with your approval.

A coding agent can ask Nearhost to add the project it is working in, can read whether a project is served and where, and can find and fix what stops it being served. It works the same when the agent runs on your laptop or on a server Nearhost is connected to, for example in an SSH session. The agent proposes and you decide: every add opens the add form in Nearhost, filled in, for you to save or dismiss.

* [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/add-a-project/): the agent proposes the project, and Nearhost opens the add form, filled in, for you to save.
* [Fix a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/fix-a-project/): the agent runs Nearhost’s checks on the project and fixes what it can, with your agreement.
* [Browser previews from a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/browser-previews/): the agent asks to forward its dev server’s port, and the preview opens in your laptop’s browser.
* [Documents from coding agents](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/documents/): the agent asks to show a plan, spec or mockup it wrote, and Nearhost opens it in your browser.

An add waits for your yes in Nearhost. A browser preview or a document asks first too, unless you chose Always allow for it. You answer in the interface or, with none open, on Nearhost’s page. See [Prompts and Always allow](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/).

## Install the skill

The `nearhost` skill installs with the [skills](https://skills.sh) CLI, which puts it where your agents look for skills: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot and many more.

```sh
npx skills add nearhost/nearhost -g
```

`-g` installs it for your user rather than into the current project. Add `-a codex`, `-a cursor` and so on to choose the agents; without it, the CLI asks. Install it where the agent runs: on the laptop, on the server, or both.

In Claude Code you can install it as a plugin instead:

```text
/plugin install nearhost --marketplace nearhost/nearhost
```

The skill needs `sh` and `curl`, and nothing else. On a Windows laptop it uses PowerShell and the `curl.exe` that Windows ships instead. A server that reaches a Windows laptop needs curl 7.55 or later. See [Windows laptops](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/#windows-laptops). Nothing is installed with it. The plugin also brings a `SessionEnd` hook, which closes browser previews when the session ends.

# Add a project from an agent

> Ask a coding agent to add the project it is working in, then save or dismiss the add form Nearhost fills in.

With the [`nearhost` skill installed](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/#install-the-skill), ask your coding agent to serve the project it is working in, and Nearhost opens the add form for you to review.

In the project’s directory, run `/nearhost add` in Claude Code, or `$nearhost add` in Codex. Asking in your own words, such as “serve this with Nearhost”, works too.

1. The agent proposes the project’s directory to Nearhost, with the dev server’s port when the project’s files say it plainly.
2. With the interface open, it notifies the terminal it runs in: `Agent on mini wants to add /home/dev/code/myapp`. Most terminals show it only when Nearhost is not the window or tab in front. With no interface open, Nearhost writes the request and a link to it in its log, and the agent prints the same link.
3. The add form opens over the view with the server and path filled in, and the line `Proposed by an agent on mini`. Nearhost reads the project as it does for any add, and you choose the routes and the name as usual.
4. Save it, and the agent reports `https://myapp.test`. Press `esc` on the path, and the agent is told you declined.
5. The agent waits up to 30 seconds for the project to start, then runs the doctor on it and offers to work through any errors or warnings it finds. See [Fix a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/fix-a-project/).

If a form is already open, the proposal waits, and Home shows `1 request waiting · p to review`. It opens when the form closes, or when you press `p`. An agent waits 10 minutes for an answer.

`/nearhost status` reports the project holding the current directory: its address, every address it serves in `urls`, its state and any error. A project with several web routes or hosts has one URL for each, so you can see where each service lives. `/nearhost status --all` reports every project on the machine the agent runs on.

A proposal waits for you whenever Nearhost can ask: with the interface open, or with Nearhost’s page served, as it is for the background Nearhost and `nearhost up`. With no interface open, the agent prints a link to the request on the page, and the page lets you decline it. To accept it, run `nearhost`, where the add form opens filled in. See [Answer from the page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#answer-from-the-page).

# Browser previews from a server

> Let a coding agent on a server open its dev server's preview in your laptop's browser, after you allow it in Nearhost.

With the [`nearhost` skill installed](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/#install-the-skill), an agent on a server can start a dev server, but you cannot see it in your browser until its port is forwarded to your laptop. With a passthrough, the agent asks Nearhost to forward that one port for the rest of the session, and you approve it first. The preview then opens on your laptop. It works for any HTTP dev server, whatever it is built with, as long as the page loads everything from that one port. Needs Nearhost 0.10.0 or later; an older Nearhost answers without passthrough, and the agent tells you to update it.

1. The agent asks for a port, and Nearhost opens a prompt over the interface, or, with no interface open, waits for your answer on its page, at a link the agent prints: `Claude Code on mini wants to open port 5173 on this laptop (browser preview).` If that port is in use on the laptop, the prompt says so and that it will open on another port; the agent reports the laptop URL once it opens.
2. Answer the prompt. See [Prompts and Always allow](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#the-prompt) for the keys, and [Always allow](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#always-allow) to stop being asked. If you allow it and the port cannot be opened, the prompt shows why, and the agent is told it failed rather than that you refused, so it passes the reason on. If the port opens but Always allow cannot be saved, the passthrough stays open and the log says Always allow was not saved. If the request has ended by then, because it expired or the agent’s session ended, pressing `y` or `A` tells you so; `n` or `esc` closes the prompt.
3. Once you allow it, Nearhost forwards the port and the agent gives you the laptop URL. Asking again for a port that is already open, from the same agent session, returns the same passthrough without a second prompt. A port that a running project already forwards is answered at once, with no prompt.

A server can have at most 16 passthroughs open or opening at once, with or without Always allow. The next request is refused with `16 passthroughs are open for this server; close one first`, and the agent passes that on rather than asking again. A prompt you allow after the limit is reached ends with the same reason. Close a passthrough to make room.

## See what is open

The `passthroughs` row at the bottom of the sidebar shows `● 2` while two are open, and a dim `none` when none are. It stays in place while the list above it scrolls. Select it to list every open passthrough across all your servers:

```text
passthroughs                                       2 open


▌ http://localhost:7480   preflash demo
    from leto, port 7480 · Claude Code · 12m


  http://localhost:5174   storybook
    from apollo, port 6006 · Codex · 2h
```

Each row starts with the address to open on your laptop, then the agent’s label. The dim line under it says which server the passthrough came from, that server’s port, which agent asked and how long ago. Rows are in the order of your servers, `local` first, then by port. When there are more than fit, they scroll with the selection, and a `+N more` line says how many are hidden above or below.

Press `tab` to move into the rows, then:

| Key      | Action                                 |
| -------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `↑`, `↓` | Choose a passthrough. `k` and `j` too. |
| `o`      | Open its address in your browser.      |
| `y`      | Copy its address.                      |
| `x`      | Close it at once.                      |
| `esc`    | Go back to the sidebar.                |

With none open, the panel says `No ports are open for agents. When an agent asks to open one, Nearhost asks you first.` A server’s panel shows only a line such as `open 1 passthrough, 2 documents`, and Home has no line for them. While anything is open, Nearhost shows this layout instead of the first-run screen, so the row is there to find.

Nearhost lists the passthroughs it opened. A tunnel an agent or you made with `ssh -L` is invisible to it.

## When the app runs on another machine

Sometimes an agent works on one machine while the app runs on another it reaches over SSH. The skill then asks for the passthrough on the machine the app runs on, with `--on <host>`: `passthrough <port> --on <host>`, and the same option on `passthrough-wait` and `passthrough-close`. Nothing needs installing on that host. The passthrough comes from that server, and Nearhost lists it under that server’s name, so the panel shows where the app is. Always allow works there as it does for any server, and the token is kept on that host.

If no Nearhost reaches that machine, the skill falls back to forwarding the port itself with `ssh -L`, opens the passthrough from the machine it is on, and puts where the app runs in the label, for example `preflash on apollo`. The passthrough then lists the agent’s own machine as its server, and the label says where the app is. If SSH cannot reach the host at all, the agent tells you and stops, because forwarding the port itself would fail the same way.

A session can open passthroughs on several machines. When the session ends, Claude Code’s `SessionEnd` hook closes all of them, within about 2.5 seconds. One it cannot close in time, because that host is unreachable, stays open until Nearhost drops that server’s connection or you close it with `x` in the `passthroughs` panel. The same option works from `nearhost.ps1` on Windows; the host it runs on must be a Linux or macOS server.

## When a passthrough ends

A passthrough ends when any of these happens:

* the session ends, which Claude Code’s `SessionEnd` hook reports;
* you disconnect the server in Nearhost, remove it, or its connection fails (for example, authentication);
* the server has been away for 10 minutes in a row;
* the forwarded port stops answering for 5 minutes, checked every 30 seconds while the server is connected;
* you close it, or the background Nearhost stops (`nearhost stop`, or a restart by `nearhost update`). Quitting the interface alone leaves it open while the background Nearhost keeps running.

The `SessionEnd` hook ships with the Claude Code plugin, so it runs only for plugin installs. With the skill installed through the skills CLI, or in another agent, the other conditions apply. If the laptop port was taken by something else while the server was away, that passthrough closes when the server comes back. If closing a passthrough’s forward fails, Nearhost keeps its laptop port and tries again on each check until it closes.

## Without Nearhost connected

When Nearhost is not connected to the server, the agent cannot ask for a passthrough. It tells you to select the server in Nearhost and press `c`, then ask again, or to forward the port yourself from the laptop. Adding `-o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` to the command it gives makes `ssh` stop with an error when the laptop port is already taken, rather than stay connected without the forward:

```sh
ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -L <port>:localhost:<port> <server>
```

# Documents from coding agents

> Let a coding agent show a plan, spec or mockup it wrote in your laptop's browser, after you allow it in Nearhost.

With the [`nearhost` skill installed](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/#install-the-skill), when an agent writes a plan, spec, report or HTML mockup for you to read, it can ask Nearhost to show it. Nearhost serves the document at an address on your laptop and opens it in your browser. This works for an agent on the laptop and for one on a server Nearhost is connected to, so you no longer need a second terminal to read a path on a server. Markdown is shown as a page; HTML is served as written. Agents offer this only for documents they wrote for you, never for code or config files. You can also ask directly with `/nearhost open <path>` in Claude Code, or `$nearhost open <path>` in Codex. Needs Nearhost 0.11.0 or later; an older one answers without them, and the agent tells you to update it.

1. The agent asks, and Nearhost opens a prompt over the interface, or, with no interface open, waits for your answer on its page, at a link the agent prints: `Claude Code on mini wants to show plans/2026-10-28-x.md`, with a line saying which folder Nearhost will serve.
2. Answer the prompt. See [Prompts and Always allow](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#the-prompt) for the keys, and [Always allow](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#always-allow) to stop being asked. If you refuse, the agent does not offer that folder again in the session and only gives you the path.
3. Once you allow it, your browser opens the document and the agent gives you the address. It looks like `https://nearhost.localhost:<web port>/d/<random>/plans/2026-10-28-x.md`, where `<web port>` is Nearhost’s web port, and `<random>` is a long random string that other pages cannot guess.

If the background Nearhost cannot open a browser, as when it runs outside your desktop session, the agent still gives you the address; open it yourself. `nearhost doctor` shows `core: browser` when the core cannot open links.

With Always allow, the document opens in your browser at once, and Nearhost shows `Claude Code on mini opened plans/2026-10-28-x.md` in the status line. That holds for folders you have approved; a document in another folder prompts first. A server may open 5 documents a minute without a prompt, and past that you are asked. The same document opened again by the same agent within 5 seconds opens no second tab.

## What is served

Nearhost serves the document’s git repository, so its images, stylesheets and linked documents work. A document that is not in a repository serves its own folder. A repository at your home folder, or above it, is never served whole: Nearhost serves the document’s own folder instead. A document directly in your home folder, or in `/`, is refused with `save the document in a project or a folder of its own`. Nearhost never serves dotfiles or the contents of dot folders inside that folder, and never follows a link out of it.

A folder inside a hidden folder, one whose path has a part starting with `.`, such as `~/.claude`, serves only Markdown, HTML and web assets such as scripts, stylesheets and images. Any other file there, such as a key or a credentials file, shows as missing, judged by the name of the file a link leads to. The prompt says when the folder is in a hidden folder. A served folder also stays tied to where it was when you approved it: if its path later leads somewhere else, such as a folder swapped for a link, it serves nothing.

A second document in the same folder reuses the address without a prompt for the agent you approved, and prompts any other.

Nearhost keeps no copies. Each time the page loads, it reads the file again, from the laptop or over the server’s SSH connection, so reloading shows the current file. A file that has moved or gone shows as missing, never as an old version. A server that is not connected shows a page saying so; select it in Nearhost and press `c`.

## Documents cannot reach your other pages

Every file Nearhost serves from a document’s folder is sandboxed by the browser. Its scripts run, but they cannot read Nearhost’s page, your projects’ cookies or storage, or other documents. Rendered markdown runs no scripts at all. Pages also send no referrer, so the address does not leak to sites a document links to.

A page’s script can load the folder’s scripts, stylesheets, fonts, images, audio, video and WebAssembly, but cannot read its other files, such as `config/secrets.json`. It can still read the files it may load, such as the folder’s scripts, stylesheets, fonts and images, since modules and styles need that to load. So an HTML report that fetches its own JSON data does not work; put the data in the page or in a script.

## When a served folder goes away

The `documents` row at the bottom of the sidebar shows `● 2` while two folders are served, and a dim `none` otherwise. Select it to list every served folder across all your servers. Each row names the folder, then, on a dim line, the server it came from, which agent asked and how long ago. Press `tab` to move into the rows: `↑` and `↓` choose, `enter` or `o` opens the document in your browser, `x` stops serving it after you confirm, and `esc` goes back. There is no key to copy the address, because a plain address may not open in a browser that lacks Nearhost’s page key. A server’s panel shows a line such as `open 1 passthrough, 2 documents` instead of a list. A folder stays served until:

* the background Nearhost stops or restarts, as nothing is saved across restarts (`nearhost update` restarts it). Quitting the interface alone does not clear them;
* you press `x` on it in the `documents` panel and confirm;
* you remove the server from Nearhost, or rename it.

Disconnecting a server does not remove its folders. Their pages say the server is not connected until it reconnects. The agent’s session ending does not remove them either, so you can read yesterday’s plan again while Nearhost runs. Home’s web page also lists the folders served since Nearhost started, with links to each document. It lists them only in a browser that has opened a document link, or opened the page from Nearhost’s interface or from the address `nearhost status` prints at a terminal: each sets the cookie that the list needs. Elsewhere the page shows no list. Nearhost sets and reads that cookie at `nearhost.localhost` only, so a dev server or container you browse at `localhost` does not receive it. See [TLS and the proxy](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/).

If Nearhost has no web port, there is no page to serve from, and the agent is told so. With `--web-port 0` the message is `Nearhost's page isn't served: --web-port is 0`. When the port was taken, it is `Nearhost's page isn't served: port 6327 wasn't available when Nearhost started`, with the port you asked for.

# Fix a project

> Let a coding agent run Nearhost's project checks and fix what stops the project being served.

With the [`nearhost` skill installed](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/#install-the-skill), ask your coding agent to find and fix what stops a project being served.

When a project is not served as you expect, run `/nearhost doctor` in its directory, or `$nearhost doctor` in Codex. The agent asks Nearhost to run the same [project checks](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#project-checks) as `nearhost doctor` on this project, and works through the errors, then the warnings. Unlike `nearhost doctor`, this first reads the project’s `.nearhostrc` again, as described under [Agent API](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/#agent-api). Each finding’s fix has a kind, and the agent handles each kind in its own way:

* **`project`.** The agent shows you the change, the snippet and where it goes, and makes it in the project’s files once you agree. When the setup is more than Nearhost can work out for itself, such as several hosts, a pattern, `localhost` or callbacks from Docker, it writes or edits the project’s [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/).
* **`nearhost`.** Something you do in Nearhost, such as adding a port in the edit form. The agent passes it on, or offers to write the port or host into `.nearhostrc` instead.
* **`manual`.** Something only you can do, such as a DNS record. The agent tells you what it says.

After editing `.nearhostrc`, and for `nearhostrc.pending` and `nearhostrc.not-applied`, the agent asks Nearhost to read the file again. A change that needs no approval applies at once. One that needs it waits, and the agent tells you to approve it in Nearhost, then waits for your answer. See [Approval](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#approval).

Then it runs the doctor again, and stops when nothing is left that it can fix. It never edits Nearhost’s `config.yaml` itself; Nearhost saves a change there when it applies one. You approve a change in the interface, or on Nearhost’s page by the link the agent prints, so it works with no interface open. See [Answer from the page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#answer-from-the-page).

# How agents reach Nearhost

> The socket a coding agent reaches Nearhost on, how Nearhost forwards it to each server, and the agent API.

This page explains the socket an agent talks to Nearhost on, and the calls it makes.

Nearhost listens on `~/.nearhost/<id>.sock` on your laptop, where `<id>` is six letters and digits made when Nearhost first runs and kept in `~/.config/nearhost/id` (`%APPDATA%\nearhost\id` on Windows) with a fingerprint of the machine. A config directory copied to another machine gets a new id there, so two laptops never share a socket. On each server it is connected to, it forwards a socket of the same name over its own SSH connection:

```sh
ssh -S <sock> -O forward -R <home on the server>/.nearhost/<id>.sock:<socket on the laptop> -- <host>
```

A request is answered for the machine its socket belongs to, so an agent on `mini` sees and proposes only projects on `mini`. sshd creates the socket readable by your account only.

A socket path can be at most 103 bytes on macOS and 107 on Linux. With a home directory long enough to pass that, agents can’t reach Nearhost. From Nearhost 0.8.0, its log says `socket path is too long`.

* **The one change on a server.** Nearhost creates `~/.nearhost` there, private to your account, and removes its own socket from an earlier run before forwarding again. From Nearhost 0.12.0, where the server gives your account a private runtime folder (`/run/user/<uid>`), the socket is made in `nearhost` inside it and `~/.nearhost/<id>.sock` is a link to it, because SELinux on Fedora and its relatives stops sshd making a socket in a home folder. sshd leaves the socket behind when the connection ends; the skill skips sockets that do not answer.
* **Two laptops on one account.** Each install has its own id and socket, so both work. When more than one answers, the agent asks which laptop you mean.
* **A server with no tunnel.** The forward exists while Nearhost is connected to the server, which is from when one of its projects starts, or when you select the server and press `c`. Otherwise the agent says to start Nearhost and connect the server, or gives the `nearhost add --server` command to run on the laptop for a server Nearhost does not know yet.
* **A server that is this machine.** A server whose home is the laptop’s own, such as `ssh_host: localhost` on your account, gets no forward: agents there already reach Nearhost on the laptop’s socket. Nearhost tells this from another machine whose home has the same path, such as a second Mac with the same user name, by checking whether the server sees a file it has just made on the laptop. That machine gets its forward like any other.

To use one socket explicitly, set `NEARHOST_SOCKET` to its path where the agent runs.

## Windows laptops

On a Windows laptop, Nearhost listens on `~\.nearhost\<id>.sock` as on macOS and Linux. Windows’ `ssh.exe` cannot forward a server’s socket to a Unix socket on the laptop, so the socket on each server leads to a port on the laptop’s `127.0.0.1` instead:

```sh
ssh -N -R <home on the server>/.nearhost/<id>.sock:127.0.0.1:<port> -- <host>
```

Any program on the laptop can connect to that port, so Nearhost answers there only requests that carry a token. It writes the token beside the socket on the server, as `~/.nearhost/<id>.token`, readable only by your account, and makes a new one each time Nearhost starts. The skill’s script sends it with curl, which reads it from that file, so it never appears on a command line. Two things follow on the server:

* **curl 7.55 or later.** Older curl cannot read a header from a file, so an agent there cannot reach a Windows laptop.
* **A current skill.** A skill installed before Windows support sends no token, and Nearhost answers `this request has no valid Nearhost token: update the Nearhost skill on this machine`. Run `npx skills add nearhost/nearhost -g` again on the server or, if you installed it as a Claude Code plugin, update the plugin from `/plugin`. See [Install the skill](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/#install-the-skill).

On the laptop itself, the skill runs its PowerShell script, which needs only Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7 and the `curl.exe` that Windows ships.

## A passthrough on another machine

An agent can ask for a passthrough on a machine other than its own, with `--on <host>`, where `<host>` is an SSH host the agent’s machine reaches. The skill’s script runs itself on that host over SSH (`ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -- <host> 'sh -s'`, with the script on standard input), so nothing is installed there. Because the environment does not cross SSH, the script passes the agent’s name and session along as arguments. On that host the script finds Nearhost’s socket as usual, so the passthrough comes from that server and is listed under it.

The script records every place a session opened a passthrough, as one line per target in the session’s marker file. When the session ends, `passthrough-close --session` closes them all at once, over the same `ssh` that opened them. The close gives each SSH connection 2 seconds to connect and stops the whole session close after about 2.5 seconds, inside the hook’s 3 second limit. A target that cannot be closed stays open. If SSH itself fails, the script exits with status 2 and says SSH could not reach the host. See [Browser previews](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/browser-previews/#when-the-app-runs-on-another-machine).

## Agent API

The skill’s script talks to Nearhost over that socket, with `curl --unix-socket`. Nearhost answers JSON for the machine the socket belongs to. These calls are the ones the doctor uses:

* `GET /v1` says which API this is. Its `capabilities` list names the calls added since the first release of API 1: `doctor`, `reload`, `passthrough` and `documents`. An older Nearhost leaves them out, and the skill tells you to update it. When passthroughs are available it also gives `id`, the laptop’s install id, which the skill uses to keep a token per laptop.
* `GET /v1/doctor?path=…` returns `project` and `findings` for the project holding the absolute path, in the shape that [`nearhost doctor --json`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#json-output) gives its findings. For a project already in Nearhost, it first reads the project’s `.nearhostrc` again, as a reload does: a change that needs no approval is applied, restarting the project if it runs under `nearhost up`, and one that needs approval waits in Nearhost. For a directory that is not in Nearhost yet, `project` is `null`, each finding’s `project` is empty, and the findings are for the project as it would be added.
* `POST /v1/projects/reload`, with `{"path": "/abs/dir"}`, asks Nearhost to read the `.nearhostrc` of the project holding the path again. The project must be added first. It answers `applied` when nothing needs approval, or `pending` with an `id` the agent waits on, as it does for a proposal, while you decide. A change you declined stays declined until the file changes or Nearhost restarts.
* A request that waits for your answer replies `202` with an `id` and, when Nearhost’s page is served, an `approve_url` for it. A proposal also carries `advice`, because the page can only decline it. `GET /v1` reports `interface`, whether anyone can answer right now.

### Errors and warnings

An error answers with `Content-Type: application/problem+json`, as [RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) defines, and with the status code it has always had. `error` comes first and holds the same text as before, so a skill installed before these fields reads it as it did:

```json
{
  "error": "Nearhost on dev@laptop has no page or window to ask you in; open nearhost there, then ask again.",
  "type": "https://nearhost.dev/docs/reference/errors/#agent.no-reviewer",
  "title": "Nearhost on dev@laptop has no page or window to ask you in; open nearhost there, then ask again.",
  "status": 409,
  "code": "agent.no-reviewer",
  "level": "error"
}
```

`code` is the error’s code, and `type` links to its entry in [Errors](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/errors/). When the error has them, `detail` says why, `fix` lists the steps, each with its `text` and any `command`, `doctor` is `true` when `nearhost doctor` checks the cause, and `data` holds facts such as a port or a path.

`GET /v1/projects` gives a project with a problem, such as one in `error`, a `problem` beside its `error` text: the same message, with its `code`, `level`, `title` and any `detail` and `fix`. A reply that came with warnings lists them last, under `warnings`, in the same shape. A reply with none has no `warnings` key.

# Prompts and Always allow

> How Nearhost asks before an agent opens a preview or a document, what Always allow covers, and how to revoke it.

Browser previews and documents ask you first, in the same way. This page covers the prompt, what Always allow does, and how to take it back.

## The prompt

Press `y` to allow it, `n` to refuse, or `A` (shift-a) for Always allow. `esc` counts as No. A prompt that waits 10 minutes expires.

For the first 750 ms after a prompt opens, it ignores every key but ctrl+c and hides its keys, then shows them. A key you meant for the screen behind it, pressed as the request arrived, does nothing. The add form an agent’s proposal opens waits the same way, and each prompt in a queue waits again when it opens. Lowercase `a` does nothing in a prompt.

When you refuse a preview or a document, that server’s requests of the same kind are held back for 30 seconds: a new one is refused at once, with no prompt, and the agent is told when it may ask again. Its other waiting requests of that kind are dropped. A request that carries a valid Always allow token still goes through. The prompt queues with proposals and passthroughs, and Home shows the same hint as for a [proposal](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/add-a-project/).

## Answer from the page

Nearhost’s page, at `https://nearhost.localhost:6327` or on the port `--web-port` gives, takes answers whenever it is served, so a request does not need the interface open. That covers the background Nearhost, a service and `nearhost up`. The page shows what the prompt shows, with the same choices: Yes, No and, where it applies, Always allow. The first answer wins, from the page or from the interface. A request to add a project is the exception: the page shows it and lets you decline it, and accepting it takes `nearhost`, where the add form opens filled in.

When a request waits and the agent knows the page’s address, the skill prints a link to it:

```text
Answer in Nearhost on dev@laptop, or open https://nearhost.localhost:6327/approve/k3f9q2
```

For a proposal, it says to run `nearhost` on the laptop to review it, and gives the link to decline it. Open the link in your browser. The page shows the request only to a browser that holds its cookie, which `nearhost status` and the interface give you with their links, so a link that someone else opens shows nothing and approves nothing. Nearhost prints the same link in its own output, in `nearhost up` and in the core’s log, and `nearhost status` lists what waits.

With no interface attached and the page off, because you gave `--web-port 0` or its port was taken, there is nowhere to ask, and the agent is told so. See [Nearhost has no page or window to ask you in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/troubleshooting/#nearhost-has-no-page-or-window-to-ask-you-in).

## Always allow

Always allow covers one tool on one server: Claude Code on `mini`, say, but not Claude Code on another server, and not another tool on `mini`. Only Claude Code is offered it. Codex documents no variable that identifies it, so Codex and every other agent are shown as `An agent`, are always prompted and are never offered Always allow.

Previews and documents are approved separately, so revoking one leaves the other working.

For documents, Always allow covers the folders you have approved, not every folder on the server. A document in a folder you approved opens without a prompt. One in any other folder prompts, and the prompt names the folder. Always allow there adds that folder to the same approval; Yes opens the document and adds nothing. Approvals saved by an earlier version name no folders, so after you update, each folder prompts once.

To revoke one, press `tab` on the server’s panel to reach its `always allowed` section, and `x` on a row. Nearhost asks you to confirm first. Revoking leaves open passthroughs and documents in place. They are listed under `passthroughs` and `documents` at the bottom of the sidebar, not on the server’s panel.

## What the token protects

When you choose Always allow, Nearhost makes a token for that tool on that server. The skill keeps the token on the server, in `${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/nearhost/tokens/<laptop id>/<requester>`, readable by your account only. For documents, the file ends in `.documents`, beside the preview token. The skill sends it with later requests, so Nearhost does not ask again. The laptop keeps only a SHA-256 hash of the token, in `grants.json` beside the install id in `~/.config/nearhost` (`%APPDATA%\nearhost` on Windows, or under `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`).

The token stops a different tool from borrowing an approval, and it stops anything from using one after you revoke it. It does not protect against anything else running as your account on the server: such a process can read the token file and use the approval. Treat Always allow as trust in everything that runs as you on that server. A wrong or revoked token gets a `401`; the skill drops it and asks again, so you are prompted.

Removing a server from Nearhost, or renaming it, revokes its Always allow grants, so a server added later under the same name starts with none. Nearhost does this when it next applies the config or starts, and the log says how many it removed. It does this only for its default config file, not one given with `--config`, and never while that file is missing, so a config file that disappears for a moment does not cost you your grants.

If `grants.json` cannot be read, Nearhost still serves coding agents but turns passthrough off, and says which file it could not read. Fix or remove the file, then restart Nearhost.

## Turn notifications off

The interface notifies the terminal it runs in when an agent asks to add a project, open a preview or show a document. To stop that, add this to the [config](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/). The prompts still open in Nearhost:

```yaml
notifications: false
```

# When agents cannot reach Nearhost

> Fix an sshd that refuses Nearhost's socket forward, or an agent sandbox that blocks the socket.

Three things can stop an agent reaching Nearhost: the server’s sshd, the agent’s own sandbox, or Nearhost having nowhere to ask you.

**The server refuses the forward.** Its sshd has `AllowStreamLocalForwarding no`. The server’s panel shows `agents unavailable` with sshd’s message, and so does `nearhost doctor`. Set `AllowStreamLocalForwarding yes` in the server’s `sshd_config`, reload sshd and press `r` on the server to reconnect. Projects serve either way, and `r` on Home leaves such a server connected.

**The agent’s sandbox blocks the socket.** Agents that run commands in a sandbox block Unix sockets by default, so the skill’s script cannot reach `~/.nearhost`. Allow only what Nearhost needs.

* **Approve the one command.** Claude Code and Codex ask before they run a command the sandbox blocks outside it. Approving that for the skill’s script opens nothing else, so it is the narrowest choice.

* **Claude Code on macOS** can allow the one socket by its full path, which `ls ~/.nearhost` shows, in `~/.claude/settings.json` where the agent runs:

  ```json
  { "sandbox": { "network": { "allowUnixSockets": ["/Users/dev/.nearhost/k3f9q2.sock"] } } }
  ```

Two settings also work, but open far more than Nearhost:

* **Claude Code on Linux** cannot allow one socket, only every one, with `"allowAllUnixSockets": true`.
* **Codex’s** `network_access = true` under `[sandbox_workspace_write]` gives its sandbox the network and every socket.

Every socket includes ones like Docker’s `/var/run/docker.sock`, and a command that reaches Docker’s socket can take over the machine. Use these settings only if that is acceptable where the agent runs; otherwise approve the command when the agent asks.

## Nearhost has no page or window to ask you in

The agent reports that the request was refused, with:

```text
Nearhost on dev@laptop has no page or window to ask you in; open nearhost there, then ask again.
```

In the skill’s script this is exit status 3, and the agent tells you to open `nearhost` on the laptop. Nearhost answers a request that needs your answer with this when it has no way to ask: no interface is open, and Nearhost’s page is off because it runs with `--web-port 0`, or because the page’s port was taken. Open `nearhost` and ask again, or run Nearhost with a page. `nearhost doctor` warns when the port is taken, and `nearhost status` prints the page’s address. See [Answer from the page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/prompts-and-always-allow/#answer-from-the-page).

# Dev servers and hot reload

> How assets and live reload reach your browser, and when a project needs a loopback forward.

A page served from `https://<alias>` usually needs a second thing to work: the dev server that builds its scripts and pushes live updates. There are two ways that server shows up, and Nearhost handles both.

## The dev server is the web app
