A Vite, Next.js or similar project serves pages and assets from one port. Give that port the `web` role and you are done. Hot reload uses a WebSocket on the same origin, and the proxy passes WebSocket upgrades through.

Vite checks the `Host` header, so it needs the alias in `server.allowedHosts`. With the `nearhost/vite` preset enabled, Nearhost shows the exact lines to add. See [Advisories](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/advisories/).

## The dev server sits beside a backend

A backend framework renders the HTML, and the page loads its scripts from a separate dev server at an address like `http://localhost:5173`. Rails, Django and Laravel projects that use Vite all work this way.

That address is resolved by your browser, on your laptop. Nothing listens there, so scripts fail to load and hot reload never connects.

A `loopback` route fixes it. Nearhost forwards the same port number on your laptop to the dev server on the remote machine, so `localhost:5173` in the browser reaches port 5173 over there. The remote project needs no changes, as long as the page asks for `localhost`.

A Laravel project outside Sail whose Vite listens on `::1` writes `http://[::1]:5173` to `public/hot`. The forward answers on both `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`, so the page reaches the dev server either way.

### Vite on `[::1]`

The forward answers on `[::1]` from Nearhost 0.7.0, on a laptop with the IPv6 loopback. Run `nearhost update` to get it. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update). With an older Nearhost, or on a laptop with IPv6 turned off, the forward answers on `127.0.0.1` only, and nothing answers `http://[::1]:5173`. Set `server.hmr.host` to `'localhost'` in `vite.config.js` and restart `npm run dev`, so that `public/hot` says `localhost` instead:

```js
export default defineConfig({
  // The rest of the config stays as it is.
  server: {
    hmr: { host: 'localhost' },
  },
});
```

Discovery proposes a loopback route only under Laravel Sail. For other backends, select the project, press `tab`, choose the dev server’s route and press `space` to make it `loopback`. See [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/#changing-roles).

To see which forwards plain `ssh -L` would need for the same project, see [Vite hot reload fails over SSH port forwarding](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/vite-hot-reload-over-ssh/).

## What happens when a project starts

1. For a project on a server, Nearhost waits for its SSH connection. If the server cannot connect, the project does not start.
2. The hosts block is checked. It holds `127.0.0.1 <alias>` and `::1 <alias>` for every `.test` project, and for an enabled project with another [main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name) unless DNS already sends that name only to loopback. An enabled project’s exact web hosts are listed the same way. Nearhost asks for your password only if it needs to change.
3. For a project on a server, one `-L` forward is added per `web` route, each on an ephemeral local port, and one per `loopback` route, on the same port locally. A local project needs no forwards.
4. The proxy rebuilds its Caddy config with the new site and applies it in-process.
5. The project’s state becomes `running`.

A request to `https://myapp.test` reaches Caddy on 443, then the ephemeral local port, then the web port on the remote. A script tag pointing at `http://localhost:5173/...` reaches the loopback forward on 5173, then port 5173 on the remote. The hot reload client connects to the origin its script came from, so it works with no remote configuration.

## Example: Laravel Sail

Under Sail, `laravel-vite-plugin` writes `public/hot` as `http://localhost:<VITE_PORT>`. With the official presets trusted and `nearhost/sail` enabled, discovery reads the Compose file, makes the port published for container port 80 the `web` route, and proposes `VITE_PORT` as a `loopback` route. A Sail project then needs no manual setup. See [Presets and registries](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/).

## Running several projects at once

A loopback route uses the same port number on both machines, so two running projects cannot share one. Give each project’s dev server its own port. Nearhost warns you before the clash happens, and suggests a free port when the port comes from a variable. Adding a clashing project is refused unless you add it with `--disabled`. See [Advisories](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/advisories/).

If another program already holds the port on your laptop, the project goes into `error` and names the program. Its other routes still start.

## Reloads and reconnects

Starting or stopping a project reloads the proxy without closing open WebSockets, so hot reload in other tabs stays connected. If the SSH connection drops, Nearhost reconnects and puts every forward back. The project shows `degraded` meanwhile.

# Discovery

> How Nearhost reads a project's files to propose routes without running anything.

Discovery takes a server and a path, reads the project’s files and proposes routes with labels and roles, plus advisories. It saves typing. It is not a requirement: a project it knows nothing about works once you give its web port.

Discovery only reads. No command runs on the remote machine. On a server the files are read over SFTP, through an SSH connection of discovery’s own. On `local` they are read from disk.

## The .env rule

Without presets, Nearhost reads `.env`, then `.env.local`, and the later file wins. A port variable is any variable with `PORT` or `PORTS` as one of its parts, split on `_` or `-`, whose value is a whole number from 1 to 65535. `APP_PORT`, `FORWARD_DB_PORT` and `vite-port` all count.

Each one becomes a route labelled with the rest of its name and the variable itself:

```text
  8080  app (APP_PORT)
  3307  forward-db (FORWARD_DB_PORT)
```

When several variables hold the same port, the first in alphabetical order names it and the others are added in brackets.

With no registry trusted, this is all discovery does, and it makes no network request.

## What presets add

Each enabled preset that applies to the project adds to what is found. See [Presets and registries](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/).

* **Compose files.** A preset that asks for Compose ports, such as `nearhost/compose` or `nearhost/sail`, makes discovery read the Compose file as Compose does: the first of `compose.yaml`, `compose.yml`, `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.yaml`, with the first override file beside it, of `compose.override.yml`, `compose.override.yaml`, `docker-compose.override.yml` and `docker-compose.override.yaml`, merged over it. An override’s ports and `extra_hosts` add to the service’s, its `environment` replaces values by key, and `!reset` and `!override` apply. A port both files publish is found once. Each published TCP port becomes a route, labelled with its service, or `service (VAR)` when a variable sets it. `${VAR}`, `${VAR:-default}`, `${VAR-default}` and `$VAR` are filled in from `.env`, as Compose fills them, never from `.env.local` or your shell. When `.env.local` gives a port variable a different value, discovery notes it. Ranges, UDP ports and ports that are not published are skipped. Without such a preset the Compose file is not read, and Nearhost says so.
* **Other files.** A preset can scan files such as `vite.config.ts` for values with a regular expression, and check `package.json` for a dependency. Nothing is executed, and JavaScript is not parsed.
* **Labels and roles.** A preset can relabel a port variable, propose a route as `loopback`, and hint which port should be the web route.
* **Advice.** Most advisories come from presets. See [Advisories](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/advisories/).

## Who claims a port

Each port is claimed once, by the first source that finds it:

1. Compose’s published ports, when a preset asked for them.
2. Each preset that applies, in the order they declare.
3. The `.env` rule, for ports nothing else claimed.

A later preset can replace an earlier one’s route or advice by using the same id, or remove it.

## Roles

Every proposed route starts as `ignore`, unless a preset proposes `loopback`. Then one route is made `web`, in this order:

1. A route a preset prefers as the web route.
2. A Compose port whose container port is 80.
3. A route a preset offers as a fallback, such as Vite’s configured port.
4. The only route, when no preset recognised the project.

If none of these applies, the interface asks you for the web port, and `nearhost add` asks at a terminal or needs `--web <port>`. See [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/).

## When something cannot be read

A file that does not exist is skipped. A file that exists but cannot be read stops discovery with its error, rather than being treated as absent. If nothing at all is found, the interface asks for the web port.

# Multi-host projects

> How one project serves several web routes, each at hosts of its own, and where those hosts come from.

A project can serve more than one name. An app, its WebSocket server and its file store can each answer at a host of their own, all from one project in Nearhost.

## Several web routes

A project can have several `web` routes. The first is the primary: it is served at the project’s [main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name), and at any hosts you give it too. Every other web route is served only at its own hosts, so it needs at least one.

You give a route hosts in three ways:

* **In the interface.** On the routes step of the add or edit form, choose a web route and press `h`. Type its hosts separated by spaces, and press `enter`.
* **On the command line.** `nearhost add --host <host>` adds a host to the primary web route. Repeat it for more.
* **In the project’s files.** A [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#keys) lists hosts for each route, and presets can find them in `.env`. See [Hosts from presets](#hosts-from-presets).

In the routes view on the main screen, `w` makes a route web. If it has no hosts, it becomes the primary. Other web routes with no hosts become `ignore`, so a route with hosts of its own keeps serving them.

## Host patterns

A host is an exact name, such as `api.local.example.com`, or a pattern with `*` in place of one label, such as `*.status.local.example.com`.

* `*` stands for exactly one label. `*.status.local.example.com` matches `eu.status.local.example.com`, but not `status.local.example.com` or `a.eu.status.local.example.com`.
* `*` can be the leftmost label or one in the middle, as in `internal.*.local.example.com`.
* The part to the right of the last `*` must be at least two labels, and more than a public suffix. A pattern that is only wildcards is refused, and so are `*.test`, `*.com` and `*.co.uk`. `*.myapp.test` is allowed.
* `localhost` is allowed as an exact host. Any other name needs at least two labels, and an IP address is refused.
* `nearhost.localhost` is refused with `nearhost.localhost is Nearhost's own page`, since [Nearhost’s page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/) is served there.
* Hosts are lowercase.

## Which route answers

When several hosts match a name, the most specific one answers:

1. An exact host beats any pattern.
2. Among patterns, the one with more fixed labels wins, so `internal.*.local.example.com` beats `*.*.local.example.com`.
3. Patterns with as many fixed labels are taken in lexical order.

A host can be served by only one enabled project. Two exact hosts clash when they are the same name, and two patterns when they are written the same. An exact host under another project’s pattern does not clash, because the exact host wins. Saving an enabled project, or starting one, that would serve a host another enabled project serves is refused with `host <host> is already served by project "<other>"`. `nearhost doctor` warns, as `hosts.overlap`, when a pattern overlaps another project’s without being the same.

## Certificates and DNS

Each exact host gets its own certificate. A name under a pattern gets one the first time it is visited. See [TLS and the proxy](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/#per-name-certificates).

An exact host goes in the hosts file while its project is enabled. One that does not end in `.test` is left out when DNS already points it only at loopback addresses, and `localhost` is never added. Patterns never go in the hosts file, because the file cannot hold them, so a pattern’s names need DNS that points them at this machine. `nearhost doctor` reports a pattern that does not resolve here as `hosts.unresolved-pattern`. See [The hosts file](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/).

## What needs approval

A host that does not end in `.test`, any pattern and `localhost` wait for your approval before they are served. A host you type with `--host` or `h` is approved by typing it. See [Approval](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#approval).

## Hosts from presets

A preset can name hosts as well as ports. The [`nearhost/sail`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/#the-official-presets) preset reads them from `.env`:

| Variable                          | Served on the port in          |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `APP_URL`                         | `APP_PORT`, or 80              |
| `REVERB_HOST`                     | `FORWARD_REVERB_PORT`, or 8080 |
| `FILES_URL`, `MINIO_URL`, or both | `FORWARD_MINIO_PORT`, or 9000  |

Only the host is taken from each value. A port in the URL is ignored, and the route’s port comes from the variable beside it. The Reverb and MinIO hosts are read only when their port variable is set in `.env` or named in the Compose file.

* Inference never proposes `localhost`, an IP address or a name without a dot. A malformed name is left out with a warning, and so is `nearhost.localhost`, as `nearhost.localhost is Nearhost's own page, so it is left out`.
* A route that has inferred hosts becomes a web route. A `loopback` route cannot have hosts, so they are dropped with a warning.
* A `.nearhostrc` that lists a route wins over the hosts presets found for it. See [Keys](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#keys).
* `nearhost add` leaves out an inferred host that another enabled project already serves, with a note: `Note: Not serving <host>: project "<other>" already serves it.` A later web route left with no hosts becomes `ignore`. A project added with `--disabled` keeps them, since it serves nothing yet. The interface does not leave them out: it refuses to save, and you remove the host with `h`.

Inferred hosts are fixed when the project is added or edited. Changing `APP_URL` later does not change what is served. Editing the project, with `e` in the interface, adds any newly inferred hosts to a saved web route and never removes a saved one. `nearhost doctor` reports a host the project’s settings name that no web route serves, as `routes.unserved-host`, and tells you to edit the project.

## Where the URLs show

The project view in the interface lists every URL under the project’s name. A pattern is shown dim, since a browser cannot open it. For a coding agent, `/nearhost status` reports the main URL as `url`, and every URL the project serves, the main one first, as `urls`. See [Add a project from an agent](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/add-a-project/).

## An example

A Sail project with an app, Reverb and MinIO, whose Compose file publishes `APP_PORT`, `FORWARD_REVERB_PORT` and `FORWARD_MINIO_PORT`, has this in its `.env`:

```ini
APP_URL=https://shop.local.example.com
APP_PORT=8010
REVERB_HOST=ws.shop.local.example.com
FORWARD_REVERB_PORT=8090
FILES_URL=https://files.shop.local.example.com:9010
FORWARD_MINIO_PORT=9010
```

With `nearhost/sail` enabled, `nearhost add` asks you to approve the three hosts, since none ends in `.test`. Nearhost then serves:

| URL                                    | Port |
| -------------------------------------- | ---- |
| `https://shop.test`                    | 8010 |
| `https://shop.local.example.com`       | 8010 |
| `https://ws.shop.local.example.com`    | 8090 |
| `https://files.shop.local.example.com` | 9010 |

`shop.test` is the main name, so it is served on the primary route with the app’s own host. Add the project with `--alias shop.local.example.com` to make the real name the main one.

# Presets and registries

> How Nearhost learns what a framework's ports mean, and where that knowledge comes from.

On its own, Nearhost knows one thing about a project: the port variables in its `.env` files. Everything it knows about a particular tool, such as Docker Compose, Vite or Laravel Sail, comes from a preset. Presets come from registries, and Nearhost trusts none until you say so.

## What a preset is

A preset is a small YAML file that says when it applies, which ports to propose and how to label them, and what advice to give. It is data, not code:

* It reads files inside the project. It cannot run a command, make a request or change a file.
* Its expressions are [CEL](https://cel.dev) with a cost limit, and its patterns are RE2, which runs in linear time.
* A preset that fails to load is skipped with a warning. It never stops a command.

Presets combine. On a Sail project with a Vite frontend, `sail`, `laravel` and `vite` all apply, and `sail` changes what `vite` would advise for a dev server that runs in a container.

## The official presets

The official registry is [nearhost/presets](https://github.com/nearhost/presets).

| Preset             | Turns on when                                                               | What it adds                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nearhost/compose` | The project has a Compose file                                              | A route for every TCP port the Compose file publishes, labelled with its service. A service on container port 80 becomes the web route.                                                                                                  |
| `nearhost/laravel` | The project has an `artisan` file                                           | Advice when `APP_URL` is not one of the project’s addresses, with `https` and no port, since generated links use it.                                                                                                                     |
| `nearhost/sail`    | The Compose file mentions `laravel/sail`, a `sail-` image or `LARAVEL_SAIL` | Compose’s published ports, with the Vite dev server forwarded to `localhost` through `VITE_PORT`. The hosts in `APP_URL`, `REVERB_HOST` and `FILES_URL`, `MINIO_URL`, or both, served on their ports. Vite advice that fits a container. |
| `nearhost/vite`    | A `vite.config.*` file exists, or `package.json` depends on `vite`          | The dev server port from `server.port` as a route. Advice when the port is the default 5173, or when `server.allowedHosts` would reject the alias.                                                                                       |

## Hosts from presets

A preset can name hosts as well as ports. `nearhost/sail` reads them from `APP_URL` and `REVERB_HOST`, and from `FILES_URL`, `MINIO_URL` or both, and serves each on its port. The hosts are fixed when you add or edit the project. A project’s `.nearhostrc` wins over them, a real domain among them is asked about first, and `nearhost add` leaves out one that another enabled project serves, with a note. See [Multi-host projects](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/multi-host-projects/#hosts-from-presets).

## Trusting a registry

A fresh Nearhost trusts no registry and makes no request for presets. The first time you add a project, at a terminal or in the interface, it offers to trust the official registry. Answer yes, no, or don’t ask again. You can also trust it yourself:

```sh
nearhost preset registry add nearhost/presets
```

From then on, adding a project suggests the presets that suit it, and asks before enabling each one. In the interface they are listed ticked on the presets step. At a terminal:

```text
This looks like a Vite project. Enable nearhost/vite from nearhost/presets? [Y/n]
```

Without a terminal, `nearhost add` prints the `--preset` flag for each suggestion instead, and enables nothing.

## Pinned and checked

A registry is a public GitHub repository with an `index.yaml` on its default branch and the presets in `presets/`. The index names a commit and a SHA-256 for every preset. Nearhost downloads each file at that commit and refuses it if its hash differs.

* An installed preset never changes until you run `nearhost preset update`.
* The index is cached for a day. If a fetch fails, the cached copy is used.
* A preset written for a newer Nearhost is refused, with a message to upgrade.

Presets from a registry are named after it, as in `nearhost/vite`, so you can see where each one came from. The name before the slash is the registry’s alias, which is the repository owner unless you choose another with `--as`.

## Commands

| Command                                     | What it does                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nearhost preset list`                      | The enabled presets and where they came from, then what each trusted registry offers.     |
| `nearhost preset enable <name>`             | Download, check and enable a registry preset, or enable a local one.                      |
| `nearhost preset disable <name>`            | Stop using a preset. Its file is kept.                                                    |
| `nearhost preset update [name\|registry]`   | Move registry presets to the current versions, and say what changed.                      |
| `nearhost preset registry add <owner/repo>` | Trust a registry. `--as <alias>` names it.                                                |
| `nearhost preset registry list`             | The trusted registries and how old their cached indexes are.                              |
| `nearhost preset registry remove <alias>`   | Stop trusting a registry, once none of its presets are enabled. Installed files are kept. |

`nearhost add --preset <name>` enables a preset without asking, and `--no-presets` uses none.

## Where they live

Presets are files beside the config, under `presets/` in Nearhost’s config folder: `~/.config/nearhost/presets/` (`%APPDATA%\nearhost\presets\` on Windows), or under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nearhost` when that variable is an absolute path. Each registry’s cached index is beside them, at `registry/<alias>/index.yaml`. One from a registry is `presets/<alias>/<name>.yaml`. A local preset is `presets/<name>.yaml`, with a plain name, and is enabled with `nearhost preset enable <name>`.

The config records what is trusted and enabled:

```yaml
registries:
  - alias: nearhost
    repo: nearhost/presets
presets:
  - name: nearhost/vite
    ref: e6c0be9e14dc89ec5c19bb1bc7d155c1029c298d
    sha256: 024643158cc1d55819e3f62d9d3e429cc8b15dae396cf036db9d573815c9d80e
```

`registry_prompt: false` stops Nearhost asking about the official registry. Choosing “don’t ask again” sets it.

## Writing your own

Write a preset when a framework’s ports or advice are not covered. The [nearhost/presets README](https://github.com/nearhost/presets#writing-a-preset) describes every key and expression. Check a file with `nearhost preset validate <file>`, and test it against sample projects with `nearhost preset test`.

Any public GitHub repository laid out like nearhost/presets is a registry. `nearhost preset index` writes its `index.yaml`, and others trust it with `nearhost preset registry add <owner/repo>`.

See [Discovery](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/discovery/) for how presets and the `.env` rule combine.

# Routes and roles

> How each discovered port becomes a web, loopback or ignored route.

A project has a list of routes. Each route is a port on the server, a role and a label. The role decides what Nearhost does with the port.

```yaml
routes:
  - port: 8080
    role: web
    label: 'app'
  - port: 5173
    role: loopback
    label: 'Vite (vite.config)'
  - port: 5432
    role: ignore
    label: 'db'
```

## web

Served through the proxy. A project has at least one. The first is served at `https://<alias>`, and each later one only at hosts of its own, so it needs at least one.

Discovery proposes one: a route a preset prefers, then a Compose port mapped to container port 80, then a route a preset offers as a fallback, such as Vite’s configured port, then a project’s only port. See [Discovery](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/discovery/#roles). You can move the role to any route.

For a project on a server, Nearhost picks an ephemeral local port for the forward and the proxy sends requests for the alias to it. For a local project the proxy sends them straight to the port.

## loopback

A raw TCP forward to `127.0.0.1:<port>` on the laptop, using the same port number as the remote. From Nearhost 0.7.0, it answers on `[::1]:<port>` too. Use it for a dev server whose URLs point at `localhost`, such as Vite behind a backend framework.

A loopback route means nothing for local projects, because the port is already local, so a local route is either `web` or `ignore`. See [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/) for when you need one.

## ignore

Discovered and listed, not forwarded. Discovery proposes every route as `ignore` unless it is the web route or a preset proposes `loopback`. In a project’s panel, ignored routes fold into one line with their ports, such as `3 ignored: 3306 6379 1025`. Press `i` to list them, and `i` again to fold them.

## Changing roles

In the interface, select the project and press `tab` to move into its routes. Choose a route with `↑` and `↓`, then:

* `space` switches it between `loopback` and `ignore`
* `w` makes it a web route, the primary if it has no hosts, and other web routes with no hosts become `ignore`

Press `tab` or `esc` when you are done. The change is saved and applied at once. `e` on the project reads its files again and walks through the routes step of the form. From the command line, `nearhost add --web <port>` chooses the web route.

## Uniqueness rules

* Aliases must be unique across projects, ignoring case.
* Loopback ports must be unique across enabled projects. Adding a project whose loopback port another enabled project uses is refused, and a config file with such a clash does not load.
* Each project has at least one `web` route. Every web route after the first needs at least one host.

# SSH transport

> How Nearhost drives OpenSSH with one supervised control master per server, or on Windows one ssh.exe per forward.

Nearhost shells out to OpenSSH, so your `ssh_config` applies. If `ssh <host>` works without a prompt, Nearhost works.

## One master per server

Each remote server gets one OpenSSH ControlMaster process, supervised by Nearhost and started when a project there first needs it:

```sh
ssh -N -M -S ~/.config/nearhost/run/<server>.sock \
    -o BatchMode=yes -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
    -o ServerAliveInterval=15 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 \
    -o ControlPersist=no -o ClearAllForwardings=yes \
    -o RemoteCommand=none -- <host>
```

The control socket is in `run/` in Nearhost’s config folder. The example shows the default, `~/.config/nearhost`; with an absolute `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, it is `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nearhost/run` instead. When the socket’s path would be too long for a Unix socket, it is named `h-<hash>.sock`.

The last three options keep the master to Nearhost’s own forwards: `LocalForward` and `RemoteForward` lines in your config are left out, and a `RemoteCommand` is not run. The `local` server needs no transport.

Discovery and the add forms open a separate connection of their own, so reading a project’s files never disturbs a running one.

## Forwards added live

Forwards are added and removed on the running master, with no reconnect:

```sh
ssh -S <sock> -O forward -L 127.0.0.1:<local>:localhost:<remote> -- <host>
ssh -S <sock> -O cancel -L 127.0.0.1:<local>:localhost:<remote> -- <host>
```

The forward always listens on `127.0.0.1`. From Nearhost 0.7.0, a `loopback` route also gets a relay that Nearhost runs on `[::1]:<port>` and passes to that forward, so the port answers on both loopback addresses. On a machine without the IPv6 loopback, it answers on `127.0.0.1` only. A program already listening on `[::1]:<port>` counts as holding the port.

[Forward several ports over SSH without retyping -L](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/forward-ports-over-ssh/) compares this with the ways to do it by hand.

Nearhost keeps the list of forwards each server should have. After a reconnect it puts them all back before the server shows as connected. A forward that fails, because something on your laptop holds the port, puts its project in `error` with the name of the program.

## The agent socket

Each master also forwards a Unix socket back to the laptop, at `~/.nearhost/<id>.sock` on the server, so that a coding agent there reaches Nearhost. It is added after the master connects and again after each reconnect, and a server that refuses it only loses that: its projects serve as usual. See [How agents reach Nearhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/).

## On Windows

The OpenSSH client in Windows, `ssh.exe`, has no connection sharing: no ControlMaster and no `-O` commands. So on Windows, Nearhost runs one long-lived `ssh.exe -N` per server for the connection and the agent socket, and one more `ssh.exe` for each forward, started when the project or browser preview needs it and stopped when it no longer does. Reading files over SFTP opens a short connection of its own. Starting or stopping one project never touches another project’s forwards. Each of these `ssh.exe` processes logs in on its own, so a key that needs a touch or an approval at each login asks once for each forward, and again for each forward every time the server reconnects. Each `ssh.exe` runs with `BatchMode=yes`, `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` and the same keepalives as above, and your `~/.ssh/config` applies as it does on macOS and Linux, with one limit. Without a control master, Nearhost cannot keep your config’s own forwards out of its connections, so the `Host` entry it uses for a server must not set `LocalForward`, `RemoteForward`, `DynamicForward`, `ForkAfterAuthentication yes` or `ClearAllForwardings yes`. If it does, Nearhost stops connecting to that server and names the setting. Move those lines to a `Host` entry Nearhost does not use, such as another alias for the same machine.

`ssh.exe` cannot forward a server’s socket to a Unix socket on the laptop, so the agent socket on the server leads to a port on the laptop’s loopback address instead. Nearhost answers there only requests that carry a token, which it writes beside the socket on the server, readable only by your account. See [Agents and Windows laptops](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/#windows-laptops).

Reconnection and backoff below work the same way on every system.

## Reconnection and backoff

If the master exits, Nearhost starts it again, waiting 1 second, then twice as long each time, up to 30 seconds. A master that does not connect within 20 seconds is stopped and tried again. While it waits, the server shows `reconnecting · attempt 3 · next in 8s`, and its projects show `degraded`.

Some errors do not go away by retrying: `Permission denied`, a host key that failed or changed, and too many authentication failures. After three of those in a row, Nearhost stops and the server shows `auth failed`, with the fix: run `ssh <host>` once in a terminal, then press `r`.

## Reconnecting and dropping

On a server’s row in the interface:

* `r` reconnects now, without waiting for the next attempt. On Home, `r` does this for every server that cannot connect.
* `c` drops the connection and holds it closed. Its projects keep their sites and show `degraded`, and starting one there is refused until you press `c` again to connect.

## Shutting down

On exit, Nearhost stops every master with `-O exit`, and stops it outright if it has not gone after 3 seconds. On Windows it stops each `ssh.exe`. A socket left by a crash is checked before each start, and cleared.

## What is stored

Nothing beyond the host string. No keys, passwords or sockets are kept in `config.yaml`.

# The hosts file

> How Nearhost keeps one delimited block in the hosts file, /etc/hosts or its Windows equivalent, to resolve project names.

`.test` is a reserved top-level domain that is never public, so Nearhost resolves aliases through the hosts file and not through DNS. The hosts file is `/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, and `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows. This page says `/etc/hosts` for either file.

## The owned block

Nearhost owns one block and touches nothing else in the file:

```text
# nearhost:start
127.0.0.1 myapp.test
::1 myapp.test
127.0.0.1 nearhost.localhost
::1 nearhost.localhost
127.0.0.1 other.test
::1 other.test
# nearhost:end
```

Each name has a `127.0.0.1` line and a `::1` line, so a browser that tries IPv6 first still reaches Nearhost. Nearhost 0.7 and earlier wrote only the `127.0.0.1` line. The block always lists `.test` names, running or not, sorted. Any other [main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name) is listed only while its project is enabled, and only if DNS does not already resolve it to loopback addresses alone. Each enabled project’s exact web hosts are listed too, under the same DNS rule for names that do not end in `.test`. `localhost` is never listed, because your system already maps it to loopback and Nearhost leaves that mapping alone. If the machine’s nameserver runs on this machine, as systemd-resolved’s does on Linux, Nearhost cannot tell what DNS would say, because that nameserver reads the hosts file too. It keeps the name in the block, so the entry stays where it is. Nearhost 0.7 and earlier dropped it. Wildcard patterns are never listed either, because a hosts file cannot express them: a pattern’s names need DNS that sends them to 127.0.0.1, and `nearhost doctor` reports any that do not resolve. With no projects, the block is removed rather than left empty.

Each block Nearhost writes also holds `nearhost.localhost`, the name of [Nearhost’s page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/), for older systems and resolvers that do not resolve it. Current macOS, Windows 11, Linux with systemd-resolved, Chrome and Firefox resolve it themselves. A block that lacks only that line counts as up to date, so Nearhost does not ask for your password to add it alone, and `nearhost doctor` does not report it. The line arrives the next time the block changes.

## How changes are applied

Each time a project starts, Nearhost works out the block the file should have. If the file already has it, nothing happens. If not, Nearhost runs itself as root to rewrite the block:

```sh
sudo nearhost hosts apply --file /etc/hosts
```

with the aliases on its standard input, one per line. The command is an internal step, so it does not appear in `nearhost --help`. Only one project’s start asks at a time.

In the interface, the password is asked for in a box, and `sudo` remembers it for a few minutes. Where `sudo` asks every time, Nearhost hands over to the terminal for it. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/#the-password-box). `nearhost up` asks in the terminal. The background Nearhost never asks: it leaves the project stopped, and `nearhost hosts update` in a terminal brings the block up to date and tells it to start the project.

On Windows, Nearhost runs itself as administrator through User Account Control instead, which shows Windows’ own prompt. The aliases go to it in a temporary file rather than on its standard input, and it checks them as strictly as the `sudo` step does. Windows does not remember the approval, so every change asks. If you choose No, the file stays as it was. After each change Nearhost clears Windows’ DNS cache, so the new names resolve at once. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/#on-windows).

From Nearhost 0.8.0, Nearhost runs `sudo` from `/usr/bin`, `/bin`, `/usr/local/bin` or `/run/wrappers/bin`, and only a copy owned by root, never one found on your `PATH`.

The rewrite changes only the content between the markers, and adds the block at the end of the file if it is absent. It writes a new file and renames it into place, keeping the file’s permissions, and on Linux its SELinux label and access lists.

If you cancel the password, the project stays stopped, and Home’s `hosts` row shows which aliases are missing. Start the project again to retry.

## Managing it yourself

Run Nearhost with `--no-hosts` to leave `/etc/hosts` alone, for example when you add the aliases yourself. `nearhost doctor` reports whether the block has every alias. A block written by Nearhost 0.7 or earlier has only the `127.0.0.1` lines. Doctor warns about that, as the block “has no IPv6 (::1) entries”, and does not fail. `nearhost up` rewrites it with the `::1` lines.

## Removing it

Nothing is removed when Nearhost quits. To remove the block, which asks for your password through `sudo`, or on Windows for your approval:

```sh
nearhost hosts clean
```

# The request log

> How Nearhost keeps each request and response in memory, and how to look at them and send them again.

Every request the proxy passes on is logged against its project, with its method, path, status and time. Nearhost also keeps the request and its response, bodies included, in memory, so you can look inside them and send them again.

## Opening it

Press `l` for the full-screen log of the selected row: a project, a server, or from Home, everything. `tab` moves between all entries, requests, events and errors, and `/` searches.

Choose a request with `j` and `k`, then:

| Key     | Action                                                  |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enter` | Open it: its headers and bodies, and the route it took. |
| `v`     | Show or hide cookies and authorisation headers.         |
| `c`     | Copy it as a `curl` command.                            |
| `r`     | Send it again.                                          |
| `G`     | Jump to the end and follow new lines.                   |
| `w`     | Wrap long lines.                                        |
| `esc`   | Clear the search, or close the log.                     |

Compressed bodies are unpacked, and JSON is laid out to read. A zstd body is unpacked with a window of up to 8 MiB, which covers zstd’s levels up to 19. One made with `--ultra` or `--long` needs more, so it shows as undecoded, like any encoding Nearhost cannot read.

When a request body did not all reach the app, the opened request shows how much did: `(app read N of M)`, or `(none of M reached the app)` when the app was down or answered without reading it. Copy as `curl` leaves such a body out, and says why.

## Sending a request again

`r` sends the request through the proxy again, so it is logged like any other, and shows the status that came back. `GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` are sent at once. Anything else could change something, so Nearhost asks first, and `y` sends it.

A request cannot be sent again when it was a WebSocket or another upgraded connection, when only part of its body was kept, or when it is no longer kept. Nor can one whose body did not all reach the app: the client stopped sending it, none of it reached the app, or the app stopped reading it. Nearhost says which.

## What is kept

* Each body up to 64 KiB.
* The latest 1000 requests, and at most 32 MiB of bodies. The oldest go first.
* Real header values, including cookies, which the log itself hides.

It all lives in memory and is gone when Nearhost quits. To keep nothing, run Nearhost with `--no-capture`. Requests are still logged, but their bodies are not kept and they cannot be sent again.

# TLS and the proxy

> How the embedded Caddy proxy and the local certificate authority serve each alias over HTTPS.

Caddy runs inside the Nearhost process, with its storage in Nearhost’s data folder, under `nearhost/caddy`: `~/Library/Application Support/nearhost/caddy` on macOS, `~/.local/share/nearhost/caddy` on Linux and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nearhost\caddy` on Windows, or `$XDG_DATA_HOME/nearhost/caddy` on any of them when that variable is set to an absolute path. It listens on 443 for HTTPS, on 80 only to redirect to HTTPS, with a 307 that browsers do not keep, and on 6327 for Nearhost’s page. To use other ports, run Nearhost with `--https-port`, `--http-port` and `--web-port`.

It answers only this machine, and, for a project whose `.nearhostrc` sets `docker_clients`, containers on this machine’s Docker networks. A request from another computer, or for a name Nearhost does not serve, has its connection closed with no answer.

While Nearhost runs, even with no projects, `https://nearhost.localhost:6327` shows Nearhost’s own page. It also shows what Nearhost is serving and any request from a coding agent waiting for your answer, so you can answer without the interface. See [Nearhost’s page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/#nearhosts-page). No project uses that port, and no project may use the name `nearhost.localhost`, so the page is there whatever the projects serve. `https://localhost:6327` shows the page too, without the document list. `localhost` on the HTTPS port belongs to projects: when no project serves it, `https://localhost` gets its connection closed, like any name Nearhost does not serve. `--web-port` moves the port, and `--web-port 0` turns the page off. If the page’s port is taken, Nearhost starts without the page and says so, and `nearhost doctor` warns. Pass `--web-port` to choose another port. A taken HTTPS or HTTP port is different: Nearhost does not start the proxy. The page needs Nearhost 0.8.0 or later.

The page’s port listens on the loopback addresses, `127.0.0.1` and `::1`, on every system, so another machine’s connection to it is refused before anything is read. One exception: on macOS, a page port below 1024, given with `--web-port` while Nearhost is not root, listens on every address, because macOS lets such a program bind a low port only that way. The page still answers only this machine.

Current macOS, Windows 11, Linux with systemd-resolved, Chrome and Firefox resolve `nearhost.localhost` to this machine themselves. For older systems and resolvers that do not, Nearhost adds `nearhost.localhost` to [its block](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/) each time it writes the block. It does not ask for your password for that line alone. If the name does not resolve, use `https://localhost:6327`. See [nearhost.localhost does not resolve](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/troubleshooting/troubleshooting/#nearhostlocalhost-does-not-resolve).

The page shows its document list, project status and approvals only to a browser that holds its cookie, `__Host-nearhost`. The interface opens the page with a link that sets the cookie, and opening any document link sets it too, so the list appears in a browser that opened a document link, or opened the page from Nearhost’s interface. Other browsers and programs see the page without the list. The cookie’s value is a secret kept in `page-secret` in Nearhost’s data folder, readable only by you. Nearhost sets and reads the cookie at `nearhost.localhost` only. At `https://localhost:6327` the page has no list, and a document link opened there sets no cookie. So a server or container you browse at `localhost` does not receive the cookie. One limit: browsers send a cookie to every port of its host, so a server you open at `nearhost.localhost` on another port receives it and can fetch the list.

## The local CA

The internal certificate authority, “Nearhost Local CA”, is created the first time Nearhost starts. Nearhost never ships a shared key or a wildcard certificate, and Caddy never installs the authority by itself.

Trusting it puts its root into the system trust store, which asks for your password once: the System keychain on macOS, your distribution’s certificate store on Linux. On Windows it goes into your user’s certificate store, which Windows confirms in a dialog of its own, with no password, and every browser there uses that store. It also updates the separate stores that Firefox and Linux Chromium-based browsers use, when `certutil` is installed. If the system already trusts it, only the browser stores are updated, with no password.

### Where its key is kept

The CA’s private key is in the `caddy` folder named above, under `pki/authorities/local`. Anyone who has it can sign certificates that your browser trusts, so keep that folder out of dotfiles repositories and shared backups. Your config, `~/.config/nearhost/config.yaml` (`%APPDATA%\nearhost\config.yaml` on Windows, or under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when that is set), holds no keys and is safe to share.

From Nearhost 0.8.0 the key is in the data folder. Earlier versions kept it in `~/.config/nearhost/caddy`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nearhost/caddy` when that variable is set. The next time you run `nearhost`, `nearhost up`, `nearhost trust` or `nearhost untrust`, Nearhost moves an existing old folder there, so the CA you already trust stays the same. It does not move it while another Nearhost is running. If a copy of the old folder is left behind, `nearhost doctor` warns with `old CA copy` and says which folder to delete.

Trust it from the welcome box the first time you start Nearhost, or at any time with `nearhost trust`. `nearhost untrust` removes the CA from the system and browser stores. It leaves the key’s folder where it is, unless you add `--delete-key`, which then deletes the CA’s folder with its key and the certificates it issued. See [`nearhost untrust`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-untrust). See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/) and, for Linux, Windows and Firefox, [Install](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/).

Home shows whether it is trusted and when it expires. The date turns amber in the last 30 days.

## Per-name certificates

Leaf certificates are issued automatically. Each exact name a project serves gets its own. A name under a wildcard pattern gets one the first time it is visited. Because the CA is created on your machine, nobody else holds a key that can sign for your `.test` names.

Each certificate lasts 7 days, signed by an intermediate that lasts 30 days. Caddy checks for renewals every minute, so after a laptop wakes from a long sleep, a certificate that is due is replaced within a minute, with no restart. At start, Nearhost removes the certificates and keys of names under a wildcard pattern that expired more than a day ago, since Caddy renews only names it still serves. A name visited again gets a new one.

## What the proxy sets

Each web route of a running project is served at its hosts, and the first one also at `https://<alias>`. Requests go to the route’s local forward, or for a local project to its port.

* The `Host` header is passed through unchanged.
* `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` and `X-Forwarded-For` are set.
* `Via` names Nearhost and its version, as `1.1 Nearhost (0.8.0)`, on the request and the response. Entries from other proxies are kept. From Nearhost 0.8.0; earlier versions said `Caddy`.
* WebSocket upgrades pass through.
* Responses are not buffered.

## Reloads without dropping connections

Config changes apply through Caddy’s in-process reload. Starting or stopping a project leaves the connections of other projects open, and open WebSockets, such as hot reload, stay connected.

The proxy also keeps the requests it passes on, so you can look at them and send them again. See [The request log](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-request-log/).

If the browser still warns about the certificate, see [The CA is not trusted](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/troubleshooting/troubleshooting/#the-ca-is-not-trusted). For why local dev wants a real HTTPS name, see [HTTPS on a local dev domain](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/https-on-a-local-dev-domain/).

# What Nearhost changes on your machine

> Every file, privilege, port and network request Nearhost uses on your laptop and your servers, and how to undo each one.

Nearhost asks for your password, trusts a certificate authority and edits `/etc/hosts`, so you should know exactly what it does. This page lists all of it, on your laptop and on your servers, and how to undo each part. The other concept pages explain the reasons; this one is the inventory.

## Files on your laptop

| Path                                                                                                                                                       | What it holds                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `~/.config/nearhost/` (macOS, Linux) `%APPDATA%\nearhost\` (Windows)                                                                                       | `config.yaml` with your servers and projects, a lock file, an install id, presets you enabled, cached registry indexes, and `run/` with SSH sockets and `control.sock`, the socket the interface, `nearhost status` and `nearhost stop` use to reach the background Nearhost                |
| `~/Library/Application Support/nearhost/caddy` (macOS) `~/.local/share/nearhost/caddy` (Linux) `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nearhost\caddy` (Windows)                   | The local certificate authority, its private key and the certificates it signed, readable only by you. Beside `caddy`, `page-secret` holds the value of the cookie that lets your browser see the document list, the status and the approvals on Nearhost’s page, also readable only by you |
| `~/.cache/nearhost/update.json` (macOS, Linux) `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nearhost\cache\update.json` (Windows)                                                       | When Nearhost last checked for a new release                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `~/.config/nearhost/core.log`, `core.log.1` (macOS, Linux) `%APPDATA%\nearhost\core.log`, `core.log.1` (Windows)                                           | The log of the [background Nearhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/#the-cores-log), set aside as `core.log.1` at 5 MiB. Written only when Nearhost runs in the background                                                                                            |
| `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.nearhost.core.plist` (macOS) `~/.config/systemd/user/nearhost.service` (Linux) The `Nearhost` task in Task Scheduler (Windows) | The service that starts Nearhost at login. Written only by `nearhost service install`, and removed by `nearhost service uninstall`                                                                                                                                                          |
| `~/.nearhost/`                                                                                                                                             | The socket coding agents on this machine use, readable only by you                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

An absolute `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME` or `XDG_CACHE_HOME` moves the first three. The install id is six random characters plus a hash of the machine id. It never leaves your machine.

Nearhost writes a log file only for the background Nearhost, `core.log`. Otherwise its log is shown in the interface, or printed by `nearhost up`. Nearhost writes nothing to your projects unless you run `nearhost export`, which writes a `.nearhostrc`. A coding agent edits files itself, not through Nearhost.

## What runs as root

Nearhost never runs as root itself. It uses `sudo` for two things, and from Nearhost 0.8.0 only the `sudo` in a system directory, such as `/usr/bin`, never one found on your `PATH`.

* **The hosts file.** When a project starts and the [block Nearhost owns](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/) in `/etc/hosts` is not what it should be, Nearhost runs its own binary as root, `sudo nearhost hosts apply --file /etc/hosts`, which rewrites that block and nothing else. If `sudo` still holds your password from the last few minutes, this happens without asking again. `--no-hosts` turns it off.
* **Trusting the certificate authority.** Only when you run `nearhost trust` or accept the welcome box. On macOS it adds the root certificate to the System keychain with `security add-trusted-cert`. On Linux it copies the certificate into your distribution’s anchors folder and runs `update-ca-certificates`, `update-ca-trust` or `trust extract-compat`. When `certutil` is installed, it also updates the stores that Firefox and, on Linux, Chromium-based browsers keep for themselves, as you, with no password.

On Windows, Nearhost uses User Account Control in place of `sudo`, and only for the hosts file: it runs its own binary as administrator to rewrite the block in `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`, and Windows asks you to approve each time. Trusting the certificate authority needs no administrator rights there: it goes into your user’s certificate store, and Windows asks you to confirm it.

On Linux, binding ports 80 and 443 needs `cap_net_bind_service`. Nearhost itself never sets it. The install script offers to run `sudo setcap` when you run a downloaded copy from a terminal, and asks first. Through `curl | sh`, or `nearhost update`, it only prints the command, as `nearhost doctor` does.

## The certificate authority

Nearhost creates its certificate authority on your machine the first time it starts: an ECDSA P-256 root, valid for ten years, with an intermediate that lasts 30 days. Certificates for your names last 7 days and renew automatically, within a minute of the laptop waking when one fell due during sleep. Nearhost issues them only for names you serve, and at start removes expired ones for names under a wildcard pattern.

Nothing limits the root to `.test`, the same as mkcert’s root. Anyone with its private key could make certificates your browser trusts for any domain. The key never leaves the `caddy` folder above, and that folder is readable only by you, but keep it out of dotfiles repositories and shared backups. See [TLS and the proxy](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/).

## Ports on your laptop

While Nearhost runs, it listens on:

* **443** for HTTPS, over TCP and, for HTTP/3, UDP
* **80**, only to redirect to HTTPS
* **6327** for [Nearhost’s page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/)
* one port on `127.0.0.1` per forwarded route, and for a `loopback` route the same port on `::1` too, when the machine has IPv6 loopback
* on Windows, one more port on `127.0.0.1` per connected server, which coding agents on that server reach Nearhost through. It answers only requests that carry that server’s token.

443 and 80 listen on every interface, because macOS lets a program that is not root bind a low port only that way. On Windows they listen on loopback addresses only, so Windows Firewall does not ask about them. 6327 listens on `127.0.0.1` and `::1` only, on every system, unless you give a page port below 1024 on macOS without root, which listens on every interface. They answer only this machine: another computer’s connection is closed before it gets a certificate or a response. A project with `docker_clients` in its [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/) is also answered for your Docker networks. Until Docker first reports them, Nearhost uses Docker’s default range, `172.16.0.0/12`, which some home and office networks share.

`--https-port`, `--http-port` and `--web-port` move the ports, and `--web-port 0` turns the page off. When Nearhost quits, all of them close.

## Network requests

Nearhost makes these requests and no others. It has no telemetry, no analytics and no account.

* **SSH to your servers**, through your own `ssh` and `~/.ssh/config`.
* **The update check.** At most once a day, `GET https://api.github.com/repos/nearhost/nearhost/releases/latest`. Set `NEARHOST_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to turn it off.
* **Preset registries.** Only registries you have chosen to trust, from `raw.githubusercontent.com`, when you add a project or manage presets. Each preset is checked against the hash in the registry’s index. With no trusted registry, Nearhost requests nothing. See [Presets and registries](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/).
* **DNS.** To decide which names need a hosts entry, Nearhost asks your configured nameserver for names that do not end in `.test`.
* **Docker**, through its local socket, for projects with `docker_clients`.
* **`nearhost update`**, only when you run it. It asks GitHub for the latest release, then runs your package manager or the install script, which download it.

## Requests through the proxy

To show request bodies and send requests again, Nearhost keeps recent requests and responses in memory while it runs: the last thousand or so, bodies up to 64 KiB, 32 MiB in all. They are never written to disk and are gone when Nearhost quits. The log hides `Cookie` and `Authorization` headers. `--no-capture` turns capture off. See [The request log](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-request-log/).

## On your servers

Nearhost installs nothing on a server and opens no ports there. It runs your `ssh`, and through that connection it:

* runs `true` once to check that the connection works
* forwards each route’s port to your laptop
* reads files over SFTP: `.env`, `.env.local`, `.nearhostrc`, Compose files and any files an enabled preset names
* creates `~/.nearhost`, readable only by you, with a socket for coding agents on the server
* from Nearhost 0.12.0, on a server with a private runtime folder (`/run/user/<uid>`, as systemd makes), creates `nearhost` in it, readable only by you, keeps the socket there, and links to it from `~/.nearhost`. SELinux on Fedora and its relatives stops sshd making a socket in a home folder
* when the laptop runs Windows, writes the token for that socket beside it, as `~/.nearhost/<id>.token`, readable only by you

When Nearhost quits, the forwards and the connection close. `~/.nearhost` stays, and may hold a stale socket or link that the next connection replaces. The system clears the runtime folder when your last session on the server ends. A `.nearhostrc` written by `nearhost export` stays in the project. See [SSH transport](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/ssh-transport/).

## What coding agents can do

A coding agent reaches Nearhost through a socket that only your user can open, and sees only the projects of the machine it runs on. Without asking you, it can list those projects, run `nearhost doctor` on a folder, and ask Nearhost to reload a project’s `.nearhostrc`. Nearhost applies changes such as ports and new `.test` hosts straight away and saves them to `config.yaml`; the agent never edits that file itself. Anything else, including other domains, wildcards, `localhost` and `docker_clients`, waits for you to approve it. See [How agents reach Nearhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/).

## Undo everything

1. If you installed the service, run `nearhost service uninstall`. Then run `nearhost stop` to stop the background Nearhost.
2. Run `nearhost untrust` to stop your system and browsers trusting the certificate authority. Add `--delete-key` to delete its private key and the certificates it issued as well.
3. Run `nearhost hosts clean` to remove the block from `/etc/hosts`.
4. On Linux, the port capability goes with the binary when you uninstall it. To drop it and keep Nearhost, run `sudo setcap -r` on the binary `nearhost doctor` names.
5. Uninstall Nearhost the way you installed it, such as `brew uninstall nearhost` or `npm uninstall -g @nearhost/cli`. For the PowerShell installer, delete `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\nearhost` and remove it from your user `PATH`.
6. Delete `~/.config/nearhost`, the data folder that holds `caddy`, `~/.cache/nearhost` and `~/.nearhost`. On Windows, delete `%APPDATA%\nearhost`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nearhost` and `~\.nearhost`.
7. On each server, delete `~/.nearhost`, and any `.nearhostrc` you no longer want.

Run steps 1 to 3 before step 5, while the `nearhost` command still exists.

## Reporting a problem

If you find a way around any of this, report it privately, as the [security policy](https://github.com/nearhost/nearhost/security/policy) explains. Please don’t open a public issue.

# Advisories

> The advice Nearhost gives about a project, when each appears and how to fix it.

Advisories are shown, never applied. Nearhost does not edit your project’s files. In the interface they appear in amber boxes under a project’s routes, and `y` copies their snippets. `nearhost add` prints each one as `Advisory (<id>): <message>`.

One advisory is built in. The others come from the official presets and appear only when that preset is enabled and applies to the project. Any preset can add its own, and a later preset can replace or remove an earlier one’s by its id. See [Presets and registries](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/presets-and-registries/).

## Loopback port clash

`loopback-clash`, built in. Appears when another enabled project forwards the same loopback port:

```text
Port 5173 is also forwarded to this machine by project "shop". Only one can bind it. Give this project its own port.
```

When the port comes from a variable, the snippet sets it to a free port:

```sh
VITE_PORT=5174
```

`nearhost add` refuses to save a project with a clash unless you add it with `--disabled`, and a config file with one does not load.

## Vite on the default port

`vite-default-port`, from `nearhost/vite`. Appears when the Vite config sets no `server.port`, unless it reads `VITE_PORT` and `.env` sets it. Any `server.port` counts, a number, an expression such as `Number(process.env.APP_VITE_PORT) || 5291` or the shorthand `server: { port }`, but not one that is commented out. A port whose value reads `VITE_PORT` counts only while `.env` sets `VITE_PORT`. Vite will use 5173, which other Vite projects also use, so set a port in the Vite config. The snippet suggests a free one:

vite.config.ts

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  server: {
    port: 5174,
  },
});
```

Under Laravel Sail, `nearhost/sail` replaces it with the same advice for `.env`. `laravel-vite-plugin` reads `VITE_PORT` from `.env` or the environment, so the advice does not appear when the Compose file’s `environment` sets `VITE_PORT` to a port other than 5173. A default under `ports`, such as `${VITE_PORT:-5176}`, does not count: it only maps the port, and Vite in the container still listens on 5173. Its snippet:

```sh
VITE_PORT=5174
```

## allowedHosts missing

`allowed-hosts`, from `nearhost/vite`. Appears when `server.allowedHosts` does not include the alias, unless Vite serves HTTPS itself or allows every host. Vite rejects requests for hostnames it does not know.

vite.config.ts

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  server: {
    allowedHosts: ['myapp.test'],
  },
});
```

`nearhost/sail` turns it off, since under Sail the browser reaches Vite at `localhost`, not at the alias.

## APP_URL mismatch

`app-url`, from `nearhost/laravel`. Appears when `APP_URL` in `.env` is missing, is not `https://`, has a port, or names a host the project does not serve. Generated links use that value, so set it to one of the project’s addresses, with `https` and no port. The suggested line keeps the host when the project serves it, and uses the alias otherwise:

```sh
APP_URL=https://myapp.test
```

See [Discovery](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/discovery/) for how advisories are produced.

# CLI

> Every nearhost command, its flags, and what nearhost doctor checks.

```text
nearhost                       the interface, on the background Nearhost
nearhost -d                    start Nearhost in the background, with no interface
nearhost stop                  stop the background Nearhost
nearhost status                what the background Nearhost serves (--json for JSON)
nearhost service install       start Nearhost at login, as a service
nearhost service uninstall     remove the service
nearhost daemon                the background Nearhost, run in the foreground; what a service runs
nearhost up [project...]       start projects without the interface, until Ctrl-C
nearhost add [path]            add a project, discovering its ports
nearhost export [project]      write a project's setup to its .nearhostrc
nearhost ls                    list projects
nearhost trust | untrust       the local CA in the system and browser stores
nearhost hosts update          bring the nearhost block in /etc/hosts up to date
nearhost hosts clean           remove the nearhost block from /etc/hosts
nearhost doctor                check ports, the CA, the hosts block, servers and projects
nearhost preset ...            presets, which say what a framework's ports mean
nearhost preset registry ...   the preset registries you trust
nearhost update                update to the latest release
nearhost completion <shell>    print a shell completion script
nearhost version               print the version (also nearhost --version)
```

Every command takes `--config <file>` to use another config file, and `--verbose` to show the code and the causes of an error, a warning or a note. A mistyped command gets a suggestion, under `Did you mean this?`, with the closest command names. From Nearhost 0.8.0.

A mistyped subcommand under `nearhost hosts`, `nearhost service`, `nearhost preset`, `nearhost preset registry` or `nearhost completion` is an error too. It names the command and the group, suggests the closest command when there is one, and exits 1, so `nearhost hosts clear` no longer looks like a clean that worked:

```text
Error: Unknown command "clear" for "nearhost hosts".


Did you mean this?


  clean
```

With no subcommand, each of them prints its help and exits 0.

## Errors, warnings and notes

Errors, warnings and notes go to stderr, so stdout holds only what the command prints when it works, for a pipe or `--json`. A blank line separates one from the next. An error starts with `Error:` and what happened. Under it come why, in plain words, the steps to fix it, each command on a line of its own so that you can copy it, and a pointer to `nearhost doctor` when it checks the cause. A warning starts with `Warning:`, and a note, which needs nothing done, with `Note:`. At a terminal the label is in colour, unless `NO_COLOR` is set. The text wraps to the terminal’s width, but a command never does. A mistyped command, an unknown flag or an argument a command does not take is an error too, which says how to see what the command takes, as `nearhost <command> --help`.

With `--json`, which `nearhost status` and `nearhost doctor` take, each error, warning and note goes to stderr as one JSON object per line instead, with its `code`, `level`, `title` and, when it has them, `detail` and `fix`:

```json
{
  "code": "core.not-running",
  "level": "error",
  "title": "Nearhost is not running.",
  "fix": [
    { "text": "Start it in the background:", "command": "nearhost -d" },
    { "text": "Or open its interface:", "command": "nearhost" }
  ]
}
```

On Linux, for example, `nearhost service install` refuses a copy of `nearhost` that may not use ports 80 and 443, such as one you built yourself:

```text
Error: The service cannot run Nearhost from this copy yet.


On Linux, a program may use ports below 1024, such as 443 for HTTPS and
80 for HTTP, only when it has been given permission. The install script
gives it; a nearhost you build or copy yourself does not have it.


To give it permission, run:


  sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep '/home/you/go/bin/nearhost'


Then run nearhost service install again.


Run `nearhost doctor` to check this and the rest of what Nearhost needs.
```

`--verbose` adds the code on the line under the title, here `(service.cannot-bind)`, and ends with what caused it, on a `Cause:` line, when that adds to the title. A code names the problem wherever it shows up: in the core’s log, in `nearhost doctor --verbose` and in the APIs. [Errors](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/errors/) lists every code.

If Nearhost itself fails unexpectedly, it prints `Error: Nearhost stopped unexpectedly.` with the path of a crash file, and asks you to report it at the Nearhost issues page with that file attached. Crash files are named `crash-<time>.log` and kept beside `core.log` in the config folder. A file holds Nearhost’s version, the system, the time and where it failed, and nothing from your config.

## Exit status

These are the exit statuses a script can rely on:

| Command                     | Status | When                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nearhost`                  | 1      | There is no terminal. Use `nearhost -d` or `nearhost up` instead.                                                          |
|                             | 1      | `--config` names another file than the running Nearhost serves, or the running Nearhost speaks another version of its API. |
|                             | 130    | Ctrl-C interrupted it while it started Nearhost in the background.                                                         |
|                             | 1      | Quitting could not stop the background Nearhost, or could not leave it running, as you chose.                              |
| `nearhost -d`               | 1      | The background Nearhost stopped while starting, or had not answered after 15 seconds.                                      |
|                             | 130    | Ctrl-C interrupted it while it started Nearhost in the background.                                                         |
| `nearhost stop`             | 0      | Nearhost stopped, or was not running.                                                                                      |
|                             | 1      | Nearhost had not stopped after 35 seconds.                                                                                 |
| `nearhost status`           | 3      | Nearhost is not running.                                                                                                   |
| `nearhost service`          | 1      | `install` or `uninstall` failed, or this system has no service manager to use.                                             |
| `nearhost up`               | 1      | Nothing can be served once every project has tried to start.                                                               |
| `nearhost add`              | 130    | Ctrl-C or another stop signal interrupted it, and nothing was added.                                                       |
| `nearhost untrust`          | not 0  | While trust remains: a system or browser store still trusts the CA, or could not be reached.                               |
| `nearhost doctor`           | 1      | A check failed, or a project has an error. Warnings leave it at 0.                                                         |
| `nearhost update --check`   | 0      | Nearhost is up to date, including when the newest release has no files for it yet.                                         |
|                             | 1      | A newer release is out.                                                                                                    |
|                             | 2      | The check failed. The reason goes to stderr.                                                                               |
| `nearhost update`           | 1      | The update command ran, but the copy that runs next did not start, printed no version, or is still the old version.        |
|                             | 1      | With `--next` on a Homebrew copy when the newest is a beta, which Homebrew does not have.                                  |
| A mistyped command or group | 1      | The command, or a subcommand under `hosts`, `service`, `preset` or `completion`, does not exist.                           |

## nearhost

Opens the interface, at a terminal. The interface is a client of the background Nearhost, which serves your projects: with none running, `nearhost` starts one in the background first, then attaches to it. `q` asks whether to stop it or leave it running when the interface started it. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/) and [Run Nearhost in the background](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/).

It needs a terminal: stdin and stdout must both be one. Without one, as in a cron job, a script or a pipe, it starts nothing, prints this to stderr and exits 1:

```text
Error: The interface needs a terminal, and there is none here.


Run it in the background:


  nearhost -d


Or serve without the interface:


  nearhost up
```

On Windows the message adds `In Git Bash, run it through winpty or use Windows Terminal.` `nearhost --help`, `-h` and `help` print the help and exit 0 without a terminal.

| Flag                  | Effect                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-d`, `--detach`      | Start Nearhost in the background, with no interface. See [nearhost -d](#nearhost--d).                                      |
| `--https-port <port>` | Serve HTTPS on this port instead of 443.                                                                                   |
| `--http-port <port>`  | Redirect HTTP on this port instead of 80.                                                                                  |
| `--web-port <port>`   | Serve Nearhost’s page at `https://nearhost.localhost:<port>` instead of 6327. `0` turns the page off. From Nearhost 0.8.0. |
| `--no-hosts`          | Leave `/etc/hosts` alone. Add the aliases yourself.                                                                        |
| `--no-capture`        | Keep no requests or responses in memory. See [The request log](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-request-log/).         |

The port flags, `--no-hosts` and `--no-capture` apply only when Nearhost starts. Given to an interface that finds one already running, they change nothing, and the interface says so in its log.

Only one Nearhost runs at a time. `nearhost` attaches to the one that runs, as long as it speaks the same version of the API. Otherwise it fails with `Nearhost in the background speaks a different version of its API.`, with the steps to stop it and open the interface again, and exits 1. When the one that runs is another release, as after an update, it asks `Nearhost in the background is <old>; this is <new>. Restart it now? [Y/n]`. A Nearhost started in a terminal is not offered a restart: a note says to restart it there. Nor is one whose service runs another copy of `nearhost`: it says so. A different `--config` file than the one it serves is refused with `Nearhost in the background serves <file>.`, and the steps: stop it with `nearhost stop` to use the other file, or open the interface on the file it serves. `nearhost up` and `nearhost daemon` stop with the error below, without the pid when it is not known. When the second one’s ports are taken, it reports the ports first.

```text
Error: Another Nearhost is already running (pid 4121).


Stop it:


  nearhost stop


Or see what it serves:


  nearhost status
```

### nearhost -d

Starts the background Nearhost, with no interface and no terminal needed, and returns once it answers. It runs `nearhost daemon`, started in a session of its own with its output in the core log. It waits up to 15 seconds.

```text
Nearhost is running in the background (pid 4121). Stop it with nearhost stop.
```

| It prints                                                                                                       | When                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Nearhost is running in the background (pid N). Stop it with nearhost stop.`                                    | It started the core.                                                                                    |
| `Nearhost is running in the background as a service (pid N). Stop it with nearhost stop.`                       | It started the core through the installed service.                                                      |
| `Warning: Starting Nearhost through its service failed (<why>), so it was started directly.`                    | The service did not start the core, so it started one itself.                                           |
| `Note: You are not signed in to Windows, so the service could not start Nearhost, and it was started directly.` | On Windows with nobody signed in, as over SSH, the service’s task cannot run, so it started one itself. |
| `Nearhost is already running in the background (pid N, started by <how>).`                                      | A core ran already. It starts nothing and exits 0.                                                      |
