# Keyboard shortcuts

> Every key in the Nearhost interface, by screen.

The footer always shows the keys that work where you are. When the window is narrow it leaves some out and shows `? more`, and `?` lists them all.

Mouse and keyboard both work. Click a sidebar row to select it, click a footer action to run it, and scroll the log with the wheel.

## Mouse

Nearhost takes the mouse for those clicks, so it selects text and opens links itself:

| Action           | Effect                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Drag             | Selects text within the panel or box where the drag starts, and copies it when you let go. A toast at the bottom right says what was copied. |
| Double-click     | Copies the word under the pointer.                                                                                                           |
| Click an address | Opens an `http` or `https` address in your browser, whether it is a link or written in a log line.                                           |

Copies made with a key or the mouse, adds, saves and removals are confirmed in a toast for two seconds and written to the log too, and so are warnings and notes. An action of yours that fails opens an alert box instead, with what went wrong, why and how to fix it, and writes it to the log as well. A problem that arrives on its own, such as a project failing in the background, never opens the alert: it shows in a toast and stays under problems on Home. Copies go to the clipboard through the terminal, over OSC 52, and through `pbcopy` on macOS, `wl-copy`, `xclip` or `xsel` on Linux, or the Windows clipboard on Windows, so they work in terminals without OSC 52 too. In most terminals, holding Shift hands the mouse back to the terminal for its own selection and links. In Ghostty, Shift+Cmd+click opens a link the terminal’s way. Needs Nearhost 0.8.0 or later.

## Anywhere

`ctrl+c` quits, even from a form or the password box, and never asks first. It stops Nearhost when this interface started it, unless `keep_running: true` is set or another interface is open on it; otherwise Nearhost keeps running in the background. While Nearhost is stopping, `q` or `ctrl+c` again stops it at once.

## Main screen

| Key      | Action                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `↑`, `↓` | Move the selection. `k` and `j` too.                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `h`      | Go to Home.                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `/`      | Filter the sidebar by name. `enter` keeps the filter.                                                                                                                                                        |
| `esc`    | Clear the filter, or go to Home.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `l`      | Full-screen log of the selected row, or of everything from Home.                                                                                                                                             |
| `n`      | Add a project, on the selected server or the selected project’s server.                                                                                                                                      |
| `s`      | Add a server.                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `p`      | Review the next request a coding agent is waiting on.                                                                                                                                                        |
| `?`      | Show or hide every key.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `q`      | Quit. When this interface started Nearhost and no other interface is open on it, asks whether to stop it or leave it running, unless `keep_running` in the config answers. Otherwise Nearhost keeps running. |

On the first screen, with nothing added yet, `c` connects a server. On Home, when a server cannot connect, `r` retries every such server now and `y` copies the `ssh` command that fixes access.

## Project

| Key     | Action                                                                                                        |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enter` | Start or stop it.                                                                                             |
| `o`     | Open `https://<alias>` in the browser.                                                                        |
| `tab`   | Move into its routes, to change them.                                                                         |
| `e`     | Edit: read its files again and change its routes or name.                                                     |
| `d`     | Remove it, after you confirm.                                                                                 |
| `y`     | Copy the snippets of its advice.                                                                              |
| `r`     | Read its `.nearhostrc` again. A change that needs no approval is applied, which restarts it if it is running. |
| `a`     | Review a pending `.nearhostrc` change.                                                                        |
| `i`     | Show or hide its ignored routes, which fold into one line with their ports. Needs Nearhost 0.8.0 or later.    |

## Routes

After `tab` on a project. Every route is listed here, ignored ones included.

| Key          | Action                                                                                               |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `↑`, `↓`     | Choose a route.                                                                                      |
| `space`      | Switch it between `loopback` and `ignore`.                                                           |
| `w`          | Make it a web route, the primary if it has no hosts. Other web routes with no hosts become `ignore`. |
| `y`          | Copy the snippets of the project’s advice.                                                           |
| `tab`, `esc` | Done.                                                                                                |

On a project on this machine, a route is only `web` or `ignore`.

## Server

| Key     | Action                                                                                                                           |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enter` | Collapse or expand its projects.                                                                                                 |
| `r`     | Reconnect now.                                                                                                                   |
| `c`     | Drop the connection and hold it closed, or connect it again.                                                                     |
| `e`     | Edit its host and name.                                                                                                          |
| `d`     | Remove it and its projects, after you confirm.                                                                                   |
| `tab`   | Move into its always allowed list: `↑`, `↓` choose, `x` revokes the selected one, `tab` or `esc` is done. Shown when it has any. |

On `local`, only `enter` and `tab` work.

## Passthroughs and documents

The `passthroughs` and `documents` rows sit at the bottom of the sidebar. Select one, then press `tab` to move into its rows.

| Key          | Action                                                                 |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `↑`, `↓`     | Choose a row. `k` and `j` too.                                         |
| `o`          | Open the passthrough’s address, or the document, in your browser.      |
| `enter`      | Open the selected document. Documents only.                            |
| `y`          | Copy the passthrough’s address. Passthroughs only.                     |
| `x`          | Close the passthrough, or stop serving the document after you confirm. |
| `tab`, `esc` | Done.                                                                  |

See [Browser previews](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/browser-previews/#see-what-is-open) and [Documents](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/documents/#when-a-served-folder-goes-away).

## Full-screen log

| Key               | Action                                                                        |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `j`, `k`          | Move. The arrow keys too.                                                     |
| `space`, `pgdown` | Page down.                                                                    |
| `pgup`            | Page up.                                                                      |
| `g`               | Go to the oldest line.                                                        |
| `G`               | Go to the end and follow new lines.                                           |
| `tab`             | Show all entries, requests, events or errors. `shift+tab` goes the other way. |
| `/`               | Search. `enter` keeps it, `esc` clears it.                                    |
| `w`               | Wrap long lines.                                                              |
| `enter`           | Open or close a request.                                                      |
| `v`               | Show or hide cookies and authorisation headers.                               |
| `c`               | Copy the request as a `curl` command.                                         |
| `r`               | Send the request again. Unsafe methods ask first.                             |
| `p`               | Open the request a coding agent is waiting on.                                |
| `esc`, `q`        | Close the log. `esc` clears a search first.                                   |

See [The request log](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-request-log/).

## Forms

`esc` goes back a step, and from the first step closes the form. The footer of each step lists its keys.

| Where         | Keys                                                                                                               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Lists         | `↑`, `↓` to choose, `enter` to pick.                                                                               |
| Path          | `tab` or `→` accepts the suggestion, `↑`, `↓` choose a match, `enter` uses the path as typed, `ctrl+r` reconnects. |
| Presets       | `space` ticks or unticks, `enter` goes on.                                                                         |
| Routes        | `space` serves or ignores a port, `←`, `→` change its role, `h` edits a web route’s hosts.                         |
| Name          | `tab` moves between name and alias.                                                                                |
| Server check  | `r` checks again after a failure.                                                                                  |
| Confirm       | `enter` adds or saves. The last step lists anything that needs approval, which `enter` approves.                   |
| Review        | `y` approves, `n` declines, `esc` leaves it for later.                                                             |
| Remove        | `y` removes, `n` or `esc` keeps.                                                                                   |
| Agent request | `y` allows, `A` always allows when offered, `n` or `esc` refuses.                                                  |

## Welcome, password, quit and alert boxes

| Box      | Keys                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Welcome  | `enter` trusts the certificate authority, `s` skips.                                                                                                                        |
| Password | `enter` continues, `esc` cancels.                                                                                                                                           |
| Quit     | `enter` stops Nearhost or leaves it running, as chosen; `tab` or `←`, `→` choose; `space` ticks Don’t ask again, which saves the answer as `keep_running`; `esc` goes back. |
| Alert    | `enter` or `esc` closes it, and `c` copies its first command.                                                                                                               |

# .nearhostrc

> Every key in a project's .nearhostrc, how its variables are filled, and what it asks you to approve.

A `.nearhostrc` is a YAML file in a project’s root directory. You commit it with the project, so everyone who adds the project gets the same ports, hosts and main name, and each worktree can fill them from its own `.env`.

The file only ever proposes. A host or main name that is not `.test`, a wildcard, `localhost`, a new loopback port and Docker access all wait for your approval before they go live. See [Approval](#approval).

```yaml
version: 1
alias: ${APP_HOST:-app.local.example.com}
routes:
  - port: ${APP_PORT:-8000}
    label: app
    hosts:
      - api.local.example.com
      - '*.status.local.example.com'
  - port: ${FORWARD_REVERB_PORT:-8080}
    label: reverb
    hosts: [ws.local.example.com]
  - port: ${FORWARD_MINIO_PORT:-9000}
    label: minio
    hosts: [files.local.example.com]
  - port: ${VITE_PORT:-5173}
    role: ignore
    label: vite
docker_clients: true
```

With this `.env` beside it, the app is served at `https://app.local.example.com` and `https://api.local.example.com` from port 8010. A name one label under `status.local.example.com`, such as `eu.status.local.example.com`, reaches the same port; the hosts file cannot hold a pattern, so its names need DNS that points them at this machine. Reverb is served at `ws.local.example.com` from port 8090, and MinIO at `files.local.example.com` from port 9010:

```ini
APP_PORT=8010
FORWARD_REVERB_PORT=8090
FORWARD_MINIO_PORT=9010
```

## Keys

| Key              | Type    | Meaning                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `version`        | integer | Required. Must be `1`.                                                                                                      |
| `alias`          | string  | Optional. The project’s [main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name): `<name>.test`, or any one domain. |
| `routes[].port`  | integer | Required. The port on the server. A number from 1 to 65535, or a variable that gives one.                                   |
| `routes[].role`  | string  | Optional. `web`, `loopback` or `ignore`. `web` when left out.                                                               |
| `routes[].label` | string  | Optional. A description, shown with the route.                                                                              |
| `routes[].hosts` | list    | Optional, web routes only. Names to serve the route at: exact names or wildcard patterns.                                   |
| `docker_clients` | boolean | Optional. `true` serves the project to Docker containers on this machine too. See [Docker clients](#docker-clients).        |

The roles mean what they mean in `config.yaml`. See [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/).

The file is the authority on the routes it lists. Their hosts replace any that presets found for those ports. A port the project has that the file does not list stays visible, but a web one becomes `ignore`, so only the file says what is served.

`nearhost add --alias` wins over `alias:`, and `alias:` wins over `<name>.test`. Removing `alias:` from the file leaves the current main name as it is.

## Rules

* A file that lists routes needs at least one `web` route among them.
* The first web route is served at the project’s main name. Every later web route needs at least one host.
* A port, or a host, listed twice is an error.
* Only web routes have hosts.
* The main name may be listed as a host only on the first web route, where it is served anyway.
* `docker_clients` works only for a project on this machine, not one on a server.
* Hosts and the main name must be lowercase. The main name cannot be a wildcard pattern, `localhost`, `nearhost.localhost` or an IP address. No host can be `nearhost.localhost`.

## Variables

`${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` work in ports, hosts, labels, roles and the alias. They are filled from `.env.local`, then `.env`, in the project’s directory, so a value in `.env.local` wins. They are never filled from Nearhost’s own environment.

A variable with no value and no default is an error that names it:

```text
.nearhostrc line 3: ${APP_PORT} has no value in .env.local or .env, and no default
```

A variable can fill part of a value, as in `app.${APP_DOMAIN}`. Worktrees of one repository can then share the committed file and each serve its own hosts. Approval works on the filled values, so you approve the names that will actually be served, and a change in `.env` that gives a new real domain asks again.

## Errors

Every error in the file itself starts with `.nearhostrc`. `nearhost add` stops with it, and the interface and `nearhost doctor` show it with the project.

A key this version of Nearhost does not know is an error, rather than being ignored:

```text
.nearhostrc: line 4: key "hostz" is not understood by this version of Nearhost; update Nearhost, or remove it
```

So is a `version` newer than this Nearhost understands:

```text
.nearhostrc is version 2; this Nearhost understands version 1, so update Nearhost
```

Run `nearhost update` for the second. For the first, check the key’s spelling against [Keys](#keys).

## Approval

These need your approval before they go live:

* a host that does not end in `.test`;
* a wildcard pattern, even one under `.test`;
* `localhost`;
* a main name that does not end in `.test`;
* a `loopback` port that the approved project did not forward as loopback, since Nearhost binds that port on `localhost` on this machine;
* `docker_clients: true`.

A `.test` host, a web port, a label or another role needs none. Neither does a host the project already serves, a new label on a loopback port you approved, or a loopback port that a preset such as Vite’s proposes. A loopback port is shown for approval as `localhost:5173 (binds localhost:5173 on this machine)`, after the hosts.

Each front end asks in its own way:

* **The interface.** When you add a project, the last step lists what needs approval, and `enter` approves it and saves. When a project’s file changes later, the project shows `.nearhostrc asks for 1 change that needs approval · a to review`. Press `a` to see what it asks for, then `y` to approve, `n` to decline or `esc` to leave it for later. A declined change is not asked about again until the file changes or Nearhost restarts.

* **`nearhost add`.** At a terminal it first says what approving a name does, then asks about each item on its own, as `<item>: approve? [y/N]`. A no drops that host, loopback port or `docker_clients`, and the add goes on without it. A refused main name falls back to the `.test` one, and the summary names what was left out. Nearhost asks about a refused item again when it next reviews the project. A host typed with `--host`, or a main name typed with `--alias`, is approved by typing it. Without a terminal it adds nothing, and names the items. For the file at the top of this page:

  ```text
  Error: Not added: this project asks for things that need your approval
  (*.status.local.example.com, api.local.example.com,
  ws.local.example.com, files.local.example.com, app.local.example.com,
  docker_clients).


  Run the add in a terminal, where it can ask:


    nearhost add


  Or approve them in the interface:


    nearhost
  ```

* **`nearhost up` and the background Nearhost.** They ask no question of their own. A project whose file asks for something new keeps serving what was approved before, and the log says what is waiting. `nearhost status` lists it with a link to answer it on Nearhost’s page. Approve it there, or open `nearhost`.

Nothing approves itself.

## When it is read

Nearhost reads the file, and applies what it finds:

* when a project starts;
* when you press `r` on a project in the interface;
* when an agent asks Nearhost to read it again, or runs the doctor on the project.

A change that needs no approval, such as a port moved in `.env`, a new label or a new `.test` host, applies at once and is saved to `config.yaml`. A change that needs approval waits, and the routes approved before keep serving until you approve it. If the file has an error, or is deleted after it was approved, the project keeps serving what was approved and shows the problem.

`nearhost doctor` on the command line reads the file too, but only reports. It applies and saves nothing. It reports a file with an error, a change that waits for approval, and a change that needs none but has not been applied yet.

## Docker clients

Nearhost answers only this machine. On Linux, a request from a container comes from a Docker network, not from this machine’s loopback address, so Nearhost drops it. `docker_clients: true` also serves the project to the networks Docker has on this machine, while other projects stay loopback-only. It works only for a project on this machine, and it always needs your approval. Docker Desktop on macOS already delivers container requests from 127.0.0.1, so this matters on Linux.

A container also needs to find the host and trust the local certificate authority. See [Callbacks from Docker containers to a local HTTPS domain](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/container-callbacks/).

## A file without routes

Note

A file without routes needs Nearhost 0.7.0 or later. Nearhost 0.6.0 stops with `.nearhostrc needs at least one web route`.

To set only the main name, and leave the routes to discovery and to you, give the file `version` and `alias`:

```yaml
version: 1
alias: ${APP_HOST:-app.local.example.com}
```

The routes stay as discovery found them or as you set them. The file removes only the hosts that an earlier, approved version of it gave, and the main name from any route other than the first web route. A later web route left with no hosts once the main name is removed becomes `ignore`.

# Troubleshooting

> Symptoms Nearhost reports and the fix for each.

Every failure attaches to the thing that failed, with why it happened and how to fix it. Each has a code, which `--verbose` shows and the core’s log always does: look it up in [Errors](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/errors/). A failure in one project or server never affects another. Home lists what needs you under problems. `nearhost doctor` checks most of the causes below at once.

## Port 443 or 80 already in use

The proxy does not start. Home shows `proxy down`, names the port and, where it can, the program holding it.

Quit that program, or run Nearhost with `--https-port` and `--http-port`. If the holder is `nearhost`, another Nearhost is running: stop it rather than moving ports. Another local proxy is the usual cause: nginx, Caddy, Herd or Valet. On Linux, also check that the binary may bind low ports. See [Install](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/).

If Home says the port needs permission to bind, nothing holds it, but this user may not use it. On Linux, the fix under it is the `setcap` command for the binary, as in [Allow binding ports 80 and 443](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/#allow-binding-ports-80-and-443); run it, then start Nearhost again. For an npm install, use the command `nearhost doctor` prints, which names the real binary. From Nearhost 0.8.0. `nearhost up` stops with the same command in its error, as in [nearhost up](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-up), and so does the core’s log when Nearhost runs in the background.

`nearhost doctor` run while Nearhost serves shows the ports Nearhost holds as `in use by the running Nearhost`, which passes. If no tool can name what holds a port while Nearhost runs, the check warns and suggests a command to find it.

On Windows, a port held by `System (pid 4)` is held by HTTP.sys on behalf of a Windows service, often IIS, so there is no program to quit. To see which service registered it, run this in a terminal opened as administrator:

```powershell
netsh http show servicestate
```

Stop that service, for IIS with `net stop w3svc`, or run Nearhost with `--http-port` and `--https-port`.

## Another Nearhost is already running

`nearhost up` and `nearhost daemon` stop at start with:

```text
Error: Another Nearhost is already running (pid N).


Stop it:


  nearhost stop


Or see what it serves:


  nearhost status
```

`nearhost` opens the interface on the one that runs instead, and `nearhost -d` says it is already running.

Two Nearhosts would end each other’s ssh connections, so only one runs at a time, whatever `--config` file each is given. The pid is left out when it is not known. Run `nearhost status` to see what runs and what started it, and `nearhost stop` to stop it, whether it runs in the background, was started by a service, or is a `nearhost up` in another terminal. Then start Nearhost again. A service starts the background Nearhost at login, so after `nearhost stop` it stays stopped until you start it again or log in.

## Nearhost in the background does not start

`nearhost -d` prints `Error: Nearhost stopped while starting.` with the last lines of the core’s log, and exits 1. Those lines say why it stopped, often a port in use or a config error. On Linux, a copy of `nearhost` that may not use ports 80 and 443 stops like this:

```text
Error: Nearhost stopped while starting.


The end of /home/you/.config/nearhost/core.log:


  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z nearhost <version> starting (pid 4121, started by detached)
  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z error [port.needs-permission] HTTPS port 443 needs permission to bind.
  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   On Linux, a program may use ports below 1024, such as 443 for HTTPS and 80 for HTTP, only when it has been given permission. The install script gives it; a nearhost you build or copy yourself does not have it.
  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Fix: sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep '/home/you/go/bin/nearhost'
  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Then start Nearhost again. Do not run nearhost with sudo.
  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Run `nearhost doctor` to check this and the rest of what Nearhost needs.
  2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Cause: HTTPS port 443 needs permission to bind: listen tcp :443: bind: permission denied
```

If it prints `Error: Nearhost is still starting.`, it has not answered in 15 seconds and goes on starting: read the log it names. The log is `core.log` in the config folder. See [The core’s log](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/#the-cores-log).

## A service’s Nearhost cannot open links, reach ssh or Docker

A service does not run with your shell’s environment. `nearhost doctor` shows it as a warning on `core: browser`, `core: ssh agent` or `core: docker`, with the fix beside it, and on `service` when the service’s log folder is missing. Most come to running `nearhost service install` again from a shell where the thing works. See [What doctor says](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/#what-doctor-says).

## A project waits for the hosts file

Nearhost in the background never asks for your password, so a project whose names are missing from `/etc/hosts` stays stopped under `nearhost -d` or a service. `nearhost status` warns `Warning: <project> waits for the hosts file to be updated.` and the log says the hosts file needs updating, both with `nearhost hosts update` to run in a terminal, and `nearhost add` ends with `Warning: The running Nearhost serves the project once the hosts file is up to date.` and the same command.

Run `nearhost hosts update` in a terminal. It updates the block, then tells Nearhost, which starts the project. Opening `nearhost` does the same, asking for the password in its box. See [The hosts file](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/run-in-the-background/#the-hosts-file).

## nearhost up stops with nothing to serve

`nearhost up` prints its summary, then `Nothing can be served, so nearhost up is stopping.`, and exits 1. Every project failed to start, and none is waiting on a server that is still connecting. The summary names each project’s error. Fix those, then start `up` again. It stops the same way when every change to the hosts block is refused.

## Nearhost without a terminal

Bare `nearhost` prints `Error: The interface needs a terminal, and there is none here.`, with the commands below, and exits 1. It was started from a cron job, a script or a pipe, where there is no terminal for the interface. Run `nearhost -d` there to serve in the background, or `nearhost up` to serve in the foreground. To start Nearhost at login, use `nearhost service install`. On Windows the message adds `In Git Bash, run it through winpty or use Windows Terminal.`

`nearhost up` without a terminal cannot ask for your password. When the hosts block needs to change, it skips the change and prints, once:

```text
Warning: The hosts file needs sudo, and there is no terminal to ask in.


Run it once in a terminal, where sudo can ask for your password:


  nearhost up


Or serve without updating the hosts file:


  nearhost up --no-hosts
```

Run `nearhost up` once at a terminal so it can update the block, or add the names to the hosts file yourself and run with `--no-hosts`. Do not give Nearhost a passwordless `sudo` rule instead: its binary is usually writable by you, so the rule would give your account root.

`nearhost add` without a terminal cannot ask you to approve anything, so it adds nothing when the project asks for approval. `nearhost untrust --delete-key` refuses without a terminal unless you also pass `--yes`.

## Port 6327 already in use

Nearhost starts, serves every project and leaves out Nearhost’s page, and the log has the warning `port 6327 is in use; serving without Nearhost's page (pass --web-port to choose another)`. The reason after the port number varies: it may name the program holding the port, or read `needs permission to bind` or `is not available`. `nearhost doctor` warns about it. Another program holding the port is the usual cause. If it is another Nearhost, see [Another Nearhost is already running](#another-nearhost-is-already-running) and stop it. Otherwise pass `--web-port` with a free port, or `--web-port 0` to turn the page off. From Nearhost 0.8.0.

Without the page, an agent that asks to show a document is told `Nearhost's page isn't served: port 6327 wasn't available when Nearhost started`.

## nearhost.localhost does not resolve

A browser or a command-line tool cannot find `https://nearhost.localhost:6327`. Current macOS, Windows 11, Linux with systemd-resolved, Chrome and Firefox resolve `nearhost.localhost` themselves. An older system, or a resolver that does not, needs the name in the hosts file.

Open `https://localhost:6327` instead. It shows the page without the document list. A document link works there too, with `localhost` in place of `nearhost.localhost`.

Nearhost adds the line for `nearhost.localhost` each time it writes [its block](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/), and does not ask for your password for that line alone, so the line arrives when a project’s start next changes the block. With `--no-hosts`, or with no projects, Nearhost writes no block. Then add these lines to the hosts file yourself, outside Nearhost’s block:

```text
127.0.0.1 nearhost.localhost
::1 nearhost.localhost
```

## A loopback port is already bound

The project goes into `error`, naming the port and the program holding it on this machine. Its other routes still start.

Stop that program, or move the project’s dev server to another port and edit the route. For Vite that is `server.port` in the Vite config, or `VITE_PORT` under Laravel Sail. Then press `enter` on the project to start it again.

From Nearhost 0.7.0, on a laptop with the IPv6 loopback, a loopback forward answers on `[::1]` as well as `127.0.0.1`, so a program listening on either address holds the port. The usual one is a Vite dev server running on your laptop, which often listens on `::1` alone. To see every program on the port the error names, on both addresses, run this with that port in place of `<port>`:

```sh
lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen -LocalPort <port> | Select-Object LocalAddress, OwningProcess
```

On older versions, such a program could answer the browser in the forward’s place, so the page loaded your laptop’s scripts instead of the server’s. Run `nearhost update` to get the check.

On Windows, a program can bind a port that another already holds. Before each forward, Nearhost checks the port with exclusive use, so a program that holds it on `127.0.0.1` puts the project into `error` as above, rather than sharing the port with the forward.

## The password was cancelled

When the hosts block needs a project’s alias, Nearhost asks for your password in a box. If you cancel it, or get it wrong three times, the project stays `stopped`, its alias is not added to `/etc/hosts`, and Home’s `hosts` row shows it as missing.

On Windows, choosing No in the User Account Control prompt does the same.

Press `enter` on the project to try again. Or add the alias to `/etc/hosts` yourself and run Nearhost with `--no-hosts`. See [The hosts file](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/).

## The hosts file is read-only

On Windows, a hosts file with the read-only attribute stops the change after the User Account Control prompt, and nothing changes on disk:

```text
Error: <path> is read-only.


Clear the read-only attribute in an administrator terminal:


  attrib -r "<path>"


Then start the project again to retry.


Or serve without updating it:


  nearhost --no-hosts
```

Under `nearhost up`, the steps after `attrib` say to start `nearhost up` again, or to run `nearhost up --no-hosts`. For Nearhost in the background, they say to run `nearhost hosts update` from a terminal once the attribute is cleared.

Nearhost does not clear the attribute itself, since a read-only hosts file is often set on purpose. Run the `attrib` command in Windows Terminal opened as administrator, or add the names yourself and run Nearhost with `--no-hosts`. A read-only file whose block is already up to date needs no change, so it causes no error.

## Too many password prompts

`sudo` remembers your password for a few minutes, so Nearhost usually asks once for several changes. If it asks in the terminal instead of the box, `sudo` is set to ask every time.

On a Mac you can use Touch ID instead of typing it. See [First run](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/first-run/#touch-id-on-a-mac).

On Windows, every change to the hosts file shows a User Account Control prompt, because Windows does not remember the approval. Changes happen only when a project starts and its names are missing, so most starts ask for nothing.

## No root-owned sudo

`nearhost trust`, `nearhost untrust` and changes to `/etc/hosts` stop with `no root-owned sudo in /usr/bin, /bin, /usr/local/bin or /run/wrappers/bin`. From Nearhost 0.8.0, Nearhost runs only a `sudo` in one of those folders that root owns, so a `sudo` elsewhere on your `PATH` is never handed your password. Install sudo there, or run the command as root.

## The CA is not trusted

The proxy still runs, but browsers warn about the certificate. Home shows `local CA ● not trusted. Run nearhost trust`. Run:

```sh
nearhost trust
```

Firefox, and Chromium-based browsers on Linux, need `certutil` too. See [Install](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/). The CA’s expiry date turns amber 30 days before it runs out.

## Doctor warns about an old CA copy or a hosts block without IPv6

Both come from an upgrade, and both are warnings, not failures.

`old CA copy` means `~/.config/nearhost/caddy` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nearhost/caddy`), where Nearhost 0.7 and earlier kept the local CA, is still there beside the new folder in Nearhost’s data folder. It holds a copy of the CA’s private key. Check that `nearhost doctor` shows the CA as trusted, then delete the old folder. See [The local CA](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/#the-local-ca).

`hosts block` saying the block has no IPv6 (`::1`) entries means an older Nearhost wrote it. Run `nearhost hosts update` in a terminal, which rewrites the block with the `::1` lines and asks for your password.

## SSH keeps reconnecting

The server shows `reconnecting · attempt N · next in Ns`, and its projects show `degraded`. Caddy returns 502 meanwhile. Nearhost keeps trying by itself.

If it keeps failing, read the error on the server, then run `ssh <host>` in a terminal. When that connects, press `r` to reconnect now.

## Authentication failed

After three errors in a row that retrying cannot fix, such as `Permission denied` or a changed host key, Nearhost stops trying. The server shows `auth failed`, with the fix:

```sh
ssh <host>
```

Run it in a terminal and handle the host key, passphrase or `ssh-add` prompt. Then press `r`. On Home, `y` copies the command.

On Windows, a key with a passphrase needs the ssh-agent service running, and Windows installs it disabled. `nearhost doctor` shows its state. See [OpenSSH](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/#openssh) to start it. If the server is reached through a `ProxyJump` host named by an alias, Windows 11’s OpenSSH 9.5 does not resolve the alias: give `ProxyJump` the jump host’s address instead.

## Doctor warns about the ssh vendor

On Windows only, `nearhost doctor` shows `ssh vendor` as `warn`, with the path of the `ssh` it found. That `ssh` is not Microsoft’s OpenSSH in `%SystemRoot%\System32\OpenSSH` or `%ProgramFiles%\OpenSSH`. It is often Git for Windows’ ssh, which reads another config and agent, so forwards can fail in confusing ways. Put `%SystemRoot%\System32\OpenSSH` first on your `PATH`, then open a new terminal. The warning does not change doctor’s exit status.

## A server’s ssh configuration sets a forward

On Windows only, Nearhost stops trying to connect to the server, which shows `auth failed` with a message such as `mini's ssh configuration sets localforward, which Nearhost can't keep out of its own connections on this system`. The `Host` entry Nearhost uses for that server sets `LocalForward`, `RemoteForward`, `DynamicForward`, `ForkAfterAuthentication yes` or `ClearAllForwardings yes`. Move those lines to a `Host` entry Nearhost does not use, then press `r` on the server. See [SSH transport](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/ssh-transport/#on-windows).

## Agents unavailable on a server

The server’s sshd refuses the socket coding agents reach Nearhost on, usually because `sshd_config` sets `AllowStreamLocalForwarding no`. Set it to `yes`, reload sshd and press `r` on the server. `nearhost doctor` shows the same check. See [When agents cannot reach Nearhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/troubleshooting/).

## Agents on a server cannot reach a Windows laptop

The skill on the server says `this request has no valid Nearhost token: update the Nearhost skill on this machine`. A Windows laptop answers only requests that carry a token, which the skill sends with curl. The server needs curl 7.55 or later and a skill installed since Windows support. Run `npx skills add nearhost/nearhost -g` again on the server or, if you installed it as a Claude Code plugin, update the plugin from `/plugin`. See [Windows laptops](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/how-it-works/#windows-laptops).

## The control socket path is too long for ssh

A project on a server goes into `error` with `control socket path <path> is too long for ssh: it is N bytes and at most M bytes fit; the run directory <dir> is too long, set a shorter XDG_CONFIG_HOME`. ssh’s control socket lives in the `run` folder beside the config, and a long home or config path leaves no room for it. Set `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` to a shorter path, move the `nearhost` folder that holds your config there, then start Nearhost again.

## A server shows dropped

You pressed `c` on it, which holds its connection closed. Its projects wait. Press `c` again to connect it.

## Discovery found nothing

The routes step says no ports were found and asks for the web port. Enter it, or from the command line use `nearhost add --web <port>`. If the project uses Compose, Vite or Laravel Sail, trust the official presets so discovery can read them. See [Discovery](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/discovery/).

## Config file invalid

Nearhost does not start, and names the file and the problem, with the line for a YAML error. Under `nearhost -d` it shows as `Error: Nearhost stopped while starting.` with the end of the core’s log. A Nearhost already running keeps serving the last good config and says so in its log. Fix it in `~/.config/nearhost/config.yaml`, or `%APPDATA%\nearhost\config.yaml` on Windows. `nearhost doctor` reports the same without exiting. See [config.yaml](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/).

## Windows stops nearhost.exe from starting

Releases before 0.16.0 are not code signed. Where Smart App Control is on, Windows blocks them outright, with no Run anyway. Elsewhere, SmartScreen may stop one downloaded in a browser the first time it runs: choose More info, then Run anyway. Updating to 0.16.0 or later, which is signed, fixes both.

A signed copy from a zip downloaded in a browser can still meet SmartScreen on its first run while the certificate builds a reputation. It names ECS Software Consulting Ltd. as the publisher: choose More info, then Run anyway. If Windows blocks a copy that should be signed, check its signature as [Code signing](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/#code-signing) shows. A copy whose status is not `Valid` is not one Nearhost published.

## An update ran but the version did not change

`nearhost update` prints `Error: The update ran, but <path> is still <old>.`, with the command to install by hand, and exits 1. The update command succeeded, but the copy your next command runs, at `<path>`, did not start, printed no version, or is still the old version. Run the command it prints, then check with `nearhost --version`.

## The nearhost command is not found on Windows

The PowerShell installer adds its folder to your user `PATH`, and a terminal that was already open keeps its old `PATH`. Open a new terminal. If it is still not found, check that `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\nearhost`, or the folder you installed into, is in your user `PATH`.

# Clerk sign-in on a remote dev server

> Run a Clerk and Next.js app at a local HTTPS domain, such as https://local.myapp.com, with hot reload working, when the dev server runs on another machine.

Note

Needs Nearhost 0.6.0 or later, which lets a project’s main name be a domain that does not end in `.test`. A `.nearhostrc` that sets only that name, as below, needs 0.7.0 or later. Run `nearhost update` to get it. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

This guide gets Clerk sign-in working at `https://local.myapp.com` while your Next.js app runs on another machine. The worked example uses Clerk’s Next.js SDK, `@clerk/nextjs`, with a Clerk development instance. The Clerk and Nearhost steps are the same for any stack.

## The symptom

A Clerk development instance is relaxed about where your app runs. It is built for an app on `localhost`, and it does not ask you to register a domain or a callback URL. When the app runs on a server or a VM, though, `localhost` in your browser is not where the app is.

A tunnel such as ngrok gets the page on screen, but often not much more. The page loads at the ngrok address, and then hot reload never connects. Recent versions of Next.js block requests for its dev resources, hot reload included, from any host it was not told about, and logs `Blocked cross-origin request to Next.js dev resource` on the server. Anything the app builds from a URL in its environment, such as an app URL set to `http://localhost:3000`, still points there. And the app is on the public internet while you work on it.

Nearhost serves the remote app on your laptop at a name you choose, with a trusted certificate, over SSH. The browser sees one stable HTTPS origin, the page and its hot reload connection come from that origin, and nothing is public.

If you only need one app and plain HTTP, forwarding port 3000 with `ssh -L` gets you `http://localhost:3000`, which a development instance accepts. Nearhost is for when you want HTTPS, a name per project, or a setup shaped like production.

## Pick a name

Use a name under a domain you own, such as `local.myapp.com`. It needs no DNS record: Nearhost points it at your laptop through `/etc/hosts` while the project is enabled. When the project is disabled, the name resolves as it normally would.

A real-domain name is shaped like production, where Clerk’s Frontend API lives on a subdomain of your domain. Clerk’s documentation does not say which local names a development instance accepts beyond `localhost`, so this guide uses a domain you own.

If your production app already uses Clerk on `myapp.com`, use a name under a different domain you own, such as `local.myapp-dev.com`. Clerk’s docs say a separate setup will not work on the production domain, even on a separate subdomain. The examples below use `local.myapp.com`; swap in your name.

## Add the project

On the command line, give the name with `--alias`:

```sh
nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp' --alias local.myapp.com
```

```text
Added myapp on mini at https://local.myapp.com
Start it with `nearhost up`.
```

A name that does not end in `.test` needs your approval, because it can hide the real site. Typing it with `--alias` counts as approval.

To keep the name with the project, put it in a [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/) in the project’s root:

```yaml
version: 1
alias: local.myapp.com
```

Run `nearhost add` without `--alias`, and it asks before using the name, since you did not type it:

```text
$ nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp'
Approving a name puts it in your hosts file on this machine, has Nearhost's local CA sign a certificate for it, and makes your browser send that site's cookies to this project.
local.myapp.com on port 3000 (a real domain): approve? [y/N]
```

The port is the one `next dev` listens on, 3000 unless you changed it. Give it the `web` role. The Next.js dev server serves pages, assets and hot reload from that one port, so it needs no `loopback` route.

See [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-project/) for the rest of the add flow, and [Main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name) for how the name is approved and written to the hosts file.

## Set up Clerk

Use a development instance. It is the default for a new Clerk application, and its publishable key starts with `pk_test_`.

A development instance has nothing to register for the new name. There is no redirect URI or allowed domain to add. Its Frontend API lives at a Clerk address ending in `accounts.dev`, and your app talks to it across sites whatever the app’s own name is. Clerk’s own docs use development keys on preview domains such as `*.vercel.app` in the same way.

The **allowed origins** setting in Clerk’s API is for browser extensions and similar apps, not for a web app on a development instance. Leave it alone.

In the Clerk Dashboard, open the **API keys** page and copy the keys into the app’s `.env.local`:

```ini
NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_...
CLERK_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_...
```

These are the names `@clerk/nextjs` reads. If you set the app up with Clerk’s `init` command, they are already there.

## Set up the app

Recent versions of Next.js only let their dev resources be requested from `localhost` and from the hostname `next dev` was started with. A page at `https://local.myapp.com` asks for them from `local.myapp.com`, so add that name to `allowedDevOrigins` in `next.config.ts`:

```ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';


const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  allowedDevOrigins: ['local.myapp.com'],
};


export default nextConfig;
```

Write the hostname alone, without `https://` or a port. Restart `next dev` after changing it. The setting only affects development, so it is safe to commit.

Clerk’s middleware stays as the quickstart has it: `clerkMiddleware()` in `proxy.ts` on Next.js 16 and later, or `middleware.ts` on Next.js 15 and earlier, at the root of the project or in `src/`. If you pass it `authorizedParties`, add the new origin, with the scheme:

```ts
export default clerkMiddleware({
  authorizedParties: ['https://local.myapp.com'],
});
```

Nearhost’s proxy passes the `Host` header through unchanged and sets `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, so the app sees the name you browse to. If the app keeps its own public URL in an environment variable, such as `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`, set it to `https://local.myapp.com`.

On another stack the idea is the same. Clerk needs nothing new, and the dev server needs to accept the new hostname. Vite, for example, wants it in `server.allowedHosts`. See [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/).

## Check it works

Start the project with `nearhost up`, or from the interface, and open `https://local.myapp.com`. The page should load, Clerk’s sign-in button should appear, and signing in should bring you back signed in. Edit a component, and the page should update without a reload.

When it does not:

* **The page loads, but edits do not show until you reload.** Next.js is blocking hot reload from the new name. The server log shows `Blocked cross-origin request to Next.js dev resource` with the hostname it saw. Add that hostname to `allowedDevOrigins` and restart `next dev`.
* **You sign in, but come back signed out, or requests return 401.** If `clerkMiddleware()` has `authorizedParties`, check that it lists `https://local.myapp.com` exactly, with `https` and no port. Check too that the publishable and secret keys come from the same instance.
* **Links or redirects you build yourself go to `localhost`.** They come from an environment variable that still says `http://localhost:3000`. Change it to `https://local.myapp.com`.

## Testing with production keys

Clerk’s production keys only work on your production domain. Clerk describes a way round that for debugging, with a local subdomain over HTTPS on port 443, which Nearhost provides, but calls it strongly discouraged. See [using production keys in local development](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/troubleshooting/using-production-keys-in-development).

## When you still need ngrok

Nearhost is local-only. The name works in your browser on your laptop, and nowhere else. Use a public tunnel when:

* **Clerk sends webhooks.** Clerk sends them through Svix, from its servers, which cannot reach your laptop. Point the endpoint on the dashboard’s **Webhooks** page at a tunnel to the server, such as `https://<your-tunnel>/api/webhooks`. Clerk’s CLI also has `clerk webhooks listen --forward-to`, a relay that forwards deliveries to a local URL. Run it on the server, next to the app.
* **Someone outside needs the link.** A colleague or a client cannot open `local.myapp.com` from their machine.

You can run both: Nearhost for your own browser, and a tunnel just for the webhook endpoint.

Checked against

These pages, on 2026-10-19:

* [Clerk: Next.js quickstart](https://clerk.com/docs/nextjs/getting-started/quickstart)
* [Clerk: Express quickstart](https://clerk.com/docs/expressjs/getting-started/quickstart) (the API keys page)
* [Clerk: clerkMiddleware()](https://clerk.com/docs/reference/nextjs/clerk-middleware)
* [Clerk: environment variables](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/clerk-environment-variables)
* [Clerk: development and production instances](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/managing-environments)
* [Clerk: how Clerk works](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/how-clerk-works/overview)
* [Clerk: update an instance](https://clerk.com/docs/reference/backend/instance/update) (allowed origins)
* [Clerk: using production keys in local development](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/troubleshooting/using-production-keys-in-development)
* [Clerk: webhooks overview](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/webhooks/overview) and [syncing data with webhooks](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/webhooks/syncing)
* [Clerk changelog: CLI webhooks](https://clerk.com/changelog/2026-07-09-clerk-cli-webhooks-and-impersonate)
* [Next.js: allowedDevOrigins](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/allowedDevOrigins)

If a step no longer matches, please [open an issue](https://github.com/nearhost/landing/issues).

# Cognito sign-in on a remote dev server

> Give an Amazon Cognito app client an HTTPS callback URL in local dev, such as https://local.myapp.com/auth/cognito/callback, when the dev server runs on another machine.

Note

Needs Nearhost 0.6.0 or later, which lets a project’s main name be a domain that does not end in `.test`. A `.nearhostrc` that sets only that name, as below, needs 0.7.0 or later. Run `nearhost update` to get it. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

This guide gets Amazon Cognito sign-in working at `https://local.myapp.com` while your Laravel app runs on another machine. The worked example uses Laravel Socialite with the community `socialiteproviders/cognito` provider and Cognito’s managed login pages. The Cognito and Nearhost steps are the same for any stack.

## The symptom

Cognito sends the browser back to your app at a callback URL you list on the app client. Every callback URL has to use HTTPS, with one exception: `http://localhost`, which Cognito allows for testing. When the app runs on your laptop, that exception is all you need.

When the app runs on a server or a VM, `localhost` in your browser is not where the app is. You can forward a port with `ssh -L` and use `http://localhost:8080`, and for one app that works. It stops being enough when:

* **You run more than one app.** Browsers do not separate cookies by port, so two apps on `localhost` can overwrite each other’s session cookies.
* **The app shares cookies across subdomains.** An app that sets cookies for `myapp.com`, or talks to an API on another subdomain, only behaves as it does on staging when it runs under that domain.
* **You want local dev to match staging.** Staging’s callback is HTTPS on your domain. With `http://localhost`, the scheme, the host and the cookie rules all differ from what you deploy.
* **The page uses browser APIs that need a secure context**, such as service workers or the clipboard. Browsers count `http://localhost` as secure, so these work there, but on any other name, such as the server’s own address, they need HTTPS.

A tunnel such as ngrok gives you HTTPS, but each new tunnel name is one more callback URL to add, and the app still builds its links from its own idea of where it lives. It also puts the app on the public internet while you work on it.

Nearhost serves the remote app on your laptop at a name you choose, with a trusted certificate, over SSH. The browser sees one stable HTTPS origin, and that is the origin you list on the Cognito app client.

## Pick a name

Use a name under a domain you own, such as `local.myapp.com`. It needs no DNS record: Nearhost points it at your laptop through `/etc/hosts` while the project is enabled. When the project is disabled, the name resolves as it normally would.

A real-domain name keeps the callback URL shaped like the one on staging and in production. Cognito’s documentation asks for HTTPS but does not say whether it accepts `.test` names, so this guide uses a domain you own.

## Add the project

On the command line, give the name with `--alias`:

```sh
nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp' --alias local.myapp.com
```

```text
Added myapp on mini at https://local.myapp.com
Start it with `nearhost up`.
```

A name that does not end in `.test` needs your approval, because it can hide the real site. Typing it with `--alias` counts as approval.

To keep the name with the project, put it in a [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/) in the project’s root:

```yaml
version: 1
alias: local.myapp.com
```

Run `nearhost add` without `--alias`, and it asks before using the name, since you did not type it:

```text
$ nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp'
Approving a name puts it in your hosts file on this machine, has Nearhost's local CA sign a certificate for it, and makes your browser send that site's cookies to this project.
local.myapp.com on port 8080 (a real domain): approve? [y/N]
```

See [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-project/) for the rest of the add flow, and [Main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name) for how the name is approved and written to the hosts file.

## Set up Cognito

Use a user pool for development, separate from production’s. Its users, app clients and settings are its own.

1. The pool needs a domain for its sign-in pages. In the [Amazon Cognito console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cognito/home), open the user pool, then **Domain** under **Branding**. If there is no domain, choose **Actions**, then **Create Cognito domain**, and pick a prefix. The domain looks like `https://myapp-dev.auth.eu-west-2.amazoncognito.com`. Either branding version, **Managed login** or **Hosted UI (classic)**, works for this guide.
2. Open **App clients** and create an app client with the application type **Traditional web application**. That type gives the client a secret, which Socialite needs. You cannot add a secret to an existing client later, so if yours has none, create a new one. When it asks for a **Return URL**, enter `https://local.myapp.com/auth/cognito/callback`.
3. Open the app client, then the **Login pages** tab. Under **Managed login pages configuration**, choose **Edit**.
4. Check that **Allowed callback URLs** has `https://local.myapp.com/auth/cognito/callback`. It must match the URL your app sends exactly: `https`, the host, the path, no trailing slash.
5. Add `https://local.myapp.com/` to **Allowed sign-out URLs**. Cognito only sends people back after sign-out to a URL on this list.
6. Under **Identity providers**, keep the user pool’s own sign-in, or whichever providers your users sign in with. Under **OAuth grant types**, choose **Authorization code grant**. Under **OpenID Connect scopes**, choose `openid`, `email` and `profile`. Save the changes.

Then set `APP_URL` in the app’s `.env` to the new name, and copy the domain and the app client’s ID and secret below it. The last two lines build on `APP_URL`, so they have to come after it:

```ini
APP_URL=https://local.myapp.com


COGNITO_HOST=https://myapp-dev.auth.eu-west-2.amazoncognito.com
COGNITO_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
COGNITO_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
COGNITO_CALLBACK_URL="${APP_URL}/auth/cognito/callback"
COGNITO_SIGN_OUT_URL="${APP_URL}/"
```

These are the names in the provider’s README. `COGNITO_HOST` is the full domain with `https://` and no trailing slash.

## Set up the app

Install the provider, which brings in Socialite:

```sh
composer require socialiteproviders/cognito
```

Add the Cognito entry to `config/services.php`:

```php
'cognito' => [
    'host' => env('COGNITO_HOST'),
    'client_id' => env('COGNITO_CLIENT_ID'),
    'client_secret' => env('COGNITO_CLIENT_SECRET'),
    'redirect' => env('COGNITO_CALLBACK_URL'),
    'logout_uri' => env('COGNITO_SIGN_OUT_URL'),
],
```

The README’s version also has a `scope` line. The provider does not read it, so this guide sets scopes in code instead.

Register the provider in the `boot` method of `app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php` (Laravel 11 and later):

```php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Event;
use SocialiteProviders\Cognito\Provider;
use SocialiteProviders\Manager\SocialiteWasCalled;


public function boot(): void
{
    Event::listen(function (SocialiteWasCalled $event) {
        $event->extendSocialite('cognito', Provider::class);
    });
}
```

Then add the routes to `routes/web.php`. The provider asks for `openid` and `profile` by default; `scopes()` adds `email` to them:

```php
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Auth;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;
use Laravel\Socialite\Socialite;


Route::get('/auth/cognito/redirect', function () {
    return Socialite::driver('cognito')->scopes(['email'])->redirect();
});


Route::get('/auth/cognito/callback', function () {
    $cognitoUser = Socialite::driver('cognito')->user();


    // Find or create your user from $cognitoUser, then Auth::login($user).


    return redirect('/dashboard');
});


Route::post('/auth/cognito/logout', function (Request $request) {
    Auth::logout();


    $request->session()->invalidate();
    $request->session()->regenerateToken();


    return redirect(Socialite::driver('cognito')->logoutCognitoUser());
});
```

`logoutCognitoUser()` sends the browser to Cognito’s sign-out page with `COGNITO_SIGN_OUT_URL`, and Cognito sends it back there.

With `APP_URL` set to `https://local.myapp.com`, the callback and sign-out URLs follow it. If you have cached the config, run `php artisan config:clear`.

Nearhost’s proxy ends HTTPS on your laptop and passes plain HTTP to the server, with `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. Laravel ignores that header until it trusts the proxy, so it thinks the request was `http://`. The callback is unaffected while `COGNITO_CALLBACK_URL` is a full URL, because Socialite uses it as it is. A path such as `/auth/cognito/callback` would be built from the request instead, as `http://`, and Cognito would refuse it. What goes wrong either way is everything Laravel builds from the request: `route()` and `url()` links, the redirect to `/dashboard` after sign-in, and `asset()` URLs.

The fix is one line in the `withMiddleware` closure in `bootstrap/app.php`:

```php
$middleware->trustProxies(at: '*');
```

The [WorkOS guide](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/#set-up-the-app) explains it, and what to list instead of `'*'` if the file also runs in production behind a known load balancer.

If the page loads its scripts from Vite at `http://localhost:5173`, that port needs a `loopback` route so your browser can reach it. See [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/). If `public/hot` says `http://[::1]:5173` instead, the forward answers there too from Nearhost 0.7.0. With an older Nearhost, see [Vite on `[::1]`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/#vite-on-1).

On another stack the idea is the same. Use any OpenID Connect client with the pool’s domain and the app client’s ID and secret. Set the app’s public URL and its callback URL to `https://local.myapp.com`, and tell the framework to trust `X-Forwarded-Proto` from the proxy, so it builds `https://` links and the callback URL it sends to Cognito matches the one you listed.

## Check it works

Start the project with `nearhost up`, or from the interface, and open `https://local.myapp.com/auth/cognito/redirect`. You should land on Cognito’s sign-in page, and after signing in come back to `https://local.myapp.com/auth/cognito/callback` and on to the dashboard.

When it does not:

* **Cognito shows an error page instead of the sign-in page.** Usually the callback URL your app sent is not in **Allowed callback URLs** on the app client whose ID you use. Compare them character by character: `https`, the host, `/auth/cognito/callback`, no trailing slash. Check that `COGNITO_CALLBACK_URL` and `APP_URL` are what you expect.
* **You come back with `error=invalid_scope` in the address.** The app asked for a scope the app client does not allow. Add `openid`, `email` and `profile` under **OpenID Connect scopes**, or ask for fewer.
* **The callback fails with `InvalidStateException`.** Socialite keeps a state value in the session when you start sign-in, and refuses the callback when the session does not come back with it. Start sign-in at `https://local.myapp.com`, not at another address for the same app, and leave `SESSION_DOMAIN` unset (`null`) or set it to `local.myapp.com`. A cookie set for another domain never reaches this one.
* **Links, the redirect after sign-in, or asset URLs use `http://`.** Laravel does not trust the proxy yet. Add `trustProxies` as above. Nearhost redirects `http://` to HTTPS, so a link may still seem to work, but `http://` scripts and styles on an HTTPS page are blocked as mixed content. Look for those warnings in the console.
* **Sign-out does not come back to `https://local.myapp.com/`.** Cognito only redirects to a URL in **Allowed sign-out URLs**. Check that `COGNITO_SIGN_OUT_URL` is on that list exactly, trailing slash included.

## When you still need ngrok

Nearhost is local-only. The name works in your browser on your laptop, and nowhere else.

Cognito itself does not need to reach your app. The browser carries the sign-in there and back, and your server calls Cognito, not the other way round. Cognito’s hooks into sign-up and sign-in are Lambda triggers, which run in AWS, not webhooks sent to your app. Use a public tunnel when:

* **Something in AWS calls your app.** A Lambda trigger, or anything else running in AWS, cannot reach your laptop or your dev server. If a trigger calls your app’s API, point it at a tunnel.
* **Someone outside needs the link.** A colleague or a client cannot open `local.myapp.com` from their machine.

You can run both: Nearhost for your own browser, and a tunnel just for whatever AWS has to call.

Checked against

These pages, on 2026-10-19:

* [socialiteproviders/cognito README](https://github.com/SocialiteProviders/Providers/blob/master/src/Cognito/README.md) and [provider source](https://github.com/SocialiteProviders/Providers/blob/master/src/Cognito/Provider.php)
* [SocialiteProviders Manager: how provider config is read](https://github.com/SocialiteProviders/Manager/blob/master/src/Helpers/ConfigRetriever.php) and [how the redirect URL is formatted](https://github.com/SocialiteProviders/Manager/blob/master/src/Config.php)
* [Laravel Socialite](https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/socialite)
* [Laravel HTTP requests: configuring trusted proxies](https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/requests#configuring-trusted-proxies)
* [Amazon Cognito: application-specific settings with app clients](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/user-pool-settings-client-apps.html)
* [Amazon Cognito: user pool managed login](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-managed-login.html)
