* [Amazon Cognito: the logout endpoint](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/logout-endpoint.html)
* [Amazon Cognito: OIDC identity providers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-oidc-idp.html) (the **Login pages** tab)
* [Amazon Cognito: Lambda triggers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-working-with-lambda-triggers.html)

If a step no longer matches, please [open an issue](https://github.com/nearhost/landing/issues).

# Callbacks from Docker containers to a local HTTPS domain

> Let a Docker Compose service, such as a queue worker or a LocalStack job, call your app at its Nearhost HTTPS name on this machine.

Note

Needs Nearhost 0.6.0 or later, which can serve a project to Docker containers. Run `nearhost update` to get it. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

A service in your Compose file often calls the app back: a queue worker reports a finished job, or a LocalStack job delivers an event to a webhook. Point it at the app’s Nearhost name, such as `https://api.local.example.com/webhooks/jobs`, and the call fails, even though the same URL works in your browser.

Three things stand between the container and Nearhost. The container cannot find the host, it does not trust the local certificate authority, and on Linux Nearhost does not let it in. The fixes go in the project’s files, which you commit. Each developer then sets one variable, for the certificate’s path, and approves the opt-in on their own machine.

This works only for a project on this machine. A container on an SSH server cannot reach the proxy on your laptop.

## The example

The project is named `shop`, and its worker is a Node service. Its app listens on port 8000 and is served at `api.local.example.com`. Its `.nearhostrc`:

```yaml
version: 1
routes:
  - port: ${APP_PORT:-8000}
    label: app
    hosts: [api.local.example.com]
docker_clients: true
```

`hosts` serves the route at a name of your own, besides the project’s main name. See [Multi-host projects](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/multi-host-projects/). `docker_clients` is explained in [Being let in](#being-let-in). Its Compose file runs the app and a worker that calls it:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - '${APP_PORT:-8000}:8000'
  worker:
    build: .
    command: ['./worker']
    environment:
      WEBHOOK_URL: https://api.local.example.com/webhooks/jobs
```

Nothing here depends on the stack. Any service that reads a URL naming a host Nearhost serves, from its `environment`, its `env_file` files, or the project’s `.env` or `.env.local` when it mounts the project directory, has the same three problems.

## Reaching the host

Nearhost puts `api.local.example.com` in your machine’s [hosts file](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/), pointing at loopback. A container does not read that file, and inside it loopback is the container itself. So the name resolves to nothing, to the public internet, or, where DNS points it at 127.0.0.1, back to the container.

Map the name to the host with `extra_hosts`. `host-gateway` is Docker’s name for the host’s address as seen from a container:

```yaml
services:
  worker:
    extra_hosts:
      - 'api.local.example.com:host-gateway'
```

List every name the service calls. `nearhost doctor` reports a service that calls a name without this mapping, as `docker.host-gateway`, and its fix is this snippet for the names it found.

## Trusting the local CA

Nearhost’s certificates are signed by its own local certificate authority. Your system trusts it, but a container has its own trust store, so the call fails with a certificate error.

Mount the root certificate into the container and point the service at it. The certificate is at `pki/authorities/local/root.crt` under Nearhost’s `caddy` folder, which is `~/Library/Application Support/nearhost/caddy` on macOS, `~/.local/share/nearhost/caddy` on Linux and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nearhost\caddy` on Windows, or `$XDG_DATA_HOME/nearhost/caddy` on any of them when that is set to an absolute path. `nearhost doctor` prints the path on your machine. Earlier versions kept it under `~/.config/nearhost/caddy`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nearhost/caddy` when that variable was set. Nearhost 0.8.0 moves that folder the first time it runs while no other Nearhost is running. After that, a `NEARHOST_CA_CERT` set for an earlier version points at a file that is gone, so set it to the new path, which `nearhost doctor` prints. Mount only `root.crt`, never the folder: the key is beside it. The doctor’s snippet, for a Node service:

```yaml
services:
  worker:
    environment:
      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS: /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/nearhost.crt
    volumes:
      - "${NEARHOST_CA_CERT:?set NEARHOST_CA_CERT to Nearhost's root certificate}:/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/nearhost.crt:ro"
```

Each developer sets `NEARHOST_CA_CERT` to the certificate’s path in their shell profile, or in `.env` when the project does not commit `.env`, so the Compose file holds no one’s path. Compose reads only `.env` and the shell, not `.env.local`. Until the variable is set, every `docker compose` command that reads this Compose file stops with `set NEARHOST_CA_CERT to Nearhost's root certificate`, so nobody runs the service without the certificate by mistake.

`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` adds the certificate to Node’s own. `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `AWS_CA_BUNDLE` and `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` replace the default bundle instead, so point them at a bundle that includes the certificate, or have the image run `update-ca-certificates`.

`nearhost doctor` reports a service that calls a name Nearhost serves and does not trust the certificate, as `docker.ca`. A service that sets `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `AWS_CA_BUNDLE`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` or `CURL_CA_BUNDLE`, or mounts the certificate’s path, counts as set up. The doctor checks only that the setting is there, not that the runtime trusts the certificate, so a worker in another language needs the setting its runtime reads.

## Being let in

Nearhost serves its projects only to this machine. A request from anywhere else is dropped without an answer. On Linux, a container’s request comes from its address on a Docker network, not from loopback, so Nearhost drops it.

`docker_clients: true` in the project’s [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#docker-clients) serves the project to the networks the Docker daemon has on this machine as well. Nearhost asks Docker for them when the project starts, and again every 30 seconds while it runs, so a network Compose creates later is let in too. It finds Docker through `DOCKER_HOST` or the current docker context, then the usual sockets of Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Rancher Desktop, Colima and Podman. From Nearhost 0.8.0. Until Docker first answers, it accepts requests from `172.16.0.0/12`, the private block most of Docker’s default networks come from, which can also take in other machines on that block your machine can reach. The project’s log says which networks it accepts requests from.

* It works only for a project on this machine. On a project on a server, the file is an error.
* It always needs your approval, as a real domain does. See [Approval](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#approval).
* Other projects stay loopback-only. Only the project that opts in is served to Docker’s networks.

With no `.nearhostrc` yet, `nearhost export` writes one from the project’s current setup, and you add the line to it.

Docker Desktop on macOS and on Windows already delivers container requests from 127.0.0.1, so this matters on Linux. On a Mac or a Windows PC, the project is reached without it. Keep it in a committed `.nearhostrc` if anyone on the team uses Linux.

`nearhost doctor` reports a project whose containers call a name it serves without the opt-in, as `docker.clients`. It is a warning on Linux, and only a note on macOS and Windows.

## The finished Compose file

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - '${APP_PORT:-8000}:8000'
  worker:
    build: .
    command: ['./worker']
    environment:
      WEBHOOK_URL: https://api.local.example.com/webhooks/jobs
      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS: /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/nearhost.crt
    extra_hosts:
      - 'api.local.example.com:host-gateway'
    volumes:
      - "${NEARHOST_CA_CERT:?set NEARHOST_CA_CERT to Nearhost's root certificate}:/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/nearhost.crt:ro"
```

Approve `api.local.example.com` and `docker_clients` when you add the project, or when Nearhost asks after the file changes. See [Approval](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/#approval). Then restart the worker with `docker compose up -d worker`.

## Check it works

Run `nearhost doctor`. After the machine checks, it lists what it finds in each enabled project. For the example before any of the fixes, with `docker_clients` not yet in its `.nearhostrc`, on a Mac, these are the first lines of its three findings, without their fixes:

```text
warn  shop             worker calls a name Nearhost serves, and does not trust Nearhost's root certificate
warn  shop             worker uses api.local.example.com, which a container resolves to itself or to the public internet, not to Nearhost
info  shop             a container calls a name Nearhost serves, and Nearhost does not accept requests from Docker's network
```

Under each, a `fix:` line says what to do, followed by the snippet to paste. These are `docker.ca`, `docker.host-gateway` and `docker.clients`, and `nearhost doctor --json` gives each finding’s `id`. On Linux the last one is a warning too. When the project is fixed, none of them is shown. See [nearhost doctor](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-doctor).

The doctor only reads the files. To see the call work, run the worker and watch the request arrive in Nearhost.

## When a public tunnel is still the right tool

This is for services you run yourself, on this machine. A webhook from a real provider, such as a payment or source control service, comes from its servers, which cannot reach your laptop. Use a public tunnel, such as ngrok, for that. See [ngrok loads the page, but assets point at localhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/ngrok-assets-on-localhost/).

# Forward several ports over SSH without retyping -L

> Ways to reach a remote app, its asset server and its other ports from your laptop over SSH, from stacked -L flags to forwards added to a running connection, and what each leaves for you to do.

A web project on a remote machine rarely uses one port. There is the app, the asset dev server, perhaps a mail catcher or a queue dashboard, and the next project wants the same set again. Typing one `-L` flag per port works until the connection drops, a port changes, or a second project needs a port the first one already holds.

## Stack the flags on one connection

One `ssh` command takes as many `-L` flags as you need. `-N` keeps it to forwarding, with no remote shell:

```sh
ssh -N -L 8000:localhost:8000 -L 5173:localhost:5173 -L 8025:localhost:8025 myserver
```

Each flag reads `local port:host:remote port`, and the host is resolved on the server, so `localhost` means the server itself. Your laptop listens on loopback only, unless you set `GatewayPorts`.

## Put them in your SSH config

`LocalForward` lines in `~/.ssh/config` set the same forwards whenever you connect:

```plaintext
Host myserver
  LocalForward 8000 localhost:8000
  LocalForward 5173 localhost:5173
  LocalForward 8025 localhost:8025
  ExitOnForwardFailure yes
  ServerAliveInterval 15
```

`ExitOnForwardFailure` makes `ssh` stop when a port is taken on your laptop, rather than connect without that forward. `ServerAliveInterval` makes a dead connection end, after about 45 seconds with the default `ServerAliveCountMax` of 3, instead of hanging. The catch: every interactive `ssh myserver` now tries the same ports, and the second one fails while the first is open. A separate `Host` alias just for the forwards avoids that.

## Add forwards to a running connection

With connection sharing, one master connection carries every session to a server, and `ssh -O` changes its forwards while it runs:

```plaintext
Host myserver
  ControlMaster auto
  ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
  ControlPersist 10m
```

```sh
ssh -O forward -L 5173:localhost:5173 myserver   # add a forward
ssh -O cancel -L 5173:localhost:5173 myserver    # remove it
```

No reconnect, and no restart of the forwards already open. Nothing re-adds them if the master exits, though.

## Use one SOCKS proxy instead

`ssh -N -D 1080 myserver` opens a SOCKS proxy, and a browser set to use it reaches every port on the server’s network. But Chrome and Firefox send `localhost` straight to your own machine, never through the proxy, so a dev server that listens only on the server’s loopback stays out of reach. It also proxies every site the browser opens, unless you set it per profile.

## What every plain-SSH option leaves to you

* **Reconnecting.** When the connection drops, the forwards go with it. `autossh` or a shell loop brings back a fixed set.
* **Port clashes.** Two projects that both use 5173 cannot both forward it to 5173 on your laptop. Change one project’s port, or forward it to another local port where the page does not hard-code it.
* **The address.** Each app is `http://localhost:<port>`. Cookies ignore the port, so every project shares one cookie jar and signing in to one can sign you out of another, and an OAuth callback or cookie domain set up for a real name does not match. See [HTTPS on a local dev domain](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/https-on-a-local-dev-domain/).

## How Nearhost does it

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

Nearhost uses the same OpenSSH mechanism as above: one supervised master per server, with forwards added and cancelled with `-O forward` and `-O cancel` as projects start and stop. On top of that:

* **It finds the ports.** It reads them from the project’s `.env`, and presets add Docker Compose, Vite and Laravel Sail. You choose which port is the web app, which need the same port on your laptop, and which to ignore.
* **It reconnects.** If the master exits, Nearhost starts it again with backoff and puts every forward back before the server shows as connected.
* **It warns about clashes** before they happen, and suggests a free port when the port comes from a variable.
* **It gives each project a name.** The web port is served at a trusted `https://myapp.test`, so you stop tracking which port is which project.

See [SSH transport](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/ssh-transport/) for the exact commands it runs, and [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/) for how ports become routes.

Checked against

These, on 2026-10-20:

* [OpenSSH: ssh(1)](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh), for `-L`, `-N`, `-D` and `-O`
* [OpenSSH: ssh_config(5)](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config), for `LocalForward`, `GatewayPorts`, `ExitOnForwardFailure`, `ServerAliveInterval` and the `Control*` options
* [Chromium: proxy support](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/net/docs/proxy.md), for the implicit `localhost` bypass

If something here no longer matches, please [open an issue](https://github.com/nearhost/landing/issues).

# HTTPS on a local dev domain

> Serve local development at a trusted HTTPS name, such as myapp.test or local.myapp.com, so secure-context browser APIs and Secure cookies work, and choose which kind of name to use.

Note

Names under your own domain, such as `local.myapp.com`, need Nearhost 0.6.0 or later. `.test` names work on every version. Run `nearhost update` to get the latest. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

Some things in local development only work over HTTPS. On your laptop you rarely notice, because browsers treat `http://localhost` as secure. Once you browse to the dev server by its address or by a name instead of `localhost`, which is usual when it runs on another machine, plain HTTP stops being enough.

## What needs HTTPS

Browsers give some features only to a secure context: a page served over HTTPS, or from `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or a `*.localhost` name. On `http://192.168.1.20:8080` or `http://myapp.test`, these are missing:

* **Service workers.** `navigator.serviceWorker` is undefined, so offline support and push notifications cannot be tested.
* **The clipboard.** `navigator.clipboard` is undefined, so copy buttons fail.
* **Web Crypto.** `crypto.subtle` is undefined, which breaks libraries that hash or sign in the browser.
* **The camera and microphone.** `navigator.mediaDevices` is undefined.
* **Passkeys and geolocation.** WebAuthn and the Geolocation API refuse to run.

Cookies have the same rule. Browsers do not set a cookie marked `Secure` over plain HTTP. Chrome and Firefox make an exception for `localhost`, but Safari does not, so test secure cookies over HTTPS. That rules out `SameSite=None` cookies, which must be `Secure`, and the `__Host-` and `__Secure-` cookie prefixes. If your app sets these in production, it behaves differently in development without HTTPS.

A self-signed certificate is not a fix. The browser warns on every visit, and some features, such as service workers, refuse to load over a certificate it does not trust.

## Choosing a name

You need a name the browser resolves to the dev server, and a certificate for it that the browser trusts.

**A `.test` name, such as `myapp.test`.** `.test` is reserved for testing and never exists on the public internet, so it cannot clash with a real site. It is Nearhost’s default, and works with no setup. Some third-party services, such as sign-in providers, may not accept a `.test` callback, or do not say whether they do.

**A name under your own domain, such as `local.myapp.com`.** It is shaped like production, so cookie scoping, cross-subdomain requests and provider settings behave as they do on staging. It needs no DNS record. Two things to know:

* Cookies your production site sets for the whole domain, with `Domain=myapp.com`, are sent to `local.myapp.com` too, if your browser has them.
* Nearhost writes the name to `/etc/hosts` only while the project is enabled. Disable the project, and the name reaches the real site again, if there is one. See [Main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name).

Avoid `.dev`, which is a real top-level domain whose every name browsers force to HTTPS, and `.local`, which macOS and many Linux systems resolve with multicast DNS, and which can be slow to look up.

## Setting it up

If the dev server runs on your laptop, a tool such as mkcert and a line in `/etc/hosts` are enough. You make a local certificate authority, trust it, issue a certificate for the name, and point the dev server at it.

If the dev server runs on another machine, Nearhost does all of this on your laptop. It creates a local certificate authority the first time it starts, which you trust once with your password, in the interface or with `nearhost trust`, and it issues a certificate for each project’s name. Its proxy serves the name over HTTPS and forwards to the dev server over SSH. See [TLS and the proxy](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/).

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

Add the project with the name you chose:

```sh
nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp' --alias local.myapp.com
```

Leave out `--alias` to use `myapp.test`. Then tell the app it lives at the HTTPS name: set its public URL, such as `APP_URL`, and trust the proxy’s `X-Forwarded-Proto` header. The [WorkOS guide](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/#set-up-the-app) shows both for Laravel. Single-port dev servers also need the name allowed: `allowedDevOrigins` in Next.js, `server.allowedHosts` in Vite. See [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/).

## Sign-in providers

Sign-in providers are the most common reason to want a real HTTPS name. The guides set one up end to end:

* [WorkOS sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/)
* [Clerk sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/clerk-sign-in/)
* [Cognito sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/cognito-sign-in/)

If the callback is what fails, see [SSO callback fails on a remote dev server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/sso-callback-on-a-remote-dev-server/).

## When ngrok is still the right tool

A Nearhost name only works on your laptop. Its proxy answers no other machine. Use a public tunnel, such as ngrok, when:

* **Another device needs the page,** such as your phone, to test a camera or a service worker on mobile.
* **Someone outside needs the link,** such as a colleague or a client.
* **A service sends webhooks,** from servers that cannot reach your laptop.

# ngrok loads the page, but assets point at localhost

> Why a dev site behind ngrok still loads its scripts, redirects or hot reload from localhost or http://, how to patch each one, and how to skip the tunnel when the dev server runs on another machine.

You put your dev server behind ngrok and open the tunnel’s address. The HTML arrives, and then something still points somewhere else: the scripts and styles try `localhost`, a redirect takes you to `http://localhost:8000`, or the page never updates when you edit a file. Sometimes the dev server refuses the request outright.

The tunnel did its job. It forwarded the request. The problem is that the page and the dev server still describe themselves with the addresses in their own config, and those addresses mean nothing in the browser that opened the tunnel.

## Why it happens

Three different things build URLs, and each one gets it wrong in its own way.

### The asset dev server

A backend framework that uses Vite renders the HTML itself, and the page loads its scripts from the Vite dev server on a separate port. In Laravel, the `@vite` directive reads the `public/hot` file, which `laravel-vite-plugin` writes when `npm run dev` starts. That file holds the dev server’s own address, such as `http://localhost:5173` under Sail or `http://[::1]:5173` elsewhere, and every script tag on the page points there.

Your browser resolves that address on your laptop. If the dev server runs on another machine, nothing listens there, so scripts and styles fail to load and hot reload never connects. Even where something does answer, the Vite dev server only allows requests from the origins `laravel-vite-plugin` lists: `localhost`, `*.test`, `*.localhost` and your `APP_URL`. An ngrok address is none of them unless you put it in `APP_URL`.

Rails, Django and other backends that pair with Vite work the same way.

### Links and redirects

Most frameworks build absolute URLs from the request, or from a URL in their config.

* **From the request.** ngrok ends HTTPS at its edge and forwards to your dev server, adding `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. A framework that does not trust the proxy ignores that header and builds `http://` links and redirects. If you started ngrok with `--host-header=rewrite`, the app sees the local address’s hostname, usually `localhost`, and builds links to that.
* **From config.** Anything built from `APP_URL` or a similar setting, such as emails, queued jobs, or an OAuth redirect URI, uses whatever that setting says, usually `http://localhost:8000`.

### Host checks in single-port dev servers

Next.js and plain Vite serve pages, assets and hot reload from one port, so their assets use relative paths. What gets in the way is the dev server’s host check:

* **Next.js** serves the page, assets included. Recent versions block its dev resources, hot reload included, from hostnames it was not told about, and log `Blocked cross-origin request to Next.js dev resource` on the server. The page loads, but edits never show.
* **Vite** refuses every request whose `Host` it does not recognise, the page included, and answers with `Blocked request. This host ("…") is not allowed.`, naming the host. Nothing loads until the host is in `server.allowedHosts`.

## Patching it with ngrok

Each patch fixes one of the three.

* **Assets.** Stop the dev server, which deletes `public/hot`, and run `npm run build`. Laravel then serves the built files from the app’s own origin. You lose hot reload. On other backends, build the assets or tunnel the Vite port. Keeping hot reload means a second tunnel for port 5173, with Vite told to advertise that tunnel’s address through `server.origin` and `server.hmr`, and that tunnel’s hostname added to `server.allowedHosts`. Once `server.origin` is set, Laravel’s Vite plugin allows only that origin through CORS, so also set `server.cors.origin` to the app tunnel’s address, or the browser blocks the scripts.
* **Links and redirects.** Set `APP_URL` to the tunnel’s address and make the framework trust the proxy. The [WorkOS guide](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/#set-up-the-app) shows the one-line `trustProxies` change for Laravel. If the tunnel name changes each time you start it, so does `APP_URL`.
* **Host checks.** Add the tunnel’s hostname to `allowedDevOrigins` in `next.config.ts`, or to `server.allowedHosts` in Vite’s config.

## How Nearhost avoids it

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

When the dev server runs on another machine, Nearhost serves it on your laptop at a name such as `https://myapp.test`, with a trusted certificate, over SSH. Nothing is public, and the name stays the same every time.

* **Assets.** A `loopback` route forwards the Vite port, so `http://localhost:5173` in your browser reaches port 5173 on the remote machine. `.test` names are already on the Vite dev server’s allowed origins. Under Laravel Sail, Nearhost proposes the route for you. See [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/).
* **Links and redirects.** The proxy passes the `Host` header through unchanged and sets `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. Set `APP_URL` to the Nearhost name once, and trust the proxy as above.
* **Host checks.** Add the Nearhost name to `allowedDevOrigins` or `server.allowedHosts` once. It does not change between runs.

### Vite on the IPv6 loopback address

A Vite dev server that listens on `::1` makes `laravel-vite-plugin` write `http://[::1]:5173` to `public/hot`. A loopback forward answers on both `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`, so that works as it is. This needs Nearhost 0.7.0 or later and a laptop with the IPv6 loopback, which every Mac and almost every Linux machine has. Otherwise, see [Vite on `[::1]`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/#vite-on-1).

## The guides

The sign-in guides walk through all of this for one app each, at a name under your own domain:

* [WorkOS sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/), with Laravel
* [Clerk sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/clerk-sign-in/), with Next.js
* [Cognito sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/cognito-sign-in/), with Laravel

## When ngrok is still the right tool

Nearhost only answers your own laptop. Keep a tunnel for:

* **Webhooks.** A payment provider, an auth provider or GitHub sends them from its own servers, which cannot reach your laptop.
* **Sharing a link.** A colleague, a client, or your phone cannot open a Nearhost name.

You can run both: Nearhost for your own browser, and a tunnel for the one endpoint that the outside world has to reach.

# Run Nearhost in the background

> Keep your projects served with no terminal open, with nearhost -d or a service that starts at login, and what the background Nearhost does when it needs you.

`nearhost up` serves until you press Ctrl-C. `nearhost` opens an interface on the background Nearhost, starting one if none runs, and when you quit it asks whether to stop it or leave it serving. That background process, called the core in these pages, serves your projects whether or not a terminal is open. Start it by hand with `nearhost -d`, or install a service that starts it each time you log in.

The core is the one Nearhost that serves: the proxy, the projects, the ssh connections, [Nearhost’s page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/) and the socket coding agents reach. The interface, `nearhost status` and the page are ways to look at it and answer it.

## Start it, check it, stop it

```sh
nearhost -d
```

This starts the core with no interface and returns once it answers. It prints:

```text
Nearhost is running in the background (pid 4121). Stop it with nearhost stop.
```

With no core running, `nearhost -d` waits up to 15 seconds for it. If the core stops while starting, `nearhost -d` prints `Error: Nearhost stopped while starting.` with the end of its log, and exits 1. If it is still starting when the wait is over, it says `Error: Nearhost is still starting.` with the path of its log, and exits 1, and the core goes on starting. Ctrl-C during the wait exits 130, and says whether the core goes on starting. Run again with a core already running, it starts nothing and says how that one was started:

```text
Nearhost is already running in the background (pid 4121, started with nearhost -d).
```

If the running one is a `nearhost up` in a terminal, it says so and tells you to stop it first.

It takes the same `--https-port`, `--http-port`, `--web-port`, `--no-hosts` and `--no-capture` flags as `nearhost`, and `--config`. They apply only when the core starts. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost--d).

With a [service](#start-it-at-login) installed, `nearhost -d` starts the core through the service, and says `Nearhost is running in the background as a service (pid 4121). Stop it with nearhost stop.` The service has its own settings, so when you give `--config` or one of those flags, Nearhost starts the core directly with yours, and says `Note: A service is installed, but it runs with its own settings, so Nearhost was started directly with yours.` on stderr.

`nearhost status` shows what the core serves:

```text
Nearhost 0.16.0 is running (pid 4121, started with nearhost -d at 2026-11-23 09:12:40).


SERVER  STATE      MESSAGE
local   connected


PROJECT  STATE    URL                 MESSAGE
myapp    running  https://myapp.test


Page: https://nearhost.localhost:6327
```

It lists each server and project, any request from a coding agent that waits for your answer, and the address of the page. At a terminal the page’s address carries the key that lets your browser see the project list and the approvals. `nearhost status --json` prints the same as JSON. When no core is running, it says `Error: Nearhost is not running.`, with the commands to start one, and exits 3, so a script can tell. Notes about the core, such as a newer release, go to stderr.

`nearhost stop` asks the core to stop and waits until its ports are free again:

```text
Stopped.
```

Stopping a core that is not running is no failure: it prints `Nearhost is not running.` and exits 0. A `nearhost up` in another terminal stops too.

You never restart the core to pick up a change to the config. It watches `config.yaml` and applies a change when the file is saved, so `nearhost add`, `nearhost preset enable` and an edit by hand all take effect in a moment.

## Open the interface on it

`nearhost` opens the interface as a client of the core. With no core running it starts one in the background first, then shows it. With one running, whoever started it, it attaches to that one. Several interfaces can follow the same core.

What quitting does depends on who started the core:

* **The interface started it, and it is the only interface open.** Pressing `q` asks `Stop Nearhost, or leave it running in the background?`, with `Stop` and `Leave running` as buttons and a `Don't ask again` box. Ticking the box saves your choice as [`keep_running`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/) in the config, and quitting does not ask again. To be asked again, remove the key.
* **Anything else started it.** `nearhost -d`, a service, or another interface that is still open. Quitting leaves it running and says `Nearhost is still running in the background. Stop it with nearhost stop.`
* **Ctrl-C, or the terminal closing,** never asks, as no one may be there to answer. Where `q` would ask, it stops the core.

When the core runs another release than the `nearhost` you opened, which is what happens after an update, the interface asks `Nearhost in the background is <old>; this is <new>. Restart it now? [Y/n]`. A core started in a terminal, or by a service that runs another copy of `nearhost`, is not restarted for you: the interface says how to. `nearhost --config <file>` refuses when the running core serves another file. See [Updating](#updating).

## Nearhost’s page

The core serves [Nearhost’s page](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/tls-and-the-proxy/) at `https://nearhost.localhost:6327`, or on the port `--web-port` gives, for as long as it runs. With no interface open, it is the place to look and to answer:

* **Status.** The servers with their health, the projects with their state and address, the open passthroughs, and the core’s version and when it started.
* **Waiting for your answer.** Each request from a coding agent has its own page, with the same choices as the interface’s prompt: Yes, No, and Always allow where it applies. Each change to a project’s `.nearhostrc` that needs your approval has one too, with Approve and Decline. The first answer wins, whether it comes from the page or the interface.
* **Documents** that agents have shown.

The page shows its project list and approvals only to a browser that holds its cookie. `nearhost status` prints the address that sets it when you run it at a terminal, and the interface opens the page with the same kind of link. An approval link on its own, without the cookie, shows nothing and approves nothing.

A request to add a project is the exception. The page shows what the agent proposes and lets you decline it; to accept it, run `nearhost`, where the add form opens filled in. See [Coding agents](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/coding-agents/).

## Start it at login

```sh
nearhost service install
```

This installs a service for your user that runs `nearhost daemon`, the core with no interface, and starts it. It starts again at each login. Run it as yourself, not as root. On the first install it prints `Installed the Nearhost service. It starts at login and runs <path>.` and starts the core. If another Nearhost already runs, the service leaves it and takes over at your next login; run `nearhost stop`, then `nearhost -d`, to hand over now.

| System     | What is written                                                                                 | Where it runs                               |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| macOS      | A launchd agent, `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.nearhost.core.plist`                               | In your login session                       |
| Linux      | A systemd user unit, `~/.config/systemd/user/nearhost.service`, enabled with `systemctl --user` | Under your user manager                     |
| Windows 11 | A Task Scheduler task named `Nearhost`, which runs at your logon                                | In your interactive session, with no window |

Linux needs systemd with a user manager. Without one, `service install` says so; run `nearhost -d` from your shell’s startup instead.

The service runs the copy of `nearhost` that you ran `service install` from, at that path. It refuses a copy that will not be there at your next login: one fetched by `npx`, `bunx` or `pnpm dlx` for a single run, one built by `go run`, and one inside Homebrew’s versioned folder, which the next upgrade removes. The message says how to install a lasting copy. On Linux it also refuses a copy that may not use ports 80 and 443, such as one you built yourself, and gives the `setcap` command to run first. See [Errors, warnings and notes](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#errors-warnings-and-notes). A copy under an nvm or fnm Node version runs from there, so install the service again if you change your default Node version; `service install` notes this.

If the core fails, it is started again. On macOS and Linux the service manager does it, and systemd gives up after five tries in a minute. Task Scheduler never restarts a program that fails, so on Windows the service’s own `nearhost` does it: it runs the core as a second `nearhost.exe`, which is why Task Manager shows two, and starts it again 5 seconds after it fails or is ended, giving up after five tries in a minute, as systemd does. Each restart is a line in [the core’s log](#the-cores-log), and while one is due `nearhost doctor` warns `installed; it is starting Nearhost again after it stopped`. A core that stops within 10 seconds of the service starting it failed to start, for example because port 443 is taken, so it is not started again, and `nearhost -d` or `service install` shows why. A clean `nearhost stop` is not a failure, so the core stays stopped until you start it again or log in.

On Windows the task runs only while you are signed in, at the screen or over Remote Desktop. With nobody signed in, as over SSH, `nearhost -d` and `service install` start the core directly and say `Note: You are not signed in to Windows, so the service could not start Nearhost, and it was started directly.` The service starts it from your next sign-in.

Run it again at any time. When nothing changed it says `The Nearhost service is installed and up to date.` and does nothing else. When something did, such as your `PATH`, it brings the service up to date. If the service’s core is running, it asks `The service's settings changed. Restart Nearhost now to apply them? Open passthroughs close. [Y/n]`. Answer no, or run it without a terminal, and the new settings apply at the next start. `--yes` restarts without asking.

```sh
nearhost service uninstall
```

This stops the core the service started, if it is running, and removes the service. A core you started with `nearhost -d` or the interface is left running. It prints `Removed the Nearhost service.`, with `Stopped Nearhost, which it ran.` after it when it stopped one, or `No Nearhost service is installed.` when there is none.

### What the service carries from your shell

A service does not get your shell’s environment, so `service install` writes what Nearhost needs into the service.

* **macOS and Linux:** `PATH`, so the service finds `ssh`, `docker` and the tools projects run, and `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONTEXT`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `XDG_DATA_HOME` when they are set. Nearhost keeps its config and its data in the folders the last two name, so a service without them would serve another config than the one you edit.
* **Linux:** `DISPLAY`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` and `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, when your session’s differ from the user manager’s, so the core can open links in your browser. The unit is wanted by `graphical-session.target` when a desktop session is running, and by `default.target` otherwise.
* **`SSH_AUTH_SOCK`,** when it points into your home folder or your runtime folder, where it lasts. When the service manager already gives the service the same socket, as launchd does for the system’s agent, nothing is written. When it points somewhere that changes at each login, such as an agent that ssh forwarded to this shell, `service install` warns `Warning: SSH_AUTH_SOCK here (<path>) changes at each login, so the service cannot use it.` and writes nothing. When it is not set, it notes `Note: SSH_AUTH_SOCK is not set here, so the service uses the agent your login session provides.` Either way, set `IdentityAgent` in `~/.ssh/config` to an agent socket that lasts. Nearhost runs your `ssh`, so the setting applies as it does in a terminal.
* **Windows:** nothing is written. The task runs with your own environment, through `conhost.exe --headless`, so no console window opens and none stays on your screen.

`nearhost doctor` checks the core’s view of this. See [What doctor says](#what-doctor-says).

A service on Linux runs while you are logged in. Nearhost does not turn on lingering (`loginctl enable-linger`), so the core stops when your last session ends, and starts again at your next login. Run `loginctl enable-linger` yourself if you want it to run without a session.

On macOS, run `nearhost service install` from Terminal on the Mac’s desktop, not over SSH. The service then runs in your desktop session, where it can open links.

## The hosts file

The core never asks for your password and never raises a User Account Control prompt: a prompt with no one at the terminal, or a dialog at login with no context, is not a thing Nearhost does. When a project’s names are missing from the [hosts file](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/the-hosts-file/), the core leaves the project stopped and says so:

```text
docdemo  stopped  https://docdemo.test  project "docdemo"'s hosts are not resolvable: the hosts file was not updated (the hosts file needs updating, and Nearhost in the background never asks for sudo.)
```

`nearhost status` also warns `Warning: docdemo waits for the hosts file to be updated.`, and the core’s log has the same refusal with `Fix: nearhost hosts update` under it. Run `nearhost hosts update` in a terminal. It asks for your password through `sudo` (on Windows, for your approval in a User Account Control prompt), brings the block up to date for every enabled project, and tells the core, which starts the projects that were waiting. `nearhost add` does the same at its end, and so does the interface, with its password box.

Most starts need no change: the hosts file is only changed when a project’s names are new, so a service that starts at login finds the block right after the first time.

The core does not trust the local certificate authority for you either. If browsers warn about the certificate, run `nearhost trust` once in a terminal. The core’s log says so when the CA is not trusted.

## The core’s log

The core writes to `core.log` in the config folder: `~/.config/nearhost/core.log`, `%APPDATA%\nearhost\core.log` on Windows, or under `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when that is set to an absolute path. Each line has a timestamp. It holds what `nearhost up` prints, a line for each request from a coding agent with the link to answer it, and why the core stopped. An error, a warning or a note is a block of lines: the first has its level and its code in brackets, and the lines under it, indented, say why, how to fix it and what caused it. Look the code up in [Errors](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/errors/).

```text
2026-11-25T14:29:57Z error [port.needs-permission] HTTPS port 443 needs permission to bind.
2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   On Linux, a program may use ports below 1024, such as 443 for HTTPS and 80 for HTTP, only when it has been given permission. The install script gives it; a nearhost you build or copy yourself does not have it.
2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Fix: sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep '/home/you/go/bin/nearhost'
2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Then start Nearhost again. Do not run nearhost with sudo.
2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Run `nearhost doctor` to check this and the rest of what Nearhost needs.
2026-11-25T14:29:57Z   Cause: HTTPS port 443 needs permission to bind: listen tcp :443: bind: permission denied
```

When the core crashes, the log has it as an error with the code `crash`, with the path of a crash file, `crash-<time>.log` beside `core.log`, that holds the details. Attach that file when you report it.

At 5 MiB the log is set aside as `core.log.1`, replacing the older one, and a new `core.log` starts. That happens while the core runs, so the log never grows without bound: the two files together stay near 10 MiB at most.

## Updating

`nearhost update` replaces the binary as it always has, and then restarts the core on the new one, so the update is not left half done. A core that a service started comes back through the service. Any other core comes back started by `nearhost -d`, with the same config file, ports and flags as before.

* **Open passthroughs and forwards close for a moment.** When there are any, it asks first, as `Restart Nearhost now to run <version>? This closes 2 passthroughs for a moment. [Y/n]`. `--yes` restarts without asking. Without a terminal, or when you answer no, it leaves the core as it is, and says `Note: Nearhost in the background still runs <old>.`, with the commands to restart it when you are ready. With nothing to close it restarts at once, and prints `Restarted Nearhost (pid <pid>); it now runs <version>.`
* **A core started by the interface closes the interface.** The open `nearhost` window ends, and you open it again.
* **A core in a terminal is yours to restart,** with Ctrl-C and then the command you started it with.
* **A service that runs another copy** of nearhost than the one you updated is left running. Run `nearhost service install` from the copy you use to bring the service across.
* **On Linux,** when the update drops the binary’s permission to bind ports 80 and 443, it prints the `setcap` command first and leaves the core running until you have run it.

The core also looks for a new release once a day, and says so in the log, the interface, `nearhost status` and the page. `NEARHOST_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` turns that off.

## What doctor says

[`nearhost doctor`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-doctor) asks the running core what it can reach from where it runs, which can differ from what your shell can reach.

| Line              | What it tells you                                                                                                 |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `core`            | Whether a core is running, its version and what started it. A core of another release than your `nearhost` warns. |
| `core: browser`   | Whether the core can open links. A warning means it runs outside your desktop session.                            |
| `core: ssh agent` | Whether the agent socket the core has answers. It explains servers that will not connect. Not shown on Windows.   |
| `core: docker`    | Whether `docker` is on the core’s `PATH` and answers.                                                             |
| `core: ssh`       | Where the core finds `ssh`.                                                                                       |
| `service`         | Whether a service is installed, runs this copy and is running.                                                    |

On a machine with no desktop, such as a server you reach over SSH, `core: browser` warns because there is no display. That is right: there is nothing to open links in.

Each warning has a fix beside it. Most come to running `nearhost service install` again from a shell where the thing works, then `nearhost stop` and `nearhost -d`.

## On Windows

Windows 11 has all of this: `nearhost -d`, `nearhost stop`, `nearhost status` and the logon task. From Nearhost 0.16.0 the Windows binaries are code signed, so it all runs where Smart App Control is on. Windows blocks an earlier, unsigned release there outright, so update first. See [Code signing](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/#code-signing).

# SSO callback fails on a remote dev server

> Why an SSO or OAuth sign-in callback fails, or lands on localhost or the wrong origin, when your dev server runs on a server or VM, and how to give it one HTTPS address that works.

Note

The fix on this page uses a name under your own domain, which needs Nearhost 0.6.0 or later. Run `nearhost update` to get it. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

Sign-in works when the app runs on your laptop. Move the dev server to a server or a VM, and it falls apart: the provider shows a redirect URI error, or you sign in and land on `localhost` with nothing there, or you come back to the app and it says the sign-in state is invalid.

## Why it happens

Sign-in with an SSO or OAuth provider is a round trip through your browser. The app sends the browser to the provider with a callback URL. The provider checks that URL against the list you registered, and after sign-in sends the browser back to it. The callback has to be right three times over: the app has to send it, the provider has to accept it, and your browser has to reach the app at it.

A remote dev server breaks one of those, depending on the address you use.

* **`http://localhost`.** Most providers accept it for development, and the app sends it happily. But your browser resolves `localhost` on your laptop, so after sign-in it lands where nothing is listening. Forwarding the port with `ssh -L` fixes that for one app.
* **The server’s own address,** such as `http://192.168.1.20:8080`. The browser reaches it, but providers that allow plain HTTP usually allow it only for `localhost`. Cognito, for example, requires HTTPS for every other callback.
* **A tunnel,** such as ngrok. It gives you HTTPS, but each new tunnel name is one more callback to register, and the app still builds its callback from its own config. If that says `http://localhost`, or the app does not trust the tunnel and builds `http://`, the URL it sends does not match the one you registered. See [ngrok loads the page, but assets point at localhost](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/ngrok-assets-on-localhost/).

There is a fourth failure that looks the same. Most integrations store a state value in a session cookie when sign-in starts, and check it on the callback. If you start sign-in at one address and come back at another, the cookie does not come with you, and the callback is refused. In Laravel, `laravel/workos` answers with a 403, and Socialite throws an `InvalidStateException`.

## The fix: one HTTPS address everywhere

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

Pick one address and use it in all three places: the URL your browser opens, the callback the app sends, and the callback the provider has registered. It has to be HTTPS, and your browser has to reach the remote app at it.

Nearhost gives you that address. It serves the remote dev server on your laptop at a name you choose, such as `https://local.myapp.com`, with a trusted certificate, over SSH. Add the project with that name:

```sh
nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp' --alias local.myapp.com
```

Then, on the app and provider side:

1. **Register the callback** with the provider, on that name: for example `https://local.myapp.com/auth/callback`. Use the provider’s development or staging environment.
2. **Set the app’s public URL** to `https://local.myapp.com`, in `APP_URL` or whatever your framework reads, so the callback the app sends matches.
3. **Trust the proxy.** Nearhost ends HTTPS on your laptop and sets `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. A framework that ignores the header builds `http://` links and redirects. In Laravel, that is one `trustProxies` line; the [WorkOS guide](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/#set-up-the-app) shows it.
4. **Start sign-in at the same name.** Open `https://local.myapp.com`, not the server’s address or an old tunnel, so the state cookie comes back.

## The guides

Each provider has its own setup, and its own way of failing. The guides cover them step by step:

* [WorkOS sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/workos-sign-in/): the redirect URI on the **Redirects** tab, with Laravel and `laravel/workos`.
* [Clerk sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/clerk-sign-in/): a development instance needs no callback registered at all, and what breaks is the dev server’s hot reload. With Next.js.
* [Cognito sign-in](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/guides/cognito-sign-in/): **Allowed callback URLs** on the app client, with Laravel and Socialite.

For other providers, such as Auth0, Okta or Google, the same four steps apply. Find where the provider lists allowed callback or redirect URLs, and add the HTTPS one.

## When ngrok is still the right tool

Nearhost is local-only. The name works in your browser on your laptop, and nowhere else. The sign-in round trip goes through your browser, so it does not need a tunnel. Keep one for:

* **Webhooks.** A provider that sends events to your app does so from its own servers, which cannot reach your laptop.
* **Sharing a link.** A colleague or a client cannot open `local.myapp.com` from their machine.

# Vite hot reload fails over SSH port forwarding

> Why Vite's scripts or hot reload fail when the dev server runs on another machine and you reach it through ssh -L, which port each setup has to forward, and how to keep it working without retyping forwards.

You run `npm run dev` on a server or a VM and forward a port to your laptop with `ssh -L`. The page loads, but edits never show up. Or the page loads without its styles and scripts. The browser console says `[vite] failed to connect to websocket`, or `[vite] server connection lost. Polling for restart...`, or the page is replaced by `Blocked request. This host ("…") is not allowed.`

The first two mean the browser is asking for an address the forward does not cover. Which address depends on whether Vite serves the page itself or sits beside a backend. The third means the forward works: the request reached Vite, and Vite refused the name you used, which `server.allowedHosts` fixes.

## Why it happens

Vite’s hot reload client opens a WebSocket to the host and port its own script came from, unless `server.ws` says otherwise (`server.hmr` in older Vite). So hot reload works wherever the scripts load, and fails wherever they do not. If your config sets a separate WebSocket port, such as `server.ws.clientPort`, forward that port too.

### Vite serves the page

A plain Vite app, or a framework built on it, serves the page, its scripts and the hot reload socket from one port. Forward that port and the browser reaches all three:

```sh
ssh -L 5173:localhost:5173 myserver
```

Open `http://localhost:5173` and hot reload works. Two things still break it:

* **Opening it by another name.** Vite checks the `Host` header and refuses names it does not know, the page included, with `Blocked request. This host ("…") is not allowed.` `localhost`, `*.localhost` names and IP addresses are always allowed. For any other name, add it to `server.allowedHosts` in `vite.config.js`.
* **The connection dropping.** When `ssh` exits, so does the forward. The console says `server connection lost`, and nothing reloads until you run `ssh -L` again.

### Vite sits beside a backend

Laravel, Rails, Django and other backends render the HTML themselves, and the page loads its scripts from the Vite dev server on a second port, at an address such as `http://localhost:5173`. In Laravel, `laravel-vite-plugin` writes that address to `public/hot` when `npm run dev` starts, and every script tag on the page uses it.

Forwarding only the backend’s port loads the HTML, and then the scripts fail, because your browser asks for `localhost:5173` on your laptop and nothing listens there. Forward the Vite port too, to the same port number on your laptop:

```sh
ssh -L 8000:localhost:8000 -L 5173:localhost:5173 myserver
```

The number has to match on both ends. `-L 3000:localhost:5173` reaches Vite, but the page still asks for 5173. If you run several projects, each needs its own Vite port, because two forwards cannot share 5173 on your laptop.

## Keeping it working with plain SSH

* **List the forwards in `~/.ssh/config`,** so one `ssh myserver` sets them all up:

  ```plaintext
  Host myserver
    LocalForward 8000 localhost:8000
    LocalForward 5173 localhost:5173
    ServerAliveInterval 15
  ```

* **Reconnect when it drops,** with `autossh` or a loop around `ssh -N`. With `ServerAliveInterval 15`, `ssh` notices a dead connection after about 45 seconds instead of hanging.

* **Add each new name** to `server.allowedHosts` if you open the app by a name other than `localhost` or a `*.localhost` name.

## How Nearhost handles it

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

Nearhost serves the project at a name such as `https://myapp.test`, over one SSH connection per server that it reconnects by itself, putting every forward back.

* **Vite serves the page.** Give its port the `web` role. The proxy passes the hot reload WebSocket through on the same origin. Add the name to `server.allowedHosts` once; with the `nearhost/vite` preset enabled, Nearhost shows the exact lines.
* **Vite sits beside a backend.** Give the Vite port the `loopback` role. Nearhost forwards it to the same port number on your laptop, so the page’s `http://localhost:5173` reaches the remote dev server. Under Laravel Sail, discovery proposes this route for you. The page at `https://myapp.test` now loads its scripts from another origin, and Vite’s default CORS policy allows only `localhost` pages. `laravel-vite-plugin` also allows `*.test` names and your `APP_URL`; with another integration, add the name to `server.cors.origin`.
* **Several projects.** Nearhost warns about two projects that want the same loopback port before they clash, and suggests a free one when the port comes from a variable.

A loopback forward answers on both `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`, so it also works when Vite listens on `::1` and `public/hot` says `http://[::1]:5173`. This needs Nearhost 0.7.0 or later and a laptop with the IPv6 loopback, which every Mac and almost every Linux machine has. Otherwise, see [Vite on `[::1]`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/#vite-on-1).

For the details, see [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/) and [Routes and roles](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/routes-and-roles/).

Checked against

These, on 2026-10-20:

* The Vite 8.3 hot reload client and host check, in `vite/dist/client/client.mjs` and `vite/dist/node`
* [Vite: server options](https://vite.dev/config/server-options.html), for `server.ws`, `server.hmr`, `server.cors` and `server.allowedHosts`
* [OpenSSH: ssh_config(5)](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config), for `LocalForward`, `ServerAliveInterval` and `ServerAliveCountMax`

If something here no longer matches, please [open an issue](https://github.com/nearhost/landing/issues).

# WorkOS sign-in on a remote dev server

> Give a WorkOS AuthKit app an HTTPS redirect URI in local dev, such as https://local.myapp.com/authenticate, when the dev server runs on another machine.

Note

Needs Nearhost 0.6.0 or later, which lets a project’s main name be a domain that does not end in `.test`. A `.nearhostrc` that sets only that name, as below, needs 0.7.0 or later. Run `nearhost update` to get it. See [CLI](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/cli/#nearhost-update).

New to Nearhost? [Install it](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/install/) and [add a server](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-server/) first.

This guide gets WorkOS AuthKit sign-in working at `https://local.myapp.com` while your Laravel app runs on another machine. The worked example uses the `laravel/workos` package from the Laravel starter kits, but the WorkOS and Nearhost steps are the same for any stack.

## The symptom

WorkOS sends the browser back to your app at a redirect URI you register in its dashboard. It has to match the URI your app sends exactly, including `https://` and the path. The staging environment accepts `http://localhost`, which is fine when the app runs on your laptop. When it runs on a server or a VM, `localhost` in your browser is not where the app is.

A tunnel such as ngrok gets the page on screen, but often not much more. The app still builds its links and assets from its own idea of where it lives, so redirects and scripts point back at `localhost` or at `http://`. Each tunnel name is one more redirect URI to register, and WorkOS’s advice is to use a stable custom domain if you must use a tunnel at all.

Nearhost serves the remote app on your laptop at a name you choose, with a trusted certificate, over SSH. The browser sees one stable HTTPS origin, and that is the origin you register with WorkOS.

## Pick a name

Use a name under a domain you own, such as `local.myapp.com`. It needs no DNS record: Nearhost points it at your laptop through `/etc/hosts` while the project is enabled. When the project is disabled, the name resolves as it normally would.

A real-domain name keeps the redirect URI shaped like the one in production. WorkOS’s documentation does not say whether it accepts `.test` names, so this guide uses a domain you own.

## Add the project

On the command line, give the name with `--alias`:

```sh
nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp' --alias local.myapp.com
```

```text
Added myapp on mini at https://local.myapp.com
Start it with `nearhost up`.
```

A name that does not end in `.test` needs your approval, because it can hide the real site. Typing it with `--alias` counts as approval.

To keep the name with the project, put it in a [`.nearhostrc`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/nearhostrc/) in the project’s root:

```yaml
version: 1
alias: local.myapp.com
```

Run `nearhost add` without `--alias`, and it asks before using the name, since you did not type it:

```text
$ nearhost add --server mini '~/code/myapp'
Approving a name puts it in your hosts file on this machine, has Nearhost's local CA sign a certificate for it, and makes your browser send that site's cookies to this project.
local.myapp.com on port 8080 (a real domain): approve? [y/N]
```

See [Add a project](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/getting-started/add-a-project/) for the rest of the add flow, and [Main name](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/reference/config/#main-name) for how the name is approved and written to the hosts file.

## Set up WorkOS

Do this in the WorkOS staging environment, which is meant for development. Its API keys, users and settings are separate from production’s.

1. In the dashboard, open **Applications**, then your application, then the **Redirects** tab.
2. Add the redirect URI `https://local.myapp.com/authenticate`, and make it the default. With `laravel/workos` the callback route is `/authenticate`. No trailing slash.
3. Set the sign-in endpoint, which WorkOS’s docs also call the initiate login URI, to `https://local.myapp.com/login`. AuthKit sends people there when sign-in starts outside your app, such as from a password reset or an invitation link.
4. On the same tab, add the sign-out URI `https://local.myapp.com/` and make it the default. Without a sign-out URI, WorkOS shows an error after sign-out, unless the app still has the older App homepage URL set. That setting is deprecated, and only kept as a fallback for existing apps.

Then copy the staging environment’s client ID and API key into the app’s `.env`, after `APP_URL`, which the redirect URL builds on:

```ini
APP_URL=https://local.myapp.com
WORKOS_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
WORKOS_API_KEY=your-api-key
WORKOS_REDIRECT_URL="${APP_URL}/authenticate"
```

These are the names the starter kits read in `config/services.php`.

## Set up the app

`APP_URL` is set to the new name above, so the redirect URL follows it. If `APP_URL` is already further down the file, move it above `WORKOS_REDIRECT_URL`, which reads it.

If you have cached the config, run `php artisan config:clear`.

Nearhost’s proxy ends HTTPS on your laptop and passes plain HTTP to the server, with `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. Laravel ignores that header until it trusts the proxy, so it thinks the request was `http://`. The WorkOS callback is unaffected, because `laravel/workos` reads it from `WORKOS_REDIRECT_URL`. What goes wrong is everything Laravel builds from the request: `route()` and `url()` links, the redirect to the dashboard after sign-in, and `asset()` URLs.

The starter kit’s `bootstrap/app.php` already has a `withMiddleware` closure. Add one line inside it (Laravel 11 and later):

```php
->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
    $middleware->trustProxies(at: '*');


    // The lines already there stay as they are.
})
```

`'*'` trusts the forwarded headers from any address. If this file also runs in production behind a known load balancer, list that load balancer’s addresses plus `127.0.0.1`, or the Docker network’s gateway under Sail, instead, or read the list from an environment variable. Nearhost’s forward arrives from `127.0.0.1`, or from the Docker network’s gateway under Sail, so leaving it out stops Laravel trusting it and brings back `http://` links.

If the page loads its scripts from Vite at `http://localhost:5173`, that port needs a `loopback` route so your browser can reach it. See [Dev servers and hot reload](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/). If `public/hot` says `http://[::1]:5173` instead, the forward answers there too from Nearhost 0.7.0. With an older Nearhost, see [Vite on `[::1]`](/pr-preview/pr-132/docs/concepts/dev-servers-and-hot-reload/#vite-on-1).

On another stack the idea is the same. Set the app’s public URL to `https://local.myapp.com`, and tell the framework to trust `X-Forwarded-Proto` from the proxy, so it builds `https://` links and the callback URL it sends to WorkOS matches the one you registered.

## Check it works

Start the project with `nearhost up`, or from the interface, and open `https://local.myapp.com/login`. You should land on the AuthKit sign-in page, and after signing in come back to `https://local.myapp.com/authenticate` and on to the dashboard.

When it does not:

* **WorkOS shows an error instead of the sign-in page.** Usually the redirect URI your app sent is not on the Redirects tab of the environment whose keys you use. Compare them character by character: `https`, the host, `/authenticate`, no trailing slash. Check that `WORKOS_REDIRECT_URL` and `APP_URL` are what you expect, and that the keys are the staging ones.
* **Links, the redirect after sign-in, or asset URLs use `http://`.** Laravel does not trust the proxy yet. Add `trustProxies` as above. Nearhost redirects `http://` to HTTPS, so a link may still seem to work, but `http://` scripts and styles on an HTTPS page are blocked as mixed content. Look for those warnings in the console.
* **`/authenticate` returns 403.** `laravel/workos` keeps a state value in the session when you start sign-in, and refuses the callback when the session does not come back with it. Start sign-in at `https://local.myapp.com`, not at another address for the same app, and leave `SESSION_DOMAIN` unset (`null`) or set it to `local.myapp.com`. A cookie set for another domain never reaches this one.

## When you still need ngrok

Nearhost is local-only. The name works in your browser on your laptop, and nowhere else. Use a public tunnel when:

* **WorkOS sends webhooks.** They come from WorkOS’s servers, which cannot reach your laptop. Point the staging webhook endpoint at a tunnel. Or use WorkOS’s events API, where your app fetches events from WorkOS rather than receiving them.
* **Someone outside needs the link.** A colleague or a client cannot open `local.myapp.com` from their machine.

You can run both: Nearhost for your own browser, and a tunnel just for the webhook endpoint.
